Disturb the roots of your plants as
little as possible when transplanting
from pots into the flower garden. Run
a thin knife blade all around the inside
of the pot to loosen the soil from the
side 50 that the soil will come out read
lily when you turn the pot upside down.
A cloudy day is best for setting out
plants, and if a good rain comes after
your work is done, all the better.


Your pansy garden must be kept wet
about the roots if you would have fine
flowers all summer. You must pluck
them every day if you would have them
bloom continually.


In transplanting pansy plants do not
set them too near together, six or sew
en- inches apart is quite near enough,
and they will spread into large thrifty
plants and bear more flowers. In July
pansy seed should be sown, or little
later. Make bed in a good soil, enrich
it well; give the plants plenty of sun
light and they will become strong
plants before winter. Then cover the

ST. PETERSBURG, May Bad as
was the rioting at Warsaw, Lodz.
Kalisz and other places in Poland
yesterday and venomous as was the
hostility everywhere displayed against
the police and the Russian authorities,
the uprising was far less formidable
and the results less bloody than an
ticipated. The authorities had given
due warning of their intention to per-
nit no demonstrations and the troops
quelled disturbances ruthlessly.


All reports, however, indicate that
the demonstrators were comparatively
few in number, and that the vast bulk
of the population, fearing trouble, re-
manned indoors. Where trouble oc-
CURED the crowds were armed with
bombs and revolvers. In Warsaw
red flag procession was dispersed by
two voleys. Cossacks and Uhlans
then charged and cut down the people
in the streets, drove them into court
yards and beat them with sabers and
whips in the cruel fashion peculiar to
these wild horsemen of the ssteppes.
About hundred persons we're killed
or seriously wounded, according to the
reports, women and even children
sharing the fate of the men.


Attack the Police


At Lodz workmen attacked the po-
lice with bombs and were charged by
dragons and Uhlans, who cut off the
bomb throwers, drove them into
house. surrounded it and then fired
upon those inside, killing three per-
sons and wounding many.


According to the reports which have
reached st. Petersburg from Kalisz the
workmen there for time had the up
per hand of the police and gendarmes,
disarming and stoning them until res
cued by a squadron of cavalry.


During service in a church here yes
terday, the congregation began sing
ing patriotic songs whereupon SOL
diers and police entered the building
and attacked the people, wounding
many of them. A free fight ensued
during which weapons were wrested
from the police, shots were exchanged
and stones were thrown. A dragoon,
woman and man were killed inside
the church. A squadron of cavalry
was summoned and dispersed the
crowds. The church was closed for re-
conservation.

Fergus Falls, Mimi, Nov. IA Great
Northern local passenger train, north
bound, ran into a burning bridge five
miles this side of GAINESVILLE last night.
The bridge was only partially consumed
and the engine passed over safely, but
the rails spread and the mailcar and
two, passenger coaches tipped over and
landed sidewise in the ditch beside the
track.


The train was going at a high rate
of speed and the escape of the passen-
gers was almost miracle, especially
in view of the fact that an acetylene
tank exploded in one of the cars. Only
seventeen passengers were on the en-
tire train and half of them sustained
bad cuts by falling against windows.
The ditch in which the train landed
contained two feet of water, and the
passengers were soaked with blood and
water when taken from the cars.


No one was fatally injured. The
train ran over the Northern Pacific
tracks last night and the bridge was
rebuilt TODAY,

YOKOHAMA, Sept. 13.-The meeting
held at a theater yesterday to protest
against the terms of the peace treaty
was followed by an anti-police demon
stration. Fourteen police boxes We're
burned.


The police say that the meeting was
the private speculation of a profess
sional agitator, who charged an adj
mission fee. The promise that there
would be popular speaker was un-
authorized, according to the police, and
the disappointed audience denounced
the swindle and demanded the refund
ing of their money. The. scramble fin
ally developed into rowdyism outside
the door.


AT o'clock this afternoon two COM
panies of troops from Toxic arrived.
They have been posted as guards at all
the consulates and other important
points.


The governor of the prefecture and
the mayor of Yokohama have issued
proclamations instructing the people to
place confidence in the ability of the
officials to restore order.


Six hundred Russian prisoners of war
from Karafuto, who were staying at
the different hotels. have been placed
under special guard. During the riot
the police used drawn swords while
the mob was armed with pistols and
sword sticks. The casualties among
the police were three severely wounded
and 81 slightly injured. Ninety-eight
of the mob are under arrest.


The mob set fire to the police boxes
by soaking hats in oil, firing them and
throwing them at the object of attack.


Quiet has apparently been restored.

alive In the latest dispatches from Sid
Abdailah. Tunis. where the tragedy oc-
CURED Their seven less fortunate com
rades perished. but these men kept
themselves alive by one of the most re-
markable exhibitions of GOODNESS ana
fortitude in naval annals.


They have been communicated with
by signals. and once the boat was
raised so that they might be talked to
END their voices distinguished Air has
been pumped into the submarine, but
So far every attempt to raise the boat
and release them has failed. In spite
of the terrible fate il. store for them,
the six survivors at last accounts were
perfectly self-possessed,


On Sunday morning. the men signaled
to those on the surface struggling to
rescue them that they were having diff
Guilty in breathing. and that their sup
ply was almost exhausted Renewed ef-
forts to raise the boat were made and
by noon 1t had been dragged along the
bottom some distance and chain haw-
Ser was got under the stern. She was
raised until her stern hatch was out Of
the water, when air was pumped into
the after compartments and the i'm
prisoned seamen were talked to and en-
couraged. They might have been res
cued then but the crane by which the
submarine had been raised. broke and
the boat sank again.


Another effort was made to raise her
but the position she assumed when she
sank made the work difficult. Last night
it was reported that fair progress was
being made, and It was still hoped that
the six men then living might eventually
be brought to the surface alive.


The courage of the imprisoned sailors
was remarkable. and they were cheered
by their comrades above the surface.

text:
Cut-COp's narrow Escape.


A delivery wagon horse left standing
by the sidewalk was scared by an auto
mobile last evening and dashed down Fifth
avenue from Eighteenth street. 1t was a
few minutes after o'clock and the avenue
was crowded.


Several men made attempts to stop the
horse, but he plunged through the tangle
of vehicles, heading down the avenue.
Drivers and coachrnen, warned by shouts,
gave him the middle OF the street.


Mounted Policeman Frank Anderson OF
the traffic squad, riding Snapper, hand
some bay horse, was at Tenth street, going
north, when the runaway hove in sight.
Wheeling his horse, Anderson galloped
beside the runaway and caught its bride
at Ninth street, but the slippery pavement
did not afford his own horse any purchase
and he could only reduce the animals
speed.


Just then westbound Eighth street
car crossed the avenue. Anderson couldn't
steer aside on account Of other ,ehicles,
nor could he stop the runaway, so the whole
outfit slammed into the side of the car.


The shafts Of the wagon snapped like
matches and the runaway's head went
through a window. snapper struck the
car sideways and. like the runaway, was
thrown from his feet. Anderson was
pulled from his saddle, but he escaped
without scratch.


The car was crowded. The collision
throw the passengers in heap and showered
them with broken glass. Several had
slight cuts and Miss Annie M. Smith Of
Orange, who had been sitting by the window
through which the runaway poked its
head, got bad cash on the back of her
head and a cut on the right cheek. She
refused to go to a hospital and after her
wounds were dressed she was sent in q cab
to the ferry. The other passengers who
were hurt refused to give their names to
the police.


The runaway horse, which is owned, the
police say, by Asa Shipman Of 4s Morris
street, was badly out about the head.
Snapper, like his rider, apparently escaped
unhurt.

TACOMA, March 5.-The most i'm
pcrtant piece of legislation passed by
the Washipg gton Legislature during the
session which ends this week has been
the radical railroad commission bill,
under which an appointive commission
will have full authority to regulate
rates, joint rates, train service and
other matters pertaining to the rail-
road service. The commission can act

During three previous biennial ses-

interests have successfully opposed the
creation of railroad commission, de-
spite the fact That's each State conven-
ton for eight years has pledged both
political parties to the passage of such
bill. The measure will become law
In ninety days.

mediately effective its anti-pass provi-
sion besides withdrawing discriminate
ing freight rates allowed Spokane. This
will hit Eastern Washington, where
the clamor has been especially loud for
a regulative railroad commission.

Japanese Commander Points Out Rus
slams Fatal Mistake


By Associated Press.


TOXIC, Japan, July 7.-Commander
Akyama, who participated in the bat
| tie of the Sea of Japan, has prepared
for publication an extended statement
relating to the great conflict and it's
weight is on the side of gunnery the
hattleships and tactics as against the
destroyer and the torpedo.


He prefaces his statement by de-
claring that good gunnery depends
mainly upon the division officers and
asserts that the Russian officers were
lamentably lacking in training.
In the early part of the battle the
landed by the Japanese. Under those
circumstances it may be said that the
Japanese had three or four guns in
action to every one of the Russians, and
there was nothing very remarkable
about the disparity of the losses.


The admiral says that Admiral Ro-
jestvensky had been criticised for elect
ing to take the chances at Tushima. On
the contrary it was the wisest course
open to him. Tsugaru strait is long and
narrow, the season foggy and there
were mechanical obstructions. Distance
and coal were against Soya and the
time consumed in reaching that en-
trance would have betrayed the design
and his plight on emerging from Soya
would have been much worse than he
might reasonably hope for at Tushima.


Shows Greatest Error


The commander insists that the great
mistake of the Russians was in mar
shaling their vessels in double column
line ahead.


From the moment of going into action
in this formation the Japanese re-
garded victory as assured. Apart from
the impossibility of maintaining an
orderly formation when pursuing such
tactics for defensive purposes there was
the fact that only a few of the ships
could bring their guns into effective
action against the japanese fleet. The
latter ships were able to concentrate
their whole fire upon the leading Rus
sian ships and in return received only
limited fire.


Had the Russians adopted the
strategy of imposing the brunt of the
action upon their battleships while the
rest of the fleet broke through and
steered direct for Vladivostok the COM
mander believes they would have
achieved partial success. Instead of
doing that they followed the plan of
mutually aiding one another, and thus
when the head of the battleship column
got into trouble the others steamed up
and thrust their heads into the lions
mouth without being able to accom-
plish anything compensatory.


Regarding the question Of sinking
armored cruisers and battleships by gun
fire, the commander expresses the
opinion that the fact that the Russian
ships were exceptionally low in the
water contributed materially to the re-
suits. The Russians carried large guam
titles of coal, stores and ammunition
and thus weighted down and in
rough sea suffered badly from hits near
the water line that ordinarily would
not have been fatal

quarter of a mile away was Elmar
Young, eighteen months old, tied hand
and foot and barely alive. The chill
dren were cousins and had been miss
ing since o'clock on Friday after
noon.


There is a deep mystery surround
ing the affair. which is being investi-
gated by the Coroner. Mrs Young in
sists that she is innocent of any crime
and states that she believes tramp
entered the house, stole the children
and tried to kill both.


Mrs. Young has been housekeeper
for months for Kingsley Melonson. She
says her husband was Fred Young, a
lawyer of Boston, who died more than
a year ago. Little May Wards mother
is dead and her aunt has cared for her.


The two children were found by
searching party in the woods or Plyrn-
ton. The baby was lying on fts face,
tied hand and foot. It's mouth had
been stopped with a cotton hood.
which had been rolled up and bound
tightly across the face. The hands
had been bound up under the chin.
In its struggle to free its hands the
hood which stopped the mouth and hose
had become displaced and the infant
thus escaped suffocation.


The elder child was dead. Her hands
and feet were bound, and across the
mouth and nose was a large burdock
leaf. over this the ch.ld's hood had
been tightly drawn and tied with
rope of yarn.


Mrs. Young and Melonson met the
searching party after the baby had
been found Tlee crowd threatened
the woman and demanded that she tell
where the other child was. Mrs. Young
protested that she did not know, and
several men IN the crowd suggested
that they hang the woman on the
spot.


Cooler counsel prevailed and the
search continued. While walking
through the woods the searchers came
to cow path, and Mrs. Young suG
gested that they turn to the right.
Being suspicious. however, the crowd
turned TO the left and soon found the
body of the elder child.


Mrs. Young was Immediately ar
rested and taken to Jail.

pectors coming into Bullfrog today re-
port that they found two men wander
ing aimlessly about in Death valley,
down beyond the Funeral range. They
were insane and absolutely naked.
Their tongues were black, swollen and
protruding. Their limbs were also
swollen.


The men had evidently become de-
lirious from thirst while prospecting
through Death valley Their misfortune
is but a repetition of the disasters of
that region during the past week. The
springs are drying up and the usual
supply of water is lacking. The pros
pectors are so scattered over the vast
region that there is no way of warn
ing them.


Carcasses of men and burros, heavy
laden and without owners, have been
found in numbers. This season of the
year is unfit for all prospecting. The
men mentioned above are being nursed
to health and steps are being taken
for their identification.

last night. The victim was about thirty
years of age.

WATERBURY, Conn, April 19.-Miss
Annie Brady, of Lafayette street. beat
out a railroad train in a terrible race
for life, but she will carry the marks
OF her adventure till death.


She was walking on the double
tracked trestle over the Naugatuck
river on rhe line of the Consolidated
road when she heard the rumble of a
train behind. She made a dash to get
across, taking three ties at every lump.


Just as the train reached the other
end of the trestle, about thiry yards
from her. Miss Brady looked back, and.
seeing that she was in the path of the
engine, sprang to the other track She
fell between the ties, and but for grasp
ing hold of the iron rail would have
gone down to the jagged rocks below.


Patrolman John Brickel ran out and
pulled her up. Her head was badly
cut and her wounds will leave scars.

MARsEILLEs, july lit Is stated that
when the Russian converted cruiser Dnieper
arrived at Port Said with the crew Of the
British steamer St. Kilda, which the Dnieper
had sunk, the British complained to their
Consul that the Captain Of the Dnieper was
determined to take them to Russia.


The Consul accompanied by the COM
manders of the British cruisers Lancaster
and Suffolk, boarded the Dnieper and re-
quested that the British subjects on board
be liberated. The Captain Of the Dnieper
rudely refused the request, whereupon
the Consul informed him that if they were
not released within an hour special meas
ures would be taken. The Consul and the
officers accompanying him then left the
Russian warship.


Immediately after, the Lance ster raised
her anchor and swung around ready to
approach the Dnieper. This hint was
sufficient for the Russian Captain, who
instantly sent the st. Kilda's crew ashore.
They were brought here on a Pennsular
and Oriental Line steamer.

enter this city, but not until the present
could they be verified. 1t now trans
pires that the Gould interests will
extend the Texas Pacific from Ell Paso
to this city and that surveying par
ties are now laying out the new route.

following closely the line of the South
ern Pacific and the other following
the Mexican border to Yuma, at which
point it will cross the Colorado river,
thence running directly west to this
city.


AS soon as these preliminary sur
veys are completed construction work
will commence and be pushed rapidly
to completion.

the Gould interests seaport terminal
which is conceded to be the best on
the Pacific coast and will open up
vast mineral and agricultural sections
which are now inaccessible.

ing. The japanese. as the attackers, have
suffered heavier than the Russians

tomorrow or Tuesday.

west of Mukden railroad station, where Gen.
eral EUROPA tkin is launching an attack
against the Japanese extreme left.

assaulted Pienchiapudgu. Kaotou pass and

When the kidneys are sick there is
always a warning to tell you of It, and
when the kidneys call for help there is
no time to lose. Kidney diseases are
common and fatal-cause more deaths
every year than any other human ills.
But nine cases out of ten this Is due
to neglect. Kidney disorders are easily
contracted, but just as easily cured
when treated properly and in time.


Common causes of kidney troubles
are colds, fevers, exposure, strains on
the back, poisoning diseases, ana
indulgence in stimulants.


The kidneys are the blood filters, and
when they become sick the blood is
soon laden with impurities which the
kidneys have failed to remove. This
causes backache, stiff, lame and sore
muscles, aching joints, spells of dizzi-
ness, headaches, rheumatic pains,
sleeplessness, nervousness and langour,
weak heart and many other bodily
aches and ills.


Meanwhile the kidneys are fast
breaking down, and from this cause
the urine becomes discolored and full
of sandy sediment; passages are too
frequent and often painful.


Uric acid crystallizes and causes
gravel and kidney stones. The bladder
cannot perform it's natural duties.
Water which should pass off in the
urine collects in different parts of the
body, causing dropsical bloating.

publican. Each Indian who could not read
English was allowed two interpreters, re-
publican and a democrat, who went with
him into the booth and assisted him in
voting his ticket. With the Ponca tribe the
election was somewhat different. They had
no fxed ideas and they wanted to vote as
their friends desired. The judges and
clerks worked hard until noon and succeed

BALTIMORE, Md, January 26.-The
weather here continues to be intensely
cold, the thermometer making four degrees
above zero. While all trains on the Balti-
more and Ohio and Pennsylvania railroads
were sent out on schedule time this morn
ing, reports indicate that delays are being
encountered, particularly between Balti-
more and Philadelphia and New York, ow-
ing to the heavy drifts of anow and the
frozen rails. =


On the Baltimore and Ohio all trains sent
out today are double headers, each being
supplied with two engines. All the incom-
ing trains due today were late, some of the
trains from New York and other points be-
ing much as seven or eight hours be
hind their regular schedule time


On the Northern Central and Western
Maryland all trains are reported late, the
latter reporting very heavy drifts of snow
in western Maryland, In the country sur
rounding Baltimore for many miles the
county roads are bloekaded with snow and
rendered irnpassable. ~. - -


Navigation on the Chesapeake bay has
been seriously interfered with. but there
has been no fatal accident. All vessels
going out and coming in; today were be-
hind their schedule time. The British
steamer Lord Erne, which went ashore on
Bodkin's Point yesterday. is still aground.
A strong wind is blowing here, but the sun
is shining brightly and street traffic has
resumed it's normal condition.

NORFOLK, Va, January 26.-The Vir-
ginia, Carolina and Maryland coasts are to-
day storm swept from end to end. Though
the wind reached velocity last night of
sixty miles hour. it continued from the
northwest. All sailing vessels unable to
make harbor were saved from being blown
ashore. Numerous other small craft ground
ed In Hampton Roads in high winds Of
last night and today, but no loss OF life has
been reported.


The Old Bay line steamer arrived here
from Baltimore today after terrible ex-
perience in the bay last night. All other
ocean coasting and bay steamers due last
night and today are yet unreported.


The storm 10 the most severe of many
winters. Numerous deaths from freezing
along distant points on the coast are fear
ed During the storm last night Bruce Park.
a colored suburb of Norfolk was wiped out
by fire and many families are today home
less A white school house in Norfolk
county was also burned.

NEW YORK, January 13.-By rare nerve
and pluck Miss Ellen Denning. twenty
three years. old, prevented two burglars
from robbing a station of the Brooklyn
Rapid Transit Company early today. Miss
Denning is ticket seller for the transit
company and was alone when the robbers
tried to force the door to the Office. Miss
Denning hastily threw the money into the
safe. locked the safe door, stepped outside
the office with revolver and threatened to
shoot.


William Young, negro porter. who had
come to the station meanwhile, grappled
with the men. Miss Denning backed to
the door of the Office and fired two shots In
the air. which brought the police The bur-
glars were arrested and held for trial Miss
Denning was complimented by the court for
her bravery. Young was slightly hurt in
his tussle with the burglars.

NEW YORK, Aug. Widespread
damage was caused by thunderstorm

burst over New York and vicinity to-
day.

killed. A dozen other persons were rem
dered unconscious but quickly recov-
cred, sustaining no serious injuries.


A Webster avenue trolley car carry

struck, the lightning running down the
trolley pole and grounding through the
tracks. Although the car and its occu-
pants were unscathed. panic was pre-
cipitated among the passengers. Four
teen persons, almost all women, were
injured in a frantic struggle to escape.
Nine Of them were severely hurt.


Many small boats were capsized In
the harbor. The immigrant steamer
John e. Moore effected several rescues.


Five hundred immigrants were IN
danger for an hour when two barges
on which they were broke away from
the dock at Ellis island and were blown
down the bay, pitching and rolling in
the heavy seas. Three tugs grappled
the barges and succeeded in holding
them until the storm subsided.


One death and three cases Of pros
tration resulted from the heat, which
was intense before the storm broke.

The Long Island Railroad Company has just COM
pleted the first alternating current single phase
electric road in commercial use that has been con-
str71cted in the State Of New-York. This road is
the Glen Cove Street Railway, which runs from
Sea Cliff, Long Island, through the town Of Glen
Cove to Glen Cove Dock, distance of eight miles.


The Long Island Railroad Company operated this
road for years by the customary direct current
trolley system, but the operation involved many
Objectionable points, including cost of operation,
maintenance and general unsatisfactory service.
This led L. s. Wells, the chief electrical engineer
of the Long Island Railroad Company, 10 invesu-
gate the single phase system. and he began nego-
fiations with the Westinghouse company, which
guaranteed the success of the project.


The reconstruction of the road was at once start
ed the motors were ordered, and about TWO months
ago experimental operation OF the road was begun.
These experiments proved the correctness of MI:
Wells's ideas the new method Of electrical
transportation.


The road has now been running week, on
a regular schedule. without the least interruption.


The power is obtained from the companys own
central station Long Island City, the current
being transmitted a distance of thirty miles 70
Glen Cove where il passes through transformer,
Is conveyed 10 the overhead wires, and then goes
through the trolley TO the motors on the cars.

Special Cablegram to The Star.


CALCUTTA, September 3O.-There has
been plenty of good foot ball up and down
and across the country of late, but quite the
best of the day has been that witnessed
at Calcutta In connection with the Indian
Foot Ball Association challenge shield. The
final was between the Calcutta club and
the Dalhousie club, also Calcutta organi-
cation. The former had won the shield the
last two years in succession, whereas Dali
housie's last success was eight years ago.
The meeting at Calcutta therefore created
tremendous excitement, and a great crowd
gathered to witness the play. After splen-
did game, brimful of incident and exciting
moments, Dalhousie defeated their rivals
by four goals to three. The narrow margin
by which the victory was gained viii show
how exciting the play was. The shield and
medals were afterward presented to the
winners amidst much enthusiasm by Mrs.
Carter, the wife of Col. Carter. The York
shire Regiment team, it may be mentioned,
has won the Bombay HARDWOOD League foot
ball cup. The league was commenced two
or three years ago on the suggestion OF
Col. HARDWOOD, R. A. n. c., and the teams
play each other throughout the monsoon
season in Bombay. The Yorkshire Regi-
ment team thoroughly deserved success, as
the result of consistently good play.

Belgian steamship Antigoon, of 1,214 tons,

at o'clock this morning. and now lies in
perilous position. The vessel struck on

Island life-saving station and sixteen miles
south of Cape Henry.

United States weather bureau seacoast
telegraph line say that the life savers who
went to the rescue Immediately after the
vessel was discovered have succeeded In
shooting life lines from shore to the vessel,
which IS some distance off, and that
hawser has been rugged for the bringing
ashore or the crew In the breeches buoy.


The Norfolk wrecking steamer Rescue has
left here for the scene of the wreck, but st
Is not believed that she will be able to APP
proach the stranded vessel until the storm
abates. The wind is now blowing forty-six
miles an hour on the coast and the storm
continues in all its fury The Antigon left
Mobile December 1 and sailed December II
from Charleston, where she coaled head
Ing direct for La Rochelle. The vessel is
lumber laden.

Special Dispatch to The Star


PORT JERVIS, N. Y, August 19-Hotel
Arlington, big boarding house at White
Lake. Sullivan county. conducted by John
Taylor and Bruce E. Sanford, was totally
destroyed by fire early this morning and
nearly two hundred guests from New York
and Brooklyn had narrow escapes and lost
thousands of dollars in clothing. money and
tewelry. The fire originated about 1 O. clock
from f1ue in the kitchen


The flames commu unicated quickly to all
parts of the building and reduced 1t to
ashes in an hour and a half. Scores of
persons rushed through the hotel warning
the sleeping guests and SO rapid was the
progress of the flames that nearly all the
people could take nothing with them but
their night clothes. Several jumped from
the windows and many women tainted.


Mrs Hughes and Mrs. Mcguire of New
York. who invalids were carried out.
Another woman broke through the crowd
after getting out and rescued her pet dog.
Many Of the guests were wandering about
the grounds this afternoon in their evening
attire worn at the regatta and dance last
night.


The Arlington built seven years ago
at cost of $4,000.

VICTORIA, B. c., September 13-Partic-
ulars regarding the disaster to the transport
Kinjo on August % in the inland sea of
Japan, involving the drowning of Major
Konori and 126 soldiers returning from For
mosa are received from passengers on the
Empress of India. The British steamer
Baralong under charter to the Nippon
Kisen Kaisha, colided with the transport,
which displayed no lights. When the cap
tains sighted each others vessel they sig
nailed and both shifted courses to starboard,
but the speed of the transport was less
than that of the Baralong, which crashed
into the stern of the transport on the port
side. The Baralong at once put out four
boats and thirty-eight men, including sew
enteen of the crew, were picked up, but 126
were drowned when the transport went
down. The Baralong was damaged about
the bows and was taken to kawasaki yards
for repairs


The Kinjo was formerly the British
steamer North Umbria. She was insured
at Toxic for $4,000.

MANILA, May 15.-Flerce fighting
has been going on the past two weeks
in the island of Jolo between the OUT
law Moro chief Pala with 900 WE'LL
armed followers and troops under the
personal command of Maj. Gen. Leon
ard Wood. Pala's losses thus far are
800 killed, while those of Gen. Wood are
seven killed and nineteen wounded.
Pala and his remaining followers, in
accordance with Moro traditions prefer
death to capture.


Gen. Wood with detachments from
the Fourteenth cavalry, the Seven
teenth, Twenty-second, twenty-third in
fantry, and constabulary scouts has
driven Pala and his followers into a
swamp which has been surrounded.
Pala was a noted slave trader and
warrior when the Americans occupied
the islands. Later he escaped with his
followers to the island Of Pula Sekar,
near Borneo. One of Pala's leaders de-
serted and took refuge in the British
settlement at Lahad. Pala discovering
his whereabouts, landed with follow
ing and demanded Of the British magis-
trate that he turn the deserter over to
him. The demand was not complied
with and Pala ordered a massacre.
Twenty-Five persons, including several
British were killed. Pala escaped to
the island of Jolo and organized the
present uprising.


1t is reported that the Borneo author
tiles requested Gen. Wood to apprehend
Pala dead or alive and turn him over
to them.

OAKLAND, May 23.-Mrs. ]. Riley,
California Cap Works at Siege, took the
law and a shotgun into her own hands
and filled the legs of Charles Murray
full of bird shot this morning. Both are
now in Jail at Martinez, the woman and
the wounded man each making charges
against the other The Rileys have lived
at Siege for some time, but Murray is a
newcomer, about whom little is known.


Murray called at the Riley home this
morning and there was decided misun-
derstanding between the two. Mrs Riley
says that Murray started rough house,
breaking windows and making disturb
ance generally. She says that she ordered
him off the place, but he continued his
actions. whereupon she got a shotgun
and let him have both barrels In the legs.
She points to the fact that the shot took
effect in his legs as proof of the fact that
she did not shoot to kill. She supple
ments her statement about the days pro-
ceedings by saying that Murray called at
the house last night and was ordered
away.


Murray declares that his visit was quiet
and orderly and that he had come from
near Merced to look for work. He says
that Mrs. Riley seemed insane in her at
tack upon him The result was that Muir
ray was taken to Point Richmond for
medical treatment and Mrs Riley was
taken to San Pablo, and this evening
both were taken to Martinez until the
case can be unraveled.

Arguments were begun in the Supreme
Court this afternoon on a case of far
reaching interest. RalstOn & Siddons are
arguing the case for South Carolina, while
the solicitor general is representing the
government. South Carolina sued the
United States for $4,000. which the fed
eral government, through its internal rev.
eEue bureau, insisted upon making the
state officers pay for wholesale and retail
liquor licenses under the operation of the
dispensary system by which South Caro-
lima controls the liquor traffic within its
borders. The suit was first brought in the
Court of Claims, the state contending that
these officers were exercising police pow
ers, and that when the federal government
compelled them to pay license fees 1t was
taxing state instrumentalities.


Court Of Claims Decision.


The Court of Claims decided unanimously
against this contention. holding that state
could not withdraw various subjects from
the scope of federal taxation under this
pretext. Had the South Carolina conten-
ton been sustained on it's broad ground the
entire internal revenue system would SEEM
ingly go to pieces. The court held that the
police power of a state must be exercised
in subOrdination to the superior rights of
the federal government.


But there is another question which has
been argued in the appeal before the Su-
preme Court To-Day, upon which South Car
DINA may win its 100000, and Congress be
compelled to enact new legislation to pre-
vent other states from initiating the South
Carolina example.


Another Chance for the State.


Congress in certain amendatory legisla-
ton some years ago defined the classes of
persons who were the subjects of these
licenses. 1t said persons included CO.
partnerships, associations and corpora
lions. The federal government is thus
compelled to argue that state is "cor-
poration' within the meaning Of this stat
ute


Many persons express the opinion that
the Supreme Court will not sustain this
definition. Congress could easily remedy
this difficulty, however, but not until South
Carolina had received it's back payments.
There is no expectation In treasury circles
that the Supreme Court will overrule the
Court of Claims on the broader question,
since the possible exercise of police powers
are so varied that little would be left upon
which the government could rely for rev.
eEue.


South Cardinals profits from the liquor
business, disclosed from the last report,
$5O0,COO year in small and Impoverished
state, suggest that its dispensary system
may yet find imitators elsewhere In spite

BAD NAUHEIM, May 26.-Secretary
Hay has finished the course of baths here
and will start tomorrow for Paris, where
Mrs. Hay awaits him. Professor Groedel
is quite satisfied with the effects the tax
ing of the baths have had on Hay, but
he has advised him to abstain from all
official business for several months, such
a course being usually necessary after
this course of treatment. Secretary Hay
expects. therefore, to spend the summer
at his country home and to remain there
until the autumn.


During his visits to London and Paris
Secretary Hay will remain very quiet
and will make no formal official calls
The call of King Leopold OF Belgium
upon him Thursday took the Secretary
completely by surprise, as the visit was
not announced beforehand.

Though manufacturing Industries have
had a remarkable growth in Japan during
recent years. agriculture still maintains it's
own as the leading source of wealth. The
oriental country can feed it's own inhabit-
ants and does not have to keep its eyes
upon the granares of other nations. To
the fact that the country Is mainly agricul-
tural some eminent Japanese statesmen
have attributed its ability to continue a
long and grueling war. The battles on
land and sea, the interruption of commerce
and the of the railroads for military
purposes do not disturb the peaceful pro-
gress of agriculture. though they would
ruin industries. The men who labor the
earth get their reward, war or no war.
commerce or no commerce. and while the
national debt must increase enormously
through the war. the country can maintain
itself indefinitely without the terrible bur-
den that a arrangement of vast industrial
undertakings, with the consequent beggary
of workingmen and their families. would
entail.

LONDON, April IAN interesting
romance ended in the Church of st.
Paul, Knightsbridge, this week, when

to Miss Constance Clark.


The admiral is 49, and the church
was full of naval contemporaries,
among them being Sir John Burgoyne.
who brought the fugitive Empress Eu-
genie to England in his yacht. There
was a great gathering, too, of his
Scotch relatives and friends: Sir David
and Lady Baird, whose useful we'd
ding gifts had been a check and a
pony carriage; Lord and Lady Cavan,
on whose yacht the pair had first met,
Lord and Lady Cassillis, and Lord and
Lady Alexander Kennedy. The brides
relatives and the friends from Devon
shire included Miss Yeo and Sir Bour-
chier Wrey and others present includ-
ed Miss Hilda Stanley and the Dowa-
ger Lady Inshiquin. The gallant ad-
mirars best man was his cousin, Hugo
Wemyss, equerry to the Grand
Duchess of Mecklenburg-S -Strelitz.


The brides dress was of opalescent
silk covered with old lace, delicately
she defied superstition by wearing a
pale sea-green hat.


A score or more Of nurses were scat
tered about the church, for Miss
Clark though not complete" hos
pital nurse, as report had it, has gone
through short course of training at
St. Bartholomew hospital, and left
many friends there, the compulsory
absentees among whom were remem-
bered by the bride at the reception af
forwards, where many pieces Of cake
were cut and sent to them.


Captain ]. A. Clark gave his sister
away, and the only bridesmaid was

ter. The service was choral, and Sir
John and Lady Baird came down the
church afterwards to the familiar
strains of Mendelssohn's wedding
march, looking radiant, the admiral
shaking hands heartily with a dozen
old friends who stretched out congrat-
ulatory arms. A crowd of interested
spectators had gathered outside the
church and greeted the old sailor with
welcoming words and smiles.


The newly married pair intend to
start on yacht cruise shortly.
Among the presents were many fit
tings for yacht, while Lady Or
mond's gift took the form of an enamel
brooch set with pearls, and silver
salver came from the tenantry of
Pennington, where, it may be recalled,
Lady Hilda Mcneil lost her life in a
heroic effort to save a drowning boy
last summer.


The reception was held by the brides
brother and sister in the palm garden
at the Hans Crescent hotel, where a
string band played and the 450 pres

condition of his little brother. who imme-
diately clutched Georges neck. both might
have been saved. However, the little fell

ers neck, while the latter struggled des-
perately to keep above the water, and at
the same time reach the empty boat, a
short distance away.


While the two boys were struggling for
their lives in the water their friends hur-
riedly rowed toward them and shouted to
some men on the gas house wharf for
help. When they arrived within a few
yards of the drowning boys the latter dis
appeared beneath the surface of the wa
ter. They went down to their deaths, OBJ
servers say, clasped in each others arms.


A rowboat containing two men from the
gas house soon reached the scene and they
began diving for the bodies, but no trace
of them could be found.


Some of the drowned lads little COM
panions went to the Dudley home and broke

BOYD'S. Md, April 1.-Three white
men, William Redmond, Eugene Lainhart
and Charles Selby, were seriously injured
at the government siding quarrtes at
Dickerson's, at $50 o'clock yesterday
evening RUNAWAY cars running into
cars which men were working. The men
were hurled from their feet into the
bottom Of the cars in which they had
been standing and were afterward picked
up badly hurt, bruised and bleeding, and,
while seriously hurt, some hopes Of re-
covery are entertained.


The siding is a long one that runs into
the quarries and a steep grade has to be
descended to the plant.
There were ten empty gondola cars for
loading standing half way up this heavy
grade five Of them were cut loose and
dropped down by hand brakes to the quar-
ries and the other five were left standing,
which afterward came down the grade
at terrific rate of over thirty miles an
hour and struck the cars which three men
were engaged in loading.


Redmond had one ear severed almost
from his head and received bad body
bruises, and the other two Lainhart and
Selby. were also badly cut, bruised and
shocked. Redmond and Selby were the
worst injured. Several of the cars were
wrecked and thrown from the tracks
These quarries furnish stone for the Dis
trict Of Columbia.

Remarkable, indeed is the life story, with


its rare experiences, of Mrs Sarah Ann


Mellen who on Thursday, April Ii, at the


home of her daughter, Mrs. E. c. Mellen,


726 San Pedro avenue, celebrated the nine


ty-seventh anniversary of her birth.


Mrs. Mellen's maiden name was Sarah


Ann Hilton. She was born April Ii, 1908,


at Gloucester. Mass. She was twice mar


ried, her first and second husbands being


brothers The first was David Mellen and


the second James Mellen. She lived in
Cambridge, Mass, for many years. and
came to San Antonio about eight years
ago AS extraordinary as 1t may seem.
since that time she has visited Boston and


Cambridge. making two trips, the last one
about four years ago. Both times she
stood the trip well, and returned feeling
much improved and in better spirits for
having visited the scenes of her earlier
life.

met personally many of the truly great

tinguished foreigners. She twice met the

street Charleston Mass. With clearness

ing saying that he endeared himself to

elder Harrison, Martin Van Buren, Abra-
ham Lincoln, Andrew johnson. Grant.
Hayes, Garfield. She was personally ac-
quainted with DIR. Oliver Wendell Holmes

/ of the Supreme Court of the United States;

Henry Ward Beeeher, Edward Everett, the
sayant Agassiz. and others whom she can
not recall now.

sixty-second annual boat race between the

Two young Italians, named Guetta
and Sorato, both in their teens, and
living in a little village near Bellinzona.
fell in love with the same girl, who
is said to have liked both suitors
equally we'll.


The young men, after many serious
quarrels, decided on very original
plan to settle the dispute. Informing
their parents that they were going on
an excursion to the mountains. they set
out for the splugen pass, which is no
torious for it's avalanches at this time
of the year.


Choosing the most exposed slope, they
agreed that each should stand for two
hours every day (between and II
a. M, the most dangerous time) in the
path of the avalanche and allow fate
to decide their destiny.


For three mornings these conditions
were carried out, but nothing serious
happened. though several avalanches
came down the slope, but not near the
foolhardy youths.


On the fourth day an enormous ava
lanche passed near Guetta. who was
knocked down by the rush of air. but
not hurt.


AS the young men had no more food
left, they returned to the village to
procure some but the authorities got
wind of the affair and threatened them
with Imprisonment. The youths then
decided to draw lots for the girl. and
sorato won Guetta left the village and
the young couple were married.

PHILADELPHIA. Nov. 1s.--At Mid
vale today a forty-ton steel ingot per-
meated with the blood and bones of
two workmen were buried with the
solemn rites of the Roman Catholic
church. The workmen who were so
strangely laid away were John Forkin
and Joseph Gaseda, two foreign-speak-
ing laborers, who met horrible death
a week ago. They were In pit near
a cupola containing $4,000 pounds of
molten steel. A plug gave way and
the fiery fluid poured from the cupola
and overwhelmed them. The men were
completely incinerated, and not trace
of them or their clothing was left.


The Midvale Steel company was
averse to selling the steel or using it
and 1t was decided to bury it with the
rites of the church to which the unfor-
tunate men had belonged. Accordingly
the forty-ton ingot, oval in shape,
twenty-eight feet long, six feet wide
and five feet thick was moved last
week by travelling crane to the rear
of the machine shop, where grave ten
feet deep had been made. The great
mass of metal was laid in the hole and
a platform built over 1t so that the
burial services could be better per-
formed.


A great crowd sought admission to
the works today but only the two sis
ters of Gaseda who depended upon
him for support and about 100 work.
men who were on Sunday duty we're
permitted to attend the services along
with the officials of the company
Among the officials was President
Charles Harrah. All heads were barred
and flags were lowered to half staff
while two priests conducted the serv-
ices After the sisters of Gaseda had
been led away the great ingot was
covered with earth and the funeral
party dispersed. The grave of the men
will be appropriately marked by the
company.

Denver, May 25.-Crop conditions
are generally favorable on the western
slope, but not so favorable on the east
ern. it is said by the weekly crop bull
letin issued by F. H. Brandenburg, the
section director of the United States
Weather Bureau. The bulletin treats
exhaustively of the crop conditions
taking reports from each county. 1t
says that while heavy rains have done
some damage and that cut worms are
active, the general outlook is good.
Gardens are backward but in good con-
dition.


An extract from the bulletin follows:


'In the western counties the weather
has been generally clear. with tempera
ture about normal, and while some rain
has fallen, the amounts have been be-
low the normal. On the eastern slope
the temperature has averaged about
one degree or two degrees below nor
NAL, with cloudy weather and numer-
Gus showers; the rainfall, however, has
been slightly below the normal, except
in the Arkansas valley and extreme
southeastern counties. The creeks in
the various parts of the state are ris-
ing rapidly, and many bottom lands are
under water. Conditions have been
generally favorable to crops on the
western, but rather unfavorable on the
eastern slope. Heavy rain and hail on
the 18th and 10th damaged grain, gar
dens and fruit in the eastern counties,
the Arkansas valley and along the di-
vide. Vegetation has been almost at
stardstill on the eastern slope, but
the various crops remain in good con-
dition, except that cut worms are injur-
ing beets and alfalfa in Weld county.
Seeding and planting are well adj
vanced, especially on the western
slope east of the mountains work is
being pushed as rapidly as conditions
permit Winter and spring wheat and
rye continue in good condition, also
other small grain; early paintings of
beets and potatoes are coming up, and
beets are being cultivated in the north
central section. Gardens, while back
ward, are coming on nicely. Ranges
are improving. The condition of fruit
is generally good and prospects excel
lent, excepting peaches plum, apple,
apricots and pear trees are in bloom"

A gas explosion in the lunch room
and saloon at 500 Also street wrecked
part of the building and severely in
jured August Escalle cook employed
in the place, and Morrison Rispaud, a
driver, also connected with the estab-
lishment.


The two men had just finished their
supper and Escalle rolled cigarette
and struck match to light it. In
stantly an explosion shook the building
and the men were hurled through the
ceiling with terrific force. Rispaud
fell on a clear space on the floor and
was not hurt by the fall, but sustained
painful burns on his face and hands.
Escalle landed across the back of a
chair and his back was severely
wrenched, rendering him helpless.


So great was the shock of the explo-
sion that the furniture of the room was
wrecked, the door blown from it's
hinges and hurled across hall into
the kitchen, the windows were demol-
ished and the plaster shaken from the
walls and ceiling.


In the room above, which was unoc-
cupied at the time. the damage was
almost as great. The furniture was
blown into the air, the plaster knocked
from the walls and the windows
broken.


The injured men say they could
smell gas in the room, but that for
several days this has been the case,
although there are no gas fixtures in
the room and no pipe on that side of
the house, electric lights being used
exclusively. They thought nothing of
the odor, except that it was nuisance,
and the effect of Escalle's match
threw the whole house into panic.


For several days the gas company
has been trying to find the source of
the gas which has made itself apparent
in Escallier's place. Escalliers theory
is that the large mains which were
recently laid down in the street near
his property and close to the curb are
leaking and that the gas escapes to
his house through crevices in the
ground.


The damage to the building amount
ed to about $780,


The injured men were treated at the
receiving hospital.

Corpses strew the debatable ground,
from which neither side can remove its
dead


Again and again the japanese
charged down the slope and up the hill.
Again and again the Russians counter
attacked, trying to gain possession of
the hill with the tower. No quarter was
asked for or given by either side. The
enmity ceased only in death.


Here sits a japanese upon a stone, a
moments pause for rest having
stretched him out into eternity. There
lie two foes with bayonets sheathed in
each others breasts.


Everywhere corpses, corpses, corpses.
For two days the Russians had been
concentrating a heavy artillery fire on
"the hill with the tower" stopping the
Japanese sapper work AT o'clock In
the morning yesterday the Russian
skirmishers heard a noise at "the hill
with the tower"


Creeping forward they discovered
that the japanese were heaping up
oorpses as defenses. The Russian field
batteries Immediately opened fire and
forced n cessation of the work.


Attack With Undying Persistence


At dawn yesterday the Japanese at
tackled the Russian positions near
Oubenepusa. The attackers were
scarcely recognizable as valiant Jap
anese, so mechanically did they move
forward and with undying persistence
attack only to be thrown back. They
repeated this at 10 in the morning after
preparatory artillery bombardment
and reached the Russian trenches,
where a bayonet fight ensued.


At the crucial moment Gen. Alieff,
commanding the vanguard arrived on
the scene with two companies and
turned the scale against the Japanese.
Among the wounded was Lieut.. Col.
Hrostitsky of the general staff, who
nevertheless remained at the front.


Toward evening the fight slackened.
The Japanese employed an ingenious
scheme to deceive the Russian artil
lery whose shells, though having the
ranges, appeared to be exploding
wrong. The officers were about to re-
sort to experimental firing when skir-
mirshers reported that the Japanese
were exploding small mines and throw
ing dirt in the air with spades to eff
feet a deception.

forces of Gen. Liubavin were repulsed

length of time The Russian artillery
forces and the Japanese guns have
been changing ground continuously.

CULLEN, Okla, Nov. 26.-Genevieve
Reddington, IL years old, was saved
from being killed by two panthers in
a canyon near here by her pony,
which set upon the beasts and drove
them away by blows from its hoofs.


The girl was riding when the great
cats rushed upon her from the Jungle.
Her pony stopped, frightened at the
sight of the beasts, and they dragged
the girl from the saddle.


They had almost stripped her cloth
ing and were rolling her over and over
on the ground when her pony ran at
them and began kicking. One of it's
hoofs struck the girl in the head, rem
dering her unconscious.


When she regained consciousness the
pony was standing quietly by her side,
and the panthers had disappeared.

sand islands in the eastern part OF the lake.
so new land masses are forming in the lake,

shallower parts Of the lake Commandment

expanse that can nowhere be navigated.

The Spanish coiners. one man and four
women, have just been tried aat the Paris
assize court for uttering spurious money.
says a Paris dispatch. They are Manoel
Caudet, aged thirty: his mother, who Is
over sixty; the widow Fernandez; the
widow Marco; a blind woman and her
daughter Eva. These people were engaged
In coming French and Spanish silver coins
in Barcelona. In Paris they succeeded in
paiming off a good many spurious / and q
franc pieces on shopkeepers. Manosl Cau-
det and his mother were first arrested, and
they agreed to inform on their accomplices
The woman Caudet had come into France
with 5000 1-franc pieces. which she was
obliged to show at Marseilles, but the Gus
toms man there made no trouble and let
her start for Paris, thinking that she was
an eccentric old person who carried her
money about with her in small coins. At
the trial Manoel Caudet and his mother
were condemned to imprisonment for two
years. The blind widow Marco was dis
charged. but her daughter Eva goes to
prison for five years, the woman Fernandez
receiving the same sentence.

Mrs. Margaret Lochte. thirty-six years
old, became suddenly insane Friday after
noon at Camp Good Will, where she had
been taken with her three children to en-
joy an outing. The ambulance in charge
of the board Of charities was summoned
and she was taken to the Washington Asy-
lum Hospital. Her home is at 433 Sd street
northeast.


Neighbors say that her home life was
anything but pleasant and they were not
surprised when they learned of her strange
conduct Her husband, who is a tilesetter,
broke his leg some months ago and was
recently injured about his hand by falling
from street car. Early this week one of
the visiting nurses reported the sad con-
dition of affairs at the home of the Lochte
family and the mother and three little
ones were sent out to the camp to recuper-
ate her health. Friday afternoon her
strange conduct made it manifest that her
mind was affected. She had had a vision
and thought she was going to die. 1t was
feared she would injure her children or
others about the camp. and the ambulance
was summoned. The children were brought
to the city and being cared for by
neighbors.

The race of the San Francisco fleet
from Vallejo to Sausalito on Sunday, the
18th inst, that was called off on account
OF lack of wind, will be resailed to-mor-
row. First prize on the former occasion
was awarded to w. G. Morrow's fast
sloop Challenger, the only yacht that
crossed the finishing line off the club
house under sail. DR.. 7. L. Hills sloop
Queen distanced all the rest of the fleet
and reached Sausalito with a lead over
all the yachts except the Challenger, but
owing TO lack of wind and an adverse
tide could not sail across the finishing
line. The second and third cups were
not awarded and will be sailed for to-
morrow.


The fleet will cruise to McNears Land
ing this afternoon and will race down to-
morrow. The tide floods from 1925 p. m
to 7:33 p. m. at Fort Point to-day, so that
any part of the upper bay can be reached
easily. Tomorrow the tide runs out at
Fort Point from 7:4S a. m. to lis p. m.
The fleet will anchor at McNears to-
night and will start on the journey down
at noon tomorrow.


The schooners Aggic and Chispa will be
the scratch boats. and the rest Of the
feet will receive arbitrary handicaps as
follows: Sloop Annie, four minutes;
sloops Thelna, Sappho and Queen and
schooner White Wings, eight minutes;

utes; sloop Amigo. sixteen minutes;
sloops Ariel and Minnetonka, twenty
minutes; sloops Thetis, Nautilus and

sloops Phoenicia and Merope and schoon-
er Josephine, thirty minutes; sloop Cur
lew and yawls Royal and Ripple, thirty
six minutes; yawl Wave, thirty eight
minutes; sloops Surprise and Juanita,
forty-two minutes; yawl Witch, forty
eight minutes; sloop Zada, one hour and
twelve minutes. The race will be under
the management of the regatta commit
tee, which consists of Roy c. Ward,
Henry G. Toll and Loring P. Rixford.


To-day and tomorrow are open dates
on the programme of the Corinthian
Yacht Club.


The feet Of the California Yacht Club
will cruise TO Vallejo to-day, returning
tomorrow on the ebb tide.


The annual regatta (the twentieth of
the Corinthian Yacht Club will be sailed,
according to custom, on Decoration day.
The feet viii be divided into six classes,
as follows: 2O-footers, yawls, 25-footers,
30-footers 36-footers and yachts whose
racing length exceeds thirty-six feet. The
20-foot class includes the yawls Witch
and Kittiwake and the sloops Caprice,
Nirrettee. Vixen, Kuku and Loiterer.
The yawls are Arcturus, Naiad, Spray,
FL Reyo, Acapulco and Truant. The %
footers are the sloops Cupid, May, Neva,
Josie, Discovery, Dixie, Hiawatha and
Ruby The SO-foot class comprises the
sloops Aeolus, Mignon, Comet and Cath
crime In the 36-foot class are the sloops
Emma, Meteor, Edna, Freda, Neptune,
Genesta, Harpoon, Presto and Kathleen.
In class one are the sloops Speedwell,
Mike, Clara. Mischief and Aloha.


The 30-foot class, which in former re-
gattas has furnished the most interest
ing racing, has dwindled to four boats,
the Presto having been enlarged to a 36-
footer, the Truant having been rebuilt
and rugged as a yawl and the Amigo
having been chartered by member of
the San Francisco Yacht Club. The rae
ing in the 25-foot and the 36-foot classes
will be interesting, the former class in
cluding eight and the latter comprising
nine boats. Among the 36-footers are the
fast yachts Meteor, Harpoon and Presto
and the old rivals Edna and Emma. In
class one the race will be between Com
modore T. Jennings Speedwell and Full
ton G.. Berry's Mike. Both are fast
boats. in the best of condition and will
be sailed for all there is in them.


The racing sloop Corinthian had trial
over the cup course with the sloop Mike
last Sunday and acquitted herself splen-
didly. The Corinthians are quite salts
fed from her behavior in the heavy sea
and strong breeze of Sunday, April 30,
that she can stand any sea or weather.
Commodore w G. Morrow will try out
the sloop Challenger during the holidays
and will decide on the makeup Of his
crew next week

Seven boys charged with soaping the
tracks of the Los Angeles Pacific rail-
road line near Colegrove on Halloween
night were severely reprimanded by
Justice Young yesterday morning and
were then sent home.


The boys admitted having soaped the
tracks, but asserted that it was sim
ply a Halloween prank and that no
damage was intended, Although moth
ing was said about the affair, it was
generally understood by the court that
these same boys were implicated in
another Halloween prank Tuesday
night when Deputy Constable Jack
Adams was rolled down the Colegrove
hill.


All the boys left the court room cry
ing, and from the looks bestowed upon
the youngsters by their fond parents
the lads will spend an unpleasant week.

Rear Admiral Charles E. Clark was placed on
the retired list yesterday after forty-five years
of active service. Like Dewey he is n native
of Vermont and was appointed from that state
to the Naval Academy. He was graduated, and
at the beginning of his career had much practi-
cal fighting experience. But it thirty-eight
years after he had entered the service before
Clark became a conspicuous figure. AT crti-
cal moment he was transferred to the command
of the first class battleship Oregon, relieving
Captain Mccormick and was ordered to pro-
ceed from the Mare Island Navy Yard San
Francisco, to join the North Atlantic Squadron
at Key West. The trip, covering distance
longer than half way around the world, through
two oceans into tOrrid heat, icy storms and
again across the Equator, always at high speed,
was watched with unusual interest by the peo-
pie of two continents; and when, after three
months the good ship arrived safe and ready
for battle a cheer went up for Captain Clark
and the Oregon wherever there We're Ameri-
cans.


Since the war with Spain Admiral Clark has
held many important places in the navy but
these services will have been forgotten when
the story of how he brought the Oregon all the
way from San Francisco to Key West will still
be told with pride by those who recount the
great achievements of our naval leaders.

reports are coming in from the southern
provinces of Luzon- Although they are

familiar call for reciprocity.

of a "maximum and minimum" tariff
law. permitting the establishment oil
reciprocal trade relations with friendly
foreign countries by the vote of Con-
gress.


Alvin H. Sanders. chairman of the
executive committee of the national
reciprocity conference. which opened
its two days session here yesterday,
is credited with originating the war
cry.


Mr.. Sanders broached his suggestion
to few friends after the word reci-
procity had received rather rough
handling on the floor OF the conven-
tion, and it met with approval among
the delegates.


They had assembled to discuss reel
procity trade relations with other
countries, amendment of the Dingley
tariff law, alterations of the interstate
commerce laws and kindTed matters.

great stock raising and farming indus

BERLIN, Feb. 2S.--The emperor of
Russia has elected to continue the war.
His position is absolutely firm, and the
German court has been advised in that
sense.


The war will be pressed with the ut
most energy, the domestic situation
being now within the control of the
authorities. Those who have advised
peace and suggested inquiries for
Japans terms. namely, the French
and British governments, are for the
present silent, and are likely to remain
so, unless events of an extraordinary
character shake the Russian emperor's
decision


His reasons, as understood here, are


First-The judgment of the army
chiefs that Field Marshal Oyama not
only cannot defeat General Kuropat-
kin, but stands in danger of defeat
himself. How cowardly, therefore, for
Russia to ask for mercy with all the
men and money essential to a success
full war.


Second-All the forces of criticism
now directed against the government
for having fought rather than yield,
and for having failed to win victories,
would be continued with increased
fury against the government A gov
ernment that would crave peace of
Russia's enemy while still capable of
winning victory would be giving the
party of change genuine grounds for
revolution.


The facts of the military situation,
love of country and arguments of ex-
pedency are all against peace and for
pressing the war hopefully.

officials were not prepared to say what would

is the official view that the company has care
fully observed every rule of neutrality

statement that President Castro had ordered the
court to annul the concession and seize the prop
erty was premature. Judgment has not yet
been delivered. The company could see no rea-

ordinary cables between Europe and Caracas are

SANTA ROSA, March 1.-For six
hours to-day several hundred men faced
each other with crowbars, picks, shovels
and fought while they pried and dug
at the rails. 1t was at the Sebastopol
avenue crossing when the Petaluma
and Santa Rosa Electric Railway force
attempted to cut the California North
western rails and cross into the city.
The Northwestern people were ON hand
to prevent the work. They succeeded
Until a restraining order arrived and
they were forced to withdraw. This
left a clear field for the electric people
and they built the crossing during the
night. AS result of the battle. several
men were hurt and several arrests
were made.


This morning Judge ]. NJ. Seawell Of
San Francisco dissolved the injunction
against the electric line and both sides
gathered for. the conflict. The North
western ran two locomotives and sew
eral flat cars on to the crossing where
the electric force was saving the rails.
The two gangs Of men fought each
othez. with their implements, and rocks.
While the men dug at the rails their
opponents. threw sand on them. The
engines were. specially fitted with steam
pipes through which hot steam was
thrown on the men at work.


Director Frank Brush Of the electric
railway lay on the ground in front Of
a Northwestern locomotive as it was
moving down to obstruct the crossing
and stopped it, the engineer not daring
TO. run over and crush him. Two
wagons were driven on to the crossing
and were wrecked between the two
locomotives as they came down the
track in opposite directions.


Warrants were subsequently served
on Superintendent Hunter, Chief Engi-
neers Zook and Barrows and a number
Of Northwestern employees, charging
them with obstructing the work of the
electric road. Superintendents Thorn
ton and Fairchild and General Passen-
ger Agent H. H. Huntington and a
number of other officials were arrested
on other charges.


About o'clock in the afternoon
President Foster arrived on a special
train with $50 employees as reinforce
merits for the fight. 1t looked as
though the conflict would grow more
serious when a restraining order ar
rived from. Judge j. Seawell in San
Francisco. 1t enjoined the California
Northwestern from interfering with the
electric road at the crossing and was
made .returnable on Monday. Foster
Immediately called off his men. ordered
the locomotive to haul the cars away
and the days war was ended.


Tonight the electric workmen put
down their rails and made the cross
ing.

Passengers on a Colegrove car of
the Los Angeles-Pa electric railway
narrowly escaped serious injury yester-
day afternoon when the car collided
with heavily loaded oil wagon which
blocked the tracks at the oil station
near the Sisters hospital.


The hand rail on the right side of the
car was demolished, the forward steps
torn off, the side stanchions loosened
and several window lights shattered.


The wagon was entirely demolished
by the collision, the driver escaping
injury by jumping.


The car left the Fourth street station
at 1:10 o'clock and was not heavily
loaded.


A woman holding little child was
sitting on the front seat of the car, but
was not aware of tho danger until she
heard the scream of another passenger.
Intuitively she grasped the child and
started toward the rear of the car.
The seat in which she was sitting was
broken into kindling wood by the force
of the collision. Other passengers had
narrow escapes.


The accident is stated by passengers
to have been due to the negligence of
the motorman, who is said to have been
joking with another employe standing
behind him.

Associated Press learns that mobs of
Lithuanians and Esthonians yesterday
attacked a hundred CossackS and dra-
goons, the only military force stationed
in Tukum.


The mobs, after wild fighting, killed
the soldiers to the last man, cut off
their arms and legs and ripped their
bodies. The streets were strewn with
bodies and dismembered parts.


Six hundred troops arrived here this
morning with three guns, shelled the
places and charged the mob of peas
ants. who surrendered or were dis.
persed. Order has now been re-estab-
lished and the soldiers are burying the
bodies of the slain and caring for the
wounded.


In all $40 soldiers and peasants were
killed and many wounded. Most of the
population have fled to Riga, which
now is the safest town in this part of
Russia.

quarters moving day at the geological
park is no small task. The birds of
the tropics represented the advance
guard of the movers. They did not
wait for even single visit from Jack
Frost but went into their winter
abodes more than two weeks ago. With
the first suspicion of the approaching
cold they quickly deserted their sum-
mer homes in the spacious grounds
and took up their winter quarters in
the snug, steam-heated little apart
ments where they will live until sum-
mer invites them out OF doors again.
Their park homes are well heated and
with plenty of windows toward the
sun, are made to resemble their tropic-
al homes as much as possible. Most
of these feathered immigrants were so
young when they came to New York
they have little recollection of their
native country, with its sunlight and
freedom and, not knowing, they are
content and even happy.

LARAMIE, Wyo., April ia little girl
named OConnor has had remarkable es-
cape from death beneath the wheels of a
locomotive. The child, with two others,
was crossing the Union Pacific tracks on
her way to school. Her companions passed
in front of an approaching freight train
and called to her to follow. She hesitated,
and then, when the train was barely ten
feet away, made the dash.

feet clipped and she fell ON her hands and
knees. The pilot Of the locomotive struck

turned a complete somersault and again

had reversed, and the locomotive stopped
with the pilot over the childs body. Had
the engine gone another foot she would
have been crushed to death. She was found
to be severely bruised.

loon

essayed deep dip. Suddenly the machine

righted ITSELF sank a considerable distance

ing to regain control of the aeroplane, but all

CHICAGO, September ALBERT Brandt.
thirty-two years old, an engineer, was NOR
tally wounded yesterday in a fight with his
brother-in-law, Thomas Harris, for the pos
session of Harris eighteen-month-ol old
daughter Brandt was taken to the County
Hospital, where he died an hour later.


Harris married Brands sister four years
ago. Mrs. Harris left her husband soon
after the marriage because she said. he
would not support her. After her first
child was born he induced her to return to
him, but she left him again six months
ago. taking her two children with her.
Since then, it is said, Harris has made
three attempts to kidnap his baby daugh-
ter. Each time Mrs. Harris or one of her
brothers recovered the child.


Harris went to the residence OF Brandl
mother yesterday. accompanied by his
brother Stephen, and demanded the child.
A fight ensued, in which the Harris broth
ers were beaten about the head with
hammer, welded by Albert Brandt. AT the
time he was shot Brandt had in his hand
revolver, with which he attempted to
repel the Harris brothers. After he fell his
brother Simon seized the weapon and fired
several shots at Harris.


After the shooting the Harris brothers
escaped. but were captured four hours
later.

resume business between here and the
orient. 1t has been officially announced
that the steamship America would leave
Yokohama for this port about September
Is, and from that time the regular serv-
ice of this line will he resumed. The two
other steamships belonging to this COM
pany. the Nippon and the Hongkong will
go into service soon as they be put
in condition. They have been out of COM

will you be mad, Jessie, if ask

ed electric car on fire and running

BY Associated Press.


MARYSVILLE, Cal, Aug. 1.-TWO
crowded oregon trains were in collision
at Lomo, siding six miles above
Marysville, early this morning and a
serious accident was narrowly averted.
Trainmen on the southbound train
claimed when they arrived here few
minutes after the accident. that they
had orders to meet the northbound
train at Lomo and that the northbound
train had orders to meet the other
train at Live Oaks, several miles be-
yond Lomo.


Owing to the fact that the south
bound train was slowing down to make
the siding and that the track for "a
long distance was straight, allowing
the engineers to see the approaching
headlights, terrible disaster was
averted. The pilots and front ends OF
both engines were badly damaged by
the force of the collision. but the jar
to the coaches on either train was felt
by but few passengers.


The engineers saved the trains by
reversing the engines and had almost
succeeded in stopping when they came
together

If any individual among the ball play

more credit than the other members of
the team it is CHRISTIE MATHEwSON,
who is unquestionably the most compe-
tent pitcher in any of the professional
leagues. But MATHEwsoN could not
have overcome the champions of the
American League without support, and
the present preeminence of the Giants
is accounted for by their magnificent
team work and Intelligent cooperation
on the diamond Manager and players
deserve the congratulations they have
received, and the Philadelphia artists,
though beaten. have displayed wonder
full skill and ability.

demonstrated how great the public in
terest in baseball continues to be. Only
few years ago the professional games
were poorly supported, but that was
due to reasons entirely unconnected
with the sport itself, The causes of
public dissatisfaction being removed,
baseball became again, and promptly,
more popular than it had ever been
before. Never has it known more sue
cessful year than 1905 Never has the
outlook for the future been better for
players, owners, managers and the ever
increasing community of fans.


A clean, wholesome, fascinating sport
is baseball, and it has never been more
admirably played than by the young
men who engaged in it under the flags
of the American and the National leagues
during the summer of 1905.

EUREKA, Jan. 1.-The Charles Mel

tain Carlson, bound for San Pedro
from Eureka, struck on the north jetty
lat the entrance to Humboldt Bay at
O'Clock this morning and had a mar
row escape from total destruction. The
buoy at the entrance had shifted and
to this fact is due the disaster.


The vessel, which carried a full car
go of lumber. struck upon the rocks at
the end of the north jetty. Her rudder
post and rudder were carried away, the
wheel was injured and a large
hole torn in the bottom. The vessel
being unmanageable drifted across the
entrance to the bay and would have
gone on the north jetty and become d
total loss, but the anchor was dropped
and she was kept off the rocks.


Distress signals attracted the life
saving station officials, who telephoned
to Eureka for tugboat, and then hur-
ride TO the distressed ship in the life
boats. Meanwhile big breakers carried
away the deck cargo and the vessel
became waterlogged. The captain and
crew were in great danger as seas
were constantly breaking over the
steamship. The tug Ranger and the
life savers arrived in good time and
the tug got a line to the Lakme, but
the hawser parted as soon as a strain
was put on it. With great difficulty
: a second line was made fast to the
vessel and a second pull moved the
Iakme and got her out of danger.

LONDON, April 6.-Four balloons
started this afternoon in cross

unique sporting event was under the
auspices of the Aero Club of Great
Britain. M. Faure, the member of
the French Aero Club, who success
fully undertook the same voyage two
months ago, again participated The
English balloons each of $4,000 to
$4,000 feet capacity started respec-
lively from Westham, the Crystal Pal
ace and Seven Oaks, while M. Faure
started from Folkestone A good
northwest wind was blowing.


Three of the balloons descended be-
fore reaching the channel. The one
which left the Crystal Palace came
down on a field near Hastings, the
second, from Westham, grounded four
miles inland from Haulings, and the
balloon from Seven Oaks descended
ten miles inland.


Faure was delayed and made his
ascent at Folkstone at II o'clock at
night, the balloon quickly disappear
ing over the channel. before a north
easterly wind.

Harrisburg. May 1.-THE coroner's jury this
afternoon returned a verdict generating the
Pennsylvania Railroad Company from any
blame for the South Harrisburg disaster last
THURSDAY when twenty-five lives were lost ana
more than one hundred persons were injured


The jury finds that the cause of the accident
was the applying of the airbrales to the freight
train, to stop it so that it would not strike the
shifting engine. The shifting crew. with its
train. was properly on the track the verdict
says, and so far the jury can learn were
guilty of no negligence.


The jury finds that 'by reason Of applying
the airbrake on the freight train, two cars OF
the said train, one of which contained twenty
thousand pounds Of Rockchef blasting powder
were thrown onto the westbound track just as
thu Cleveland and Cincinnati express was going
westward. and ran into the two cars FIRE from
the engine Of the passenger train set fire to the
powde.. and caused terrible explosion, which,
together with fire from some unknown source,
burned all passenger and Pullman cars


The Jury says that the freight train was
properly equipped with airbrakes, and that no
human agency could have stopped the passenger
cars from running into the wreck.

From the Pittsburg Dispatch.


The first dolls of which there is any knowl-
edge were found among the treasures I'M
earthed from the ruins of Babylon. They
were small figures in terra Gotta and ivory,
beautifully carved, and must have been fas-
cinating playthings for the little Assyrian
children.


The little girls of Syria had mechanical
dolls. The arms and legs were moved by
pulling strings, much after the fashion Of
jumping Jacks. -


The dolls the classic Greek children played
with were made of wax and clay, decorated
with bright colors.. One kind had movable
limbs and it's clothes were made to take off
and put on. Every doll had bed Of Its
own. These dolls represented gods and
heroes, but whatever they were meant to
represent they were dressed with loving
care by the little Greeks.


AS these children married when they were
very young they played with their dolls
until just before their wedding day. Then
they made a sacrifice of all their toys, dolls
and clothes included. They dedicated them
as a pious offering to some deity. If the
little girl died before she was grown up her
dolls were buried with her.


Thus 1t happens that the kind and fashion
of dolls which comforted these ancient chill
dren are known. All the specimens which
are kept with such great care behind glass
doors in various museums were taken from
some tiny tomb.

declared that he knew Sensoria well, hav-

At one time comets used to be the

one day a comet would bump against
the earth and either set it ablaze or
shatter il into space. In the middle OF
the nineteenth century the greatest
alarm was manifested all over Europe
lest the comet which then appeared
should crush the world to atoms. Men
and women and children came out OF
their houses and watched with white.
drawn faces the long, luminous tail
sweeping through the sky. In due
course the comet disappeared from
view, and nothing happened


London has had several end-of-the-
world panlcs. The famous Winston once
predicted the world would come to an
end on a certain October 13 The de-
struction of the mighty city of London,
1t was said, was to mark the beginning
of the end. The inhabitants We're seized
with terror Blanched faces We're at
every door. People thronged the street
terror-stricken. They rushed to Isling-
ton, to Hampstead. and congregated in
all the adjoining fields to watch and
wait. fearing the worst. hoping for the
best. Hour after hour they waited till
the dawn of another day. Then they
felt safe, and, tired and weary, went
home. leaving the world intact
