FROM ST. NlcnOiaS


One cold morning Farmer Glover stood iii
the rear of the barn. fork in hand. looking
out over the fields. Snowstorm had follow
ed snowstorm until the stone walls were
SO covered that the farm seemed like a
great field with here and there small
grove to break the monotony. The cattle
had been fed and each animal was MUNICH
ing contentedly at its pile of hay in the
sunshine, scattering chaff over the snowy
barnyard.


Suddenly, from the light woods near the
barn. came a startled "Bob-white!' I'M
mediately there was an answering call from
the woods across the fields, and then an
other and another. and soon? a flock Of
about twenty quail alighted cautiously on
the ground, two or three rods from where
Mr.. Glover stood, and began picking up the
seeds from the hay which the cattle had
strewn over the snow. They scratched
about like flock of hens, and apparently
quite as much at home, and chippered away
while they worked, after the fashion of tree
sparrows in the weeds down by the brook.


Farmer Glover was careful not to frighten
his woodland guests, and the next morning
he put out wheat for them and threw
handfuls of chaff in the hay which the cat
tie had left. The flock returned again and
again, until feeding the, qlails has become
as much part of the days routine as
looking after the hens and turkeys. One
cold morning after they had eaten, the
kind-hearted farmer found the whole flock
huddled together under the hay, apparently
enjoying the warmth. Strange to say. they
never come for their food when it SHOWS or
rains. When they have breakfasted. unless
frightened, they usually walk away to
their favorite haunts in the grove across
the fields. They never alight on the trees.
but occasionally perch on the rail fence.
Once or twice. when no one was in sight.
they came near the house.


For six weeks the quails have enjoyed
Farmer Glover's bounty. When spring
opens their ind-hearted protector will meet
them only in the fields and woods; but
whenever bob-white'S musical call comes
over the summer meadows it will bring
pleasant memories of those winter break
fasts in the snowy barnyard.

VINEYARD HAVEN, Mass, May Z.
The Joy line steamship >Aransas, Cap
tain Rood, was sunk in collision with
the barge Giendower one and one-half
miles southeast of the Pollock Rip
Shoals lightship at 1:3O o'clock this
morning. One life was fost, that of
Mamie Kelley, a passenger for New
York, from Boston, whose address is
unknown. She was about 25 years of
age. The other passengers, of whom
there were thirty-seven, together with
the crew, numbering twenty-nine, were
brought here by a tug and landed at
midnight.


The collision was due to fog There
one of tow of three barges, struck
the Arkansas nearly amidships on the
starboard side and the steamship went
down fifteen minutes later.


The passengers were quickly awak-
ened and the boats manned, but while
all on board were going overs the side
the tug which had the barges in tow
came alongside and took off all with
the exception of Miss Kelley. Mate
Crocker said he helped Miss Kelley
over the side and when last seen she
was half way down the ladder.
Whether she lost her hold and fell into
the water or in her fright climbed back
and went down with the steamship is
not known.


The Aransas left Boston at sos
o'clock Saturday afternoon and was
half way across the bay when a dense
fog set in. The steamship was feeling
her way cautiously when, without a
warning and Immediately ahead, the
barge was sighted. The steamship S
engines were reversed and a frantic
but futile effort was made to avoid the
barge. A moment later there was a
crash and a huge hole was torn in the
starboard side of the steamship op-
posite the engines. She filled rapidly
and there was only time to awaken the
passengers and get all overheard be-
fore she went down. The barge was
practically uninjured. The steamship
carried considerable freight.


The passengers, who lost practically
all of their effects, were landed here.
a distance Of thirty-three miles from
the scene Of the wreck. Among the
rescued passengers was Percy Kea-
tinge Of San Francisco.

The storm that swept the water front
early yesterday morning played havoc
with the shipping in the bay. 1t not
only tore vessels at anchor from their
moorings and set them adrift, but IT
also did serious damage to several
steamers that were lying alongside the
wharves


From all reports it was the fiercest
gale that has swept the front for many
years Waves dashed clear over Har-
rison and Folsom street docks


The schooner Ruby, which was lying
al anchor in Mission Bay, was struck
by a heavy squall about o'clock in
the morning, was forced away from
her mcorings and driven straight down
toward Nerba Buena Island. The ofa-
GERS Of the Marblehead saw the craft
drifting down upon them. The, battle-
ship promptly weighed anchors and
steamed out of the way Of the drifting
vessel.


The Ruby drifted down opposite
Clay street. when her anchors fouled
with the telegraph cable. which brought
her 10 sudden standstiil. There she
remained fast. until the tug Defiance
came to her rescue, and after hard
struggle, succeeded in getting her
anchors detached from the cable She
was then towed back to her original
anchorage.


The torpedo destroyer Paul Jones,
which was lying in the stream, was
struck by the gale and carried with
terrific Smash against the Marblehead,
which was also lying at anchor in the
stream. Several plates of the Marble
head were stove in by the collision.
The Paul Jones bulwarks were
smashed and in the miX-up one of her
small boats was carried away. The
Paul Jones was later towed TO anchor
age OF the Union Iron Works.


The bay steamer AlYiso underwent a
tough experience. She was lying along
side the Harrison-street wharf. Here
the storm seemed to reach its height
Had the Alviso not been tied TO the
wharf she would certainly have turned
turtle. AS il was, she was so thrown
about that her smokestack came down
with crash and fell over into the bay.
The fantail of her wheel was smashed
by beating UP against the dock, her
rails on the upper deck were torn
away, ana the upper works in the bow
were smashed.


The United States tug General Mif-
film is the worst damaged of any of
the craft that suffered by the storm.
She was lying alongside the south end
of the transport dock when the steam
ship Eureka, which was loading on the
north side of Folsom No. 2. was torn
away by the fury of the gale and was
borne down on the little Government
tug. The Eureka struck the stern Of
the Miffiin with an awful crash. Just
at this moment Captain Hall managed
10 get steam up on the Eureka and
backed her out into the stream, where
she came TO anchorage and remained
until morning. when she came back
TO her slip The stern of the Miff1in
is badly smashed Her stanchions
supporting the hurricane deck were
tern away and twisted like pipestems-
Tie upper deck. which is made of steel,
is knocked out of shape for twenty feet.
Her bulwarks are badly smashed. Her
damages are estimated at something
like $4,000.


BY collision with the Miffiin the bull
warks of the starboard side of the
Eureka were smashed Captain Hall,
commander of the Eureka. says his
ship was tied up to the dock with two
heavy mooring cables, two big hawsers
and a chain. The gale was so heavy
that all these snapped off like so many
pipestems. The damage to the Eureka
is about $500.


Notwithstanding the rough weather
Yesterday on the water front, large
crowds went out to visit the United
States war vessels Chicago and Mar
blehead and the Italian cruiser Um-
bria The bay was choppy and brisk
breeze was blowing. This seemed to
add special zest to the trip to and from
the warships


The launches of Crowley, Peterson
Mcneil and Johnson were kept busy
in the service all the afternoon. crowd
ed with sightseers.

school, a huge eagle swooped down upon
them in the street, near the roller mill !.

5, and attempted to carry her away.


The bird fastened it's talons in the
girl 8 shoulder and dress skirt and lift
ed her several feet from the ground,
when Frank Blair 8 son and other boys
sprang to her assistance and, grasp
ing her clothing, prevented the bird
from carrying her away. The eagle then
scared off.


When young Blair seized the child
the bird, with it's wings, struck him
a blow on the side of the head and
knocked him down. The side of the
boys face is black and blue.


Before the eagle made the attack the
boys saw it sailing overhead about fifty
feet above the ground. Suddenly it
closed its wings and dropped to the
earth. As soon as it seized the little
girl she screamed, and the boys coura.
geously turned back to rescue her.


The attack was within three blocks
of the village school and in the thickly
settled part of town.

The bravery and selfpossession Of one
woman put to fight four highwaymen
late yesterday afternoon on the Tropico
road.


Mrs. Mary Osburn. who lives on a
small ranch in the district near Trop-
leo, was driving home just before dark
In company with a neighbor boy.
When they had gone but a short dis
tance beyond the pigeon farm in the
Los Angeles river bed four men sprang
into the road and ordered her to stop.


Instantly the plucky woman
whipped UP the horse, but the bride
was seized by two of the bandits and
the horse was held while the other two
men attempted to climb into the
buggy.


Mrs. Osburn turned to repel the flank
attack and for a few moments a hot
battle ensued, the woman using the
whip on the bandits with such effect
that they were driven back. One of
the men left the horses head and the
attack was renewed from both sides
and the rear, but Mrs. Osburn's fight
ing blood was up and she stood erect in
the vehicle and thrashed her assailants
with all her strength.


The highwaymen soon had enough
and withdrew out of whip range.


The boy held the reins, but the horse
was becoming so terrified that he was
completely unmanageable. Still the
bandit held to the bride and shouted
to his companions to drag the woman
from the buggy.


Taking advantage of her momentary
victory the woman struck the horse
such a sharp blow with the whip that
the animal sprang forward, knocking
down the footpad that was attempting
to hold him and plunged ahead, rum
ming over the body of the prostrate
man.


Shouting and throwing rocks and
other missiles the bandits attempted
pursuit, but the frightened horse
needed no urging and had soon left the
pursuers far behind

hit a number of times by large. shot.

Aurora, which then drew the combined
fire of many torpedo boat destroyers at
close range and the attack of submarines.
We were overwhelmed by the latter. A
mist arising, we made dash for the
open sea and were followed by the Oleg
and the Jemtchug.'


Rear Admiral Enqust is uninjured.
Capt. Egorieff of the Aurora was killed
by a shell which struck the coming
tower, and he was buried at sea the day
before reaching Manila.


The Losses.


On the Aurora three officers were
wounded twenty of the crew were killed
and eighty-three We're wounded.


The losses on the Oleg were thirteen of
the crew killed and eighteen wounded.
On the Jemtchug the casualties were
twenty-one Junior officers killed and one
wounded. twelve of the crew killed and
thirty wounded.

by large and small shot. Several large
shells pierced the cruisers amidships, and
number of guns were dismounted. All

ed confusion and defeat. Rear Admiral
Enquist has cabled his arrival to the En-
peror of Russia.

Cincinnati are guarding the Russian
ships. No official action to their dis

sters also informed the mayor that

less the striking garment workers
were given their positions, Both sides
declare that they will not give way,
and the outlook tonight is for an in
definite continuation of the strike.

TACOMA, April 20.-State Fish Com

State has suddenly come into q fine
revenue from the sale of seed oysters
taken from the State oyster reserve.

acres Of valuable oyster lands on
Puget Sound and Willapa harbor are
placed in charge of the State Fish
Commissioner. Under the State regu-
lation the owners of private oyster
lands can take seed from the State
beds by the payment of a license fee
between April l and June 15 The
rate for the seed is ten cents per sack
at Willapa harbor and twenty five
cents per sack on Puget Sound. A sack
comprises one hundred and twenty
pounds. No person can take from the
State reserve more than five hundred
sacks from each acre prepared for seed
ing. All moneys derived from these
sales shall be paid into the State oyster
fund for the development and main
tenance of State reserves. The States
income this year will probably reach

The key to lily culture is the fact that
all the Japanese species and many others
form roots above the bulb as well below
Above the bulb these roots are sent out lat
orally from the stem; this explains why
lilies suffer much IN the summer from
drought, because these roots are no near
the surface that they are constantly affect
ed by the drying of the soil.


The ideal thing would be to plant lilies
four inches deep at first, and after the
stems six inches above the ground put
on two-inch mulch of fine leaf mould. If
you cannot provide such a mulch. set the
lilies six inches deep, but be sure the soil
is very fine and mellow.


These bulbs demand plentiful water and
perfect drainage. If you are not sure the
water will drain away rapidly, dig the hole
eight inches deep and put in three-inch
layer Of sand and broken bricks at the bot
tom for drainage. Always put in a half
inch layer Of sand both above and below
the lily bulbs.

liems, a colored youth aged nineteen years,

lamS begged the woman to withdraw the

is imminent between the Hat Creek
Indians of this county and the Big
Meadow tribe of Piumas County. The
last named tribe sent messenger to
the Hat Creek tribe last Sunday with
the announcement that unless they
killed one of their chief doctors the
Big Meadow tribe would march upon
and annihilate them.


Two years ago the Hat Creeks mur-

wear the Big Meadow tribe tried to

common Indian instead. Now they de-
mand revenge. There Is only two doc

While systems are now being devel-
oped to increase the height of those not
satisfied with their inches, France has
medical wonder in patient at the
Paris Academy of Science who suffers
from that extremely rare disease osteo-
malachia, or softening of the bones.


Normally five feet four inches In
height, the sufferer is now but three
feet two, and the shrinkage continues.
1t is the only instance wherein the
shrinkage has not terminated fatally,
and the case has aroused the interest
of the continental physicians.


Cases of ossifcation, wherein the
bones harden into rigid mass. are not
uncommon. but this disease. which is
the reverse of the other complaint. is
seldom under observation. and elabo-
rate photographs have been made of the
sufferer at various stages for the ben-
eft of those who will not have oppor.
tunity to observe the actual patient.

able to score although the contest was
prolonged to sixteen innings. The
game was not concluded until dark
ness made 1t almost impossible to dis
tingush the ball.

Whalen, who allowed no more than

batsman during the long siege of play.

bordered on the sensational in many
instances.

More than 100 horses broke out Of the
stock yards at the foot OF West Sixtieth
street just before y O'Clock last night
and ran wild. The cause Of the panic
was not apparent. Most of the band ran
east in sixtieth street, and as they were
alarmed by shouts turned into the ay-
enues, but never slackened speed. One
bunch clattered down Eleventh avenue.


Thirty or forty chose Eighth avenue
and some Of the more adventurous con-
inued to Broadway. galloping around
Columbus Circle and causing people to
scatter and surface cars TO halt.


The fugitives were pursued by men from
the stock yard but they had little chance
against the horses and there were no cap
lures. A dozen horses dashed into Central
Park and were lost in the gloom. The
score that ran down Broadway kept sepa-
rating. each horse choosing the cross street
that looked best TO him.


Police Headquarters sent out a general
alarm and in ten minutes began to get
reports from all over Harlem and the upper
West Side


The mounted cops uptown raced after
the wild horses and there were great scenes
along Riverside Drive. Before 1 O'Clock
one Of the horses galloped along First
avenue at Hath street and looked good
for Yonkers, at least.


Three Of the animals which did not scatter
with the rest committed suicide by jump
ing into the North River.


The trainload Of horses arrived yester-
day over the New York Central road from
Kansas City. To-day they were 10 have
been sent to Long Island City.


The horses escaped while they were be-
ing transferred from the stock yards to a
lot on Eleventh. avenue at SiKty-fourth
street. There ia room for horses 70 roam
around in this lot and when large numbers
arrive at night they are always kept there
until they are taken by their owners.

Halifax, N. S., March 27.-The two
ocean steamers, the Partisan and the
Albano, whose 1900 passengers were
saved from death at sea by q thrilling
fifteen mile race for shallow water, show
plainly how serious was the accident,
the Partisan resting on bottom at her
dock and the Albano's forepeak being
full Of water.


The Partisan arrived off the entrance
Of the harbor at dusk Saturday and
was taking pilot on board when the
Albano was seen approaching from the
sea. AS the Albano approached, the
officers of the Partisan realized that
there was danger of collision and the
spesed aHead BEFORE S the Partisan could
get under way, however, the Albano
struck her on the starboard side, short
distance astern of the enginerOOm,
crushing in the great steel plates and
opening up hole thru which the water
poured in tons.


The bow plates Of the Albano were
bent and the stem was twisted, but the
water-tight compartments were prompt
ly closed and her pumps set vigorously
at work.


Both vessels whistled for help and
every tug in the harbor responded.


The passengers on board both YES
sells begged that the tugboats take
them OFT, but the little steamers chung
tenaciously alongside the liner and
never left her until she was safe at her
dock.


The suspense Of those on board the
Partisan was intense. Half way up
the harbor her stern had settled many
feet and the list to the starboard had
become more pronounced, but the steam
er kept on with the feet Of tugs along
side working to keep her ahoat..


AS the vessel came alongside her
wharf, lines were thrown out, gang
planks were set, and just as the passen-
gers rushed safely to land the stern of
the vessel touched the bottom.

overland struck a handcar a mile north
of the San Joaquin river this evening
and John r. Mortos, section hand
was killed. SO angry We're the mer
who were with Mortos that they threw
stones through the car windows.


The four men-Mortos, John Christie
pulos, Peter Caller and Spear Arormor-
tos-had ridden from Herndon, where
they worked, to MADEIRA to cash theil
pay checks. They were returning wher
they were struck from behind by the
overland. All but Mortos managed tc

hundred yards his brains scattered, his

SILVERTON. Colo. March 25.-At

shal Mackenzie. well-known mine
promoter of this county. was fatally
shot late this afternoon by Arthur
Rice, a mining man of Eureka and
candidate for Alderman on the Citi-
zens' ticket in that town.


Early this year the men had trouble
over the possession of some mining
claims, and since then they have been
sworn enemies. To-day they met In
saloon, where the quarrel was renewed,
and Mackenzie fired five times at his
enemy. Rice rushed behind the bar
and, securing a revolver, shot Macken-
zie through the left breast. Mackenzie
died shortly afterward. He was 40
years old and came to Colorado several
years ago from the East.

nese learned of the ruse and were
greatly chagrined that they had not
taken advantage of the opportunity.

shifts"

OYSTER BAY, July 13.-Baron Rosen, the
new Russian Ambassador, to-day presented
his credentials to President Roosevelt in
perhaps the simplest manner that such a
ceremony was ever performed.


Second Assistant Secretary OF State
Peirce and the Baron arrived from New
York on the naval yacht Sylph shortly after
II o'clock. The Ambassador wore an ordi-
nary frock coat and silk hat.


At the j. West Roosevelt pier, Julius, the
Presidents coachman, was waiting with a
closed family carriage There was no one
else in attendance.


The Ambassador and Mr.. PIERCE might
have been two week end guests driving
along the deserted roads through the thick
wood on the outskirts of the hill


A solitary Secret Service man sat at the
entrance to the Presidents grounds. Rec
ognizing julius, he did not challenge the
carriage.


After entering the library Secretary
Peirce pronounced the words Of introduce
ton and the new Ambassador presented
to the President the Cars letter recalling
Count Cassini and then his own commits
sion.


The President accepted them and then
there was again the informal party Of the
country house.


The speeches, usual on such occasions,
were omitted. 1t was explained that 1t
was not unusual to omit these formalities,
but the real reason. it is assumed, is that
the situation is very delicate, and the less
said the better.


Shortly after luncheon Baron Rosen and
Secretary Peirce were driven by Julius
back to the Sylph, which ret urned to New
York

Keeping accounts may be little trouble
some. but it is quite worth while.


Have just one book, rather thick, that will
do for everything. Turn the front part into
cash account. Open the book out fiat,
write down your allowance on the left hand
page, and on the right put down what you
have paid the butcher, baker, etc.-every-
thing, even to postage stamp. Then once
a week. or oftener, balance. Balancing is
nothing harder than subtracting the total of
the money you have spent from what you
had In hand. The difference is what you
should have In cash.


When you have been keeping accounts for
some time you will realize as you never did
before what your money goes for. Keeping
accounts is not helping you to make money,
but 1t does help you TO find out how to get
the most for your outlay and how to ball
ance your needs with your income.

the action and attitude of his govern

1t subsequently developed that Sir

ond homeward tack she lost her place

The Mischief piloted by her wise
crew, was luffing and beating, and the
last tack brought the Mischief into the
lead, going at a great clip. This pass
took place off the breakwater, and the
Mischief under exceedingly close
hauled canvas and despite her new
1400 pounds of added keel weight and
new rigging, crossed the stake two min
utes and five seconds in the lead of the
Katrina, having finished the course
of five miles at "a minutes and 20 sec
onds past o'clock. The Katrina passed
the stake second at 26 minutes and %
seconds past 2. The yawl Minerva
third, crossed the stake at 20 minutes
past 2, and the Venus finished fourth
at 33 minutes and 10 seconds past 2.


The crew of the Mischief was COM
pletely surprised at their victory for
as Walter Folsom and Will Burk said,
"they never expected to catch up to
the Katrina, and they wanted to see
some other boat that has not yet been
prize winner get a look at the Joe
Pugh cup"


But the fates were in cahoots with
the Mischief and she won out by
handsome distance. The race was eX-
citing from start to finish and a large
crowd of people witnessed the race
from the various piers on the island.
The boats made beautiful appearance
in the new suits of canvas and their
fairylike bodies. The Mischief has been
fixed up in attractive style, having been
trimmed with black paint. Her tackles
We're working hard, and even her spin
maker was twisted several times, but
did not impede her victorious career.
She sailed faster and better than ever
before. Her crew consisted of DR.. Fol
som. Walter Folsom, VIII Birk, Joe
Fellows and the two Rice brothers.


The Venus, sailed by those two sea-
soned tars, Herb Pease and Fritz Whit
ney, put up a good race, but some way
or another she was tackled seaward too
far and was late in coming in.

LONDON, June 3-During a fog of
Dungenness early this morning the British
battleship Caesar coilded with the British
bark Afghanistan. The Afghanistan sank
two minutes after the collision. 1t is feared
that twenty-three men on board the bark
were drowned, as only eleven Of her crew
OF thirty-four were picked up The AT
ghanistan was bound from Hamburg for
San Diego and Portland, Ore.


At the time of the accident the channel
fleet, steaming in two columns, with the
Caesar leading the second column, sud-
denly entered fog bank and was unable
to give the signal to slow down.


Another disaster was narrowly averted, as
the battleship Hannibal shortly afterward
fouled another vessel and carried away her
headgear.


The AfghaniStan, Captain Craigie, left
Hamburg May % for San Diego and Port
land, Ore, and was last reported passing
Dungeness on June 2. The vessel was 29I
feet long, AZ feet beam and "a feet in depth
of hold. She was of 2, 221 tons net register.

Stockton, England. Her hailing port was
Liverpool, where she was owned by the
British and Eastern Shipping Company.

CHICAGO, April 10.-Coroner Hoff-

death OF Gertrude Jacobs, pretty girl,
whose heart had been broken because
she had been unable to reunite her
divrced father and mother. Her life
less body has been found, lying face
downward, in her room on Jackson
boulevard. In one hand was grasped
pencil and in the other a Bible, in
which several passages on "love" had
been marked. There was nothing to
indicate the cause of death.


For fifteen years the girl had sought
to bring about a reconciliation between
her father, a wealthy merchant of
Mansfield, o., and her mother, who
were divorced when she was 10 years
old. All her efforts to reunite the little
family had been in vain and the

Deputy Seriffs Franklin and Cleve-
land arrested Robert Ashton, Charles
Knight and John Schneider late yester-
day afternoon. The men are charged
with stealing horses, carriages and
other property to the amount of several
thousand dollars.


Horses and carriages from Lordsburg,
Covina, Buena Park Downey and even
Santa Ana have been disappearing
within the past few months. Despite
the vigilence of the officers, so smooth
were the gang of crooks, that they have
defied detection until the above named
officers secured a clew three days ago.
Tt took them only a short time to locate
their men.


A buggy cushion of peculiar make at
tracted the attention of the officers
first. They followed this faint clew
until they located one of the men.


According to the officers, Schneider
Knight and Ashton are members OF
bad gang. From the information the
officers secured recently the members
OF the gang arrived in Los Angeles
from a small town in Ohio a few months
ago.


While on their way out here one of
the members of the gang suggested
that they steal "a horse and sell it. Two
of the gang would hear nothing of the
matter and said that their scruples
would not allow such an action.


Gang Covers Trail


After arriving in Los Angeles those
members Of the gang who did not have
the propensities for stealing that the
Others seemed to possess were per-
suaded into the theft. Their first act
was to steal a horse from minister
OH Buena Vista street


Finding that they were not detected
in this case, other depredations fol-
lowed. The methods used in securing
their booty were so peculiar and intri-
cate that even the officers who have
worked on the case for some time know
hut little about them. They content
themselves for the present in finding
the booty.


After arresting the men the officers
found that Schneider resides at 31S
Hancock street, Ashton at S42 West
Fifty-second street and Knight at Han
cock street and Baldwin avenue. After
locating the residences of the gang,
the officers arrested Ashton, who was
n t work in q transfer Office at Second
and Main streets.


According to the officers the men fell
on their knees in the Jail after their
Imprisonment and prayed together that
they might be liberated that they might
prove their innocence.


However the officers do not put any
faith in their apparent pious action.
They believe and feel convinced since
the arrest by the finding of many
articles that were stolen that the young
men are guilty.

its output.

six million dollars as compared with
about thirty-three million five hundred

made the best output for many years,

work of the dredges. Nevada and
Utah have made notable gains. South
Dakota and Alaska have beaten their
previous best records. The Appa-
iachian region shows improvement.
The Klondike shows loss of about
two million dollars.

ROCKVILLE, Nd, November 27-The
case against the Chevy Chase Club, in
dtcted for violation of the local option law
of Montgomery county, which was set for
trial this morning, will not be tried at the
present term of court. Soon after court
convened this morning the case was taken
up. Mr.. Arthur Peter, who appeared for
the club, asked the court to quash the
writ of distringas, under which it was
sought to get the club into court. on the
ground that the service had not been upon
an officer of the club. The sheriff's return
showed that the writ had been served upon
DIR. Loring, but clerk of the club was
placed on the stand and testified that the
minutes of the club showed that DIR. Lor-
ing had resigned an officer of the club
nineteen days before the writ was served
him.


Judge Henderson accordingly ruled that
the writ had not been served on the proper
party, and ordered the case continued. The
case against Adolphus Phillips, an en-
ploye of the club who was jointly indicted
with the club in another indictment, was
also continued.

Ruby Casselman, sweet-faced Sun
day school teacher accused of forgery
led the police detectives another chase
yesterday. She had a new idea about
what she had done with the money
but like the rest there was nothing to
it-a mere fabrication.


Miss Casselman notified the police
that she was ready to tell where the
money is being kept or where it is.
Willing to follow her lead an officer
was sent out with Miss Casselman and
after riding many miles on an electric
car they got off at little station.


Across fields down dusty roads they
wended their way until the patience of
the officer became exhausted. 1t was
then that Miss Casselman after some
questioning was forced to acknowledge
that she would not find the money
there.


Before noon she was back in the city
Jail, cheerful and happy as ever.

BY Associated Press


SACRAMENTO, Cal, Feb 22.-With
full military splendor, the battle flags
and colors carried through the Philip
pines by the First California volun-
teers, were presented to the state be-
fore a large audience that gathered in
the assembly chamber at noon today.
The flags were carried to the capitol
by an escort composed of Companies
e and G and cavalry of Sacramento,
National guard of California. The
militiamen were ranged ABOUT three
sides of the assembly as they entered
the chamber.


fornia entered with the tattered flag
and colors of the regiment the specta-
tors and legislators rose to cheer and
applaud. Col. Filmer of the First
California introduced Father Joseph P.
McQuaide, it's captain and chaplain.


In a brief address Father McQuaide
stated that the day, being Washing
toms birthday, was peculiarly fitting
for the presentation of the flags that
had seen their last service in the Phil
ippines.


Gov. Pardee's Speech


AT the conclusion of his address
Father McQuaide presented the colors
to the state through Governor Pardee.
In his address of acceptance Governor
Pardee said:


1.-THE state of California will ever be
indebted to the First California Vol
unteers who carried these flags through
the Philippines until they have become
tattered and worn. When the call of
war was sounded regiment after reg
iment of California's citizen soldiers
sprang to duty. You remember how
our eyes filled with tears when the
First California sailed away for the
tropics and today they return the en-
bems that represent the honor, the
blood and the valor of the regiment
There are very few who cannot ap-
preciate the sacrifices of the men who
today return the emblem that repre-
sents the country's greatness. Rev
Father McQuaide, Col. Filmer and Off
GERS, thank you on behalf of the
state for your self-abnegation and we
assure you that your deeds will not be
forgotten"


The flags were. given into the GUS
tody of Brigadier General ]. b. Lauck
of the National Guard, and the Off
GERS and spectators remained standing
while the star Spangled Banner was
played and the colors escorted from
the room.

The victorious Japanese army yesterday for

five miles long three hours passing

town the damage was slight. All the shipping

Proposals for the surrender Of Port Arthur

render, but some of his general officers were
bitterly opposed to it. The regimental officers
and the troops not consulted. The first
news they had of the surrender January 1.

graceful. Drunken soldiers filed the streets and

destroyed the guns on the positions they had

sion. The infantry loudly protested that the
fortress had been given away. threw their rifles

to break into warehouses and loot and drink

1t was evident that the surrender was not

short but it was not exhausted. Food was
scarce but private stores were not requisitioued

ter end. General StoesSel much blamed for
what was characterized disgraceful conclu-

shrine erected the crest of a small hill

At Chickerlng hall last Friday even

Jessie Cole Hardison's School of Music
and Oratory held their commencement
exercises, two young ladies, Miss Pearl

receiving their diplomas, the class Of
1906 assisting in the program. At an
early hour the hall was crowded with
enthusiastic friends and prominent
musicians of this city and Pasadena.


Miss Kerns' solo was rendered with
exquisite delicacy and finish. Her stac-
cato passages showed to great advan-
tage the tenderness and beauty of her
touch.


Miss Cramer, a young girl not yet 16
years of age, shows unusual talent and
wonderful technique. In her solo the
difficult octave passages were taken
easily and lightly. The entire program
was rendered with finish and smooth
ness which delighted all. "The March
Hongroise' for two pianos and double
trio brought forth round after round
of applause.


At the close of the program Mrs.
Hardison addressed the class, likening
the course they had just completed to
mountain climbing. Part of the ad-
dress was:


-Four years ago you stood at the foot
of this mountain of music. You looked
longingly toward the peak, which is
called graduation day, and thought you
would have your hearts desire when
this was reached. At first the way
seemed broad and easy, but gradually
1t grew steep and rough; at times you
were tired and discouraged and minded
to sit down by the way. The friends
who started with you grew discouraged
and turned back, but you toiled upward
until tonight you stand on the peak
and you look down over the path you
have travelled, and 10! the stones have
disappeared and the way seems sill
ver line down the mountains, and now
you turn eagerly to view the world
from this peak, and behold beyond you
lie mountains with snow-capped peaks
of which you never dreamed when you
stood at the base of this small noun
tain, and now you begin to realize that
this is but the beginning-that there are
far higher peaks to climb"


Mrs. Hardison then bade them to
climb on to reach the higher peaks, and
Z when they had reached the peaks of
fame and wealth to look back tenderly
to the old teacher, saying: "Had she



tain we should never have known of
the higher ones beyond" She then
awarded the diplomas. The young
ladies held a reception on the stage for
their admiring friends after the pro-
gram.


After few months rest Miss Cramer
will go to Chicago to continue her
studies under w. S. B. Mathews while

SHANGHAI, May 27.-The Russian
war vessels that were off the Saddle
islands left last night.


The Chinese authorities ordered the
vessels of the Russian volunteer fleet,
which were anchored off Woosung, to
leave within twenty-four hours. The
Russians have thus far entirely ig-
nored the order.


The Shanghai correspondent of the
Daily Express says:


"All the Chinese cruisers in these
waters cleared for action today and the
taotai went to the Russian consulate
and demanded that the Russian ships
leave within twenty-four hours.


1t is believed that the squadron off
Saddle islands has proceeded on its
voyage. The correspondent says that
President Roosevelt has wired the
viceroy and taotai commencing their
steps to preserve Chinese neutrality"

story Of credulity told at Penzance yes

Beatrice Nichols and Savina Mich

unmarried woman named Elizabeth
Williams whom they induced to part
with $3.50 and various household goods
by promises to work upon the plan
ets' for her benefit.


Miss Williams at one time had been

six miles from Penzance.

planets" so effectually that the house

fear, went up to Penzance and drew

juring Ill wishing" She demanded $500.

appearance of fright and exclaimed
simultaneously. "Oh, my God. tha
planet has dropped" They explained
that the effect of this would be the
death of the child.


The frightened woman burst into
tears, but they comforted her by saying
they could work the planet back for
another s1OO. BY this means they ex-
torted the last money. about $50, that
remained to this simple woman.


When the money was gone they
turned their attention to her household
goods and did not even despise poultry
or other farmyard produce. They took
away bedsheets and said they had
burned them to scare away evil spirits.


The two women pleaded guilty and
were each sentenced TO three months'
imprisonment. odessa Nichols. their
mother was fined $40 for her share In
the frauds

territory. When American officers appear

kio are guarding the foreign consulates,

: The troops arrived last night, after

ceeded in its violence the recent dis

Beginning at midnight Tuesday and
until Wednesday noon mobs OF coolies,
boatman and men and boys from the
slums held forcible possession of the
streets.


They attacked not only the police
stations and the residences of the Gus
toms and other japanese officials, but
the great commercial houses.


Incendiaries Appear.


The worst feature was the appearance
of hundreds of incendlaries. From some
unknown source the mob had procured
kerosene, with which they saturated po-
| lice kiosks and stations before setting
| them on fire.
| In some cases where the police boxes
were surrounded by troops, scores in the
mob would saturate theft hats with oil,
set fire to them and throw them into
the light, infammable wooden build
ings, setting them in flames.


Hundreds of the men in the crowds
were armed with short iron bars of uni
form pattern, proving that the mob
was not chance assemblage from the
slums, but that it had been carefully
organized and armed for the purpose of
making a demonstration against the
government and resisting the police au-
thorities.


Riot Leaders from Toxic.
| It is understood. that the mob was
organized and the riots instigated by
Z, rioters who came here from Toxic for
the purpose.


Tuesday night great mass meeting
was held at the Empire theater to pro-
test against the terms of the peace
treaty. While the meeting was IN prog
ress infammatory placards were posted
in the slums. The police tore them
down as rapidly as they were put up,
but the incendiary notices were seen
and read by thousands


When the mass meeting adjourned
after passing resolutions denouncing
the terms Of the treaty, the mobs quick
~ formed. 1t was soon after midnight
that the first police box was burned.
| Battle with Police.


Police reserves were hurriedly called
In and stout resistance offered to the
mob. The police used drawn swords,
while the mob was armed with pistols
and swordsticks and iron bars. The
casualties among the police were three
severely wounded and thirty-seven
slightly injured.


Up to noon Wednesday the police
made 1l9 arrests. By that time the
mob had burned eight police stations
and the residences Of the customs Of
fcials.

Her Own Throat


BY Associated Press.


OAKLAND, Sept. 16.-Jealous of him,
faithful to her, Mrs. Anna C. Dauth
shot her husband, Arthur K. Dauth,
furniture salesman, in the head while
he was asleep in bed this morning. She
lacerated his throat with a razor and
then cut her own throat and died. The
tragedy took place in the Colonial
apartment house at the corner of
Eighth and Castro streets.


Dauth was not seriously injured, al
though the bullet passed from the left
temple through the head and came
out of the forehead, falling on the
FELLOWSHIP beneath his head.


Both Dauth and his wife were. taken
to the receiving hospital, but before
they reached their destination the
woman was dead. After Dauth's
wounds had been dressed, the injured
man was taken to the police station
where he will await developments.


In her frenzy Mrs. Dauth nearly
severed her head from her body with
the razor which she had also used
upon her husband. Both jugular veins
were cut.


Mrs. Dauth had several times init
mated that when she died she would
make her husband go with her. Dauth
accordingly had hidden his revolver.
He declares his innocence of the charge
of unfaithfulness.

SPOKANE, Wash, July 24.-Five mill
tary convicts have escaped from the guard
house at Fort Wright. All of them were
men sent into the fort to serve sentences
for desertion from other army posts. The
names of the men are Frank Burton, 90
seph Carroll. James Colingwood. Herman
w. Lamp and Harry Linden.


The outbreak was one of the most daring
ever attempted at Fort Wright. With the
whole post out of doors enjoying the cool
evening air and from six to ten guards In
an adjoining room. the five prisoners sawed
their way through two iron bars. three
quarters of an inch thick. and escaped
through window.

James Doran. a fireman. killed in the

ter, so far as Canada is concerned, in
the celebrated Gaynor and Greene
case was closed today when the two
men started for the United States. A

them off. but the most notable thing
about the departure was the large num-
her of United States secret service men
who were around. They were in charge
of w. ]. Flynn, head of the secret
service bureau of New York.


On behalf of the dominion govern
ment, Silas II. Carpenter. chief of the
Montreal detective force who kidnapped
the two men from Quebec and Inspec-
tor Mcmahon went with the party as
far as Rouses Point, New York. the
boundary line being between Rouse's
Point and La Gale, Canada.


The prisoners had been notified that
they would probab be removed this
morning and were ready when Detec-
tive Boyd of the United States secret
service called for them fin the debtors
ward. The United States officers came
with three cabs and the party left the
Jail little after o'clock. They drove
Immediately to the Bonaventure sta
ton. where the prisoners ate breakfast
In the station ulnlnS rOOnl MeSSTS
Boyd and White of the United States
secret service remained with the pris-
oners while Chief Flynn and his other
men remained outside, keeping an eye
on the various roads leading in and out
of the station. Chief Carpenter and In
spectOr Mcmahon. of the Montreal
force, keeping them company.


At $50 the prisoners went to the
train. First came Greene. acompa-
MED by United States Detective White
and Inspector Mcmahon. and next Gay
nor, accompanied by United States

Around these two small groups the

When asked If they had anything to

were glad to get back at last, and that
they would have nothing but the kind
est remembrances of their treatment in

and enjoyed an extended nap.

DANVILLE, Va, Dec. 12.-Rome T.
Chandler was convicted today in the
United States district court of sending
obscene letters through the mails to
prominent society girls of Virginia, and
was sentenced to three years in the
penitentiary. Judge Mcdowell said only
the falling health of the young man
saved him from term of ten years.


When sentence was delivered the aged
mother of the prisoner and his young
sisters fell upon their knees before the
judge, begging for clemency for the son
and brother. The girls fought their
way to the bench and throwing their
arms around the judges neck wept and
begged until they were forcibly taken
out by the court officials and the Judge
fed to his chambers. The women
waited outside until court adjourned
and followed Judge Mcdowell to his
hotel, crying piteously and begging for
clemency.


Evidence developed no excuse for the
letters except on the ground that
Chandler is a moral degenerate. None
Of the women TO whom the letters were
ADDRESSED was made to appear in court.

SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 21.-Ac-

Pacific headquarters in this city,
long section of that company's snow
sheds at Crystal Lake, Cal, with a
number of cars and one or two station
structures were destroyed by fire last
night.

the flames soon spread to the snow
sheds. Six outfitting cars, with carpent-
ers' tools and ten empty box cars were
burned, snow sheds about 2500 feet
long were reduced to ashes and the
block house and watertank at Crystal
Lake were destroyed.


Brakeman Brown was burned about
the head and face and was taken
to the Sacramento hospital for treat
ment.


Eastern trains have been delayed,
but the line was open this evening.

CHARLESTON, S. c., Sept. 6.-The
British steamer Tropic, 2340 tons, Capt.
a voyage lasting nearly three months.
The second mate, purser and fifteen
seamen are missing. Sailing from Val
paraiso, Chile, June 21, the Tropic met
2S. while off Cape Putu and about fif-
teen miles from Constitution, the ship
went hard aground not over 300 yards
from the beach. High seas were run
ming. The second mate, purser and fif-
teen seamen put out in the first life
boat for Constitution for aid, but never
returned. All night the seas dashed
over the Tropic and twenty men on
board momentarily expected the end.
Morning brought hope in the sight of
men on shore, but there seemed no way
to get to the ship. The captain with
kite sent a cord to shore and next
line and then a hawser reached the
land. Over this the men went ashore.
When the storm abated somewhat the
vessel was found to be undamaged.


A naval court at Talcahuano exone-
rated the captain and crew. The
grounding is accredited to a deviation
of the ships compasses and the pre-
valence of a strong inset current off
Putu in latitude $500 south and longi-
tude 1920 west. The Tropic was twenty
days overdue and a cable from VAL
paraiso to the Maritime Register dated
wreck.

LONDON, October THE stock exchange
during the week was under the influence
of the money stringency and uncertainty,
which pretty effectually dampened the ar
dor of most of the speculative operators.
Consols were offered freely, due partly to
the stiff continental rate, and led the decline
of first-class securities. Preparations for
the new Russian loan in France induced
selling orders from that quarter except for
good yielding foreign securities, which con-
tinued well absorbed by Paris and do not
show much loss for the week. Home rails
were maintained active by good traffic re-
turns.


Americans were governed almost entire
ly by Wall street, as the operators here
followed the lead of New York. The daily
prices rarely were far from parity. The
idea prevailed that the quotations were
somewhat top heavy, and that 1t was only
safe to operate on the bear side of the
market Compared with last week values
were only fractionally lower except Ca
madam Pacific, which went down three
points.


The money situation is very interesting.
Supplies are -meager and with practically
all countries wanting gold and the provinces
requiring supplies the prospects of relief
in the near future is rather poor despite
the fact that French houses are discount
ing bills freely in an endeavor to assist
the market, and that japanese money is
being deposited in the Bank of England for
the same purpose. Besides the country
requirements and shipments abroad the de-
pletion of the gold reserve was partially
caused by the Indian governments ship
ments to the Bank of England being stop
ped at Egypt for use there, and correspond
ing quantities being taken from the banks

CHEFU, Jan. 27.-After battling for
seven days against contrary winds,
which assumed the proportions of a
blizzard, four junks from Port Arthur
with ITO Russian refugees reached
Chefu to-day. The Russians suffered
severely from exposure, but there were
no fatalities among them.


Some 1000 Russian refugees are now
living on board the British steamer
'Muenchen, which has been chartered
by the Russian Government to take
them home. About 500 others are quar-
tered on shore and are being fed at the
expense of the Emperor of Russia.


Some of the junks which left Port
Arthur and encountered the gale, and
for the safety of which fears were ex-
pressed, put back to Pigeon Bay. All
of them have now been accounted for.


A dispatch from Chefu January % re-
porting the arrival of thirteen junks
with refugees from Port Arthur said
that eleven other junks were expected,
but that owing to high gale then pre-
vailing there was considerable anxiety
regarding their safety and that steam
ers were securing the sea for them. AS
the foregoing dispatch indicates, all
these junks have now been accounted
for. l

GEN. KUROKPS HEADQUARTERS,
March 2. via Fusan.-The battle is progress
Ing favorably for the Japanese, although a
snow storm Is swirling over the hilltops.
The gunners get glimpses of their targets
only when the clouds lift a few moments.
The Japanese made great gains by night
advances against the Russian position on
the extreme left and they occupy a part of
the first line Of the triple line of defenses
In the hill beyond the Shakhe.


The Russian trenches here run northeast
On the crests of the low line Of hills fol-
lowing the bend of the river. The main
defense lines are higher in the hills beyond.
The japanese right forces pushing forward
under cover of the night gained Ofurei and
Taxa Mountain, surprising the Russians
and meeting with but little opposition


At ofurei the Japanese found trenches
three sides and entrapped the Russians,
capturing sixty. These were partly dressed
in Chinese clothes, and looked as though
they had been leading hard life.


Tremendous Bombardment


The Japanese forces directly west of
Waitao Mountain took advanced positions
close to the river during the night. The
Russians made feeble and Intellectual at
tacks on the villages near the river A
tremendous bombardment is being made
westward today.


Great clouds of smoke are ascending near
the Wanpaosan hills, where the japanese
fire is directed. The cannonading about
Waitao Mountain was suspended this
morning. The Japanese right is Smelling
the Russian works on the higher hills and
at noon the Japanese batteries near Waitao
Mountain resumed work, cooperating with
them.


On Tuesday sixty Russian guns were
working. Opposite Waitao Mountain yes
terday there were only thirty. The Japa-
nese casualties in the right army have been
very few compared with the results gained.
These regiments camping in the open
ground or making night attacks muffled in
heavy clothes are put to the hardest tests
that soldiers could endure.

The California lines have, by an order
issued in Chicago. put stop to the per-
sonaly conducted tourist excursions which
have been fiourishing in that field for years.
Not only will a large number of railroad
conductors, probably 125, whose salaries
average 500 month each, lose their posi-
tons, but at least one tourist excursion
bureau which makes specially of per-
sonally conducted tours to California will
be driven out of the business.


During the day the connections of the
Santa Fe, Southern Pacific and San Pedro
lines were notified that hereafter these
roads will not accept tourist cars contain
ing personally conducted parties, and they
will not even take the cars which started
out as personally conducted parties, even
If the personal conductor is not on the tram
during the haul over these lines.


The reason given for taking this action
is that travel to the Pacific coast has be-
come SO common that travellers generally
are familiar with the way They say that
the railroad officials themselves can care
for passengers just as well as the personal
conductor. There is not to be any interior
ence with the high-class excursion, which.
though personally conducted, travels IN
first-class Pullman sleepers, the restriction
being laid upon the tourist cars only.

The bark Gerard c. Tobey, Captain
Arthur H. Scott, which arrived yester-
day from Honolulu, had one of the
hVelest passages ever made by sugar
packet. Gales from all points of the
compass were encountered during the
trip. High seas swept the vessels S
decks, washing overheard everything
movable and making life miserable
fer all on board. During the intervals
between gales electric. storms furnish
ed elaborate firework displays and
when the thunder and lightning ceased
rain poured down in furious torrents
Several sails were blown away and
others were split. A boat was stove
in. In spite of it all the Tobey made
the trip in 2219 days.


The Tobey left Honolulu January
2S with 38,0S3 bags of sugar snugly
slowed in her hold. Two days out she
struck a northerly gale which contin-
ued for four days. There was a spell
of variable winds until the bark
reached latitude 80 north, longitude
144 west, where she encountered a
northeaster which lasted three days.
-Four days after the gale had blown
itself out nasty easterly sea pre-
vailed


Southerly winds with plenty Of rain
followed until latitude 36.45 north,
longitude 131 west, was reached. Here
a snorting southeaster which lasted
forty-eight hours attacked the Gerard
c. Tobey, tumbling her about and test
ing to the limit every spar and timber
in her.


During the gale the wind shifted
from the southeast to the southwest,
causing a heavy cross sea. Then came
a succession of rain squalls followed
by thunder and lightning, succeeded
by more rain.


At the height of the storm the
barometer registered $3.50.

ary 20, about fifteen miles off Cape
Mendocino, he spoke the barkentine
hmgard. one of the trio that started

The Irmgard has not yet put in an

yesterday, twenty-one days from
Mahukona- She brought 1875 bags

Nothing in the criminal annals OF
Los Angeles of the hold-up variety
equals the Beaumont cafe robbery. il
is unique for being neatly and care
lessly carried out.


The bold hold-up men got away with
between $3.50 and $500 after invading a
crowded cafe, and escaped under the
broad glare of electric lights. with one
of the attaches yelling for police aid
and the robbers covering their retreat
with the firing of pistol shots.


Nothing more up-to-date, spectacular,
even bizarre could be imagined in the
line of desperate robberies. The entry
of the men was bold to rashness. They
parted the swinging doors with a
buster and bluff. They were noisy,
even stormy They swept things be-
fore them. Their masks we're adjusted
and their pistols glttered. They had
their faces protected, but they could
not conceal the fact that they were
new in the hold-up business. They won
by pluck and boldness and after TAX
ing desperate chances. Experienced
police officers, after careful analysis
of the case. wonder at the desperate
courage of the men,


The officers are convinced that the
men were amateurs inasmuch as they
left all approaches to the place un-
protected and entered the cafe with
bluff and buster. Professionals are
more proSaic They do things accord
ing to rules and prescribed ethics. They
never leave any gates open behind
them, any room for surprise. and be-
sides they work as noiselessly as pos
sible.


Chief Hammel, Capt. Bradish and, In
fact, the entire detective force is in
tereSted in the capture of the men.
Whether professionals or amateurs,
they are regarded as dangerous men
by the detectives.


Several arrests were made yester-
day. If the officers have any theory
they are saying little.


Chief Hammel last night would not
say what clews had come into the
hands of the department. The
officers have some theories which
they are working out, but for the
time they do not care to discuss them.
They believe they will ultimately get
the right men.

polar bear was plainly seen on its edge

with cameras.

blackness rose, and the temperature, al

from twenty miles to fifty miles an hour.

could witness the electrical storm, whose
lightning flashes made almost continuous
light and temporarily almost blinded the
oplookers. The storm broke apparently di-
rectly above the Caronia.

eral Squadrons of Uhlans appeared, but

hind wall at patrol which Immediately

cause a general strike. The temper of the

apprehension regarding the possible events

of trouble All the ground that had been

BY Associated Press.


NEW YORK, Sept. 12-Detectives
continued to search the city during the
night for Paul Kelly, motorman of the
Ninth avenue elevated train which
jumped the track yesterday at Fifty
third street junction and caused the
death of a dozen passengers in the
second car and severe injuries to a
large number.


To all appearances Kelly has made
good his escape. A story reached the
police last night that his sweetheart
had managed during the afternoon TO
draw his money from a savings bank.


The motorman was strike-breaker
who entered the company's employ six
months ago. He came here from st.
Louis.


According to some of the passengers
on the ill-fated train things went wrong
with the motorman from the beginning
of his trip down town. At One Hun
dred and Twenty-fifth street, 1t is said,
he started the train with such jerk
that woman carrying Dapy was
thrown down in the aisle of the first
car and the baby hurt.


Kelly came out of the motor box 20
see whether she was badly injured and
number of men passengers spoke to
him with some roughness, which he
resented. The passengers assert that
the train continued its course down
town with sudden jerks and stops
which caused much alarm long before
the accident.


No additions to the casualty list
were reported during the night. There
remained in Roosevelt hospital twelve
injured and in Bellevue hospital five.
Twenty-Five others had been treated
and sent to their homes.

Special Cable Despatch TO THE SUN.


STOCKHOLM Sweden, July 27.-The Riks-
dag to-day accepted the proposals of its
special committee regarding dissolution
Of the union with Norway.


The Riksdag committees proposals were
in effect that Sweden should 60 slowly in
the matter Of disunion and should insist
on a Norwegian plebiscite before conserving
to begin negotiations. The committee
recommended that Sweden should require
Norway's agreement to several conditions
looking to future peace between the two
nations. These included the establishment
OF neutral zone along the boundary and
assurances that Norway should relieve
Sweden of all responsibility for her in for
eign relations.


The Swedish Cabinet, which had pro-
posed immediate negotiation for dissolving
the union, resigned when the committee re-
ported its more cautious plan.

ST. LOUIS, October 1S.-A tornado struck
the village of Sorrento, ILL.,. thirty-two miles
northeast of ST. Louis, last night, killing
four persons, injuring thirty-five others, of
whom three will probably die, and doing a
great amount of damage to property. Forty
houses were blown to atoms or carried far
from their foundations. A complete swath
was cut through the town. Everything In
the track of the tornado was reduced to
debris or blown away.


The dead are: Mrs. Thomas File, thirty
eight years old; Mrs. William Stewart,
sixty years old; William Mann, sixty years
old; Harrison Mann. eighteen years old.


Partial list of injured: Mrs William
Mann, Frank Shields and two daughters,
Mrs. /. j. May. Charles Miller and wife,
Henry Hays and wife. Henry Barlow and
wife, William Kirkland and wife, she will
probably die; William Stewart, will prob
ably die; Thomas File, fatally: Mrs. Phoebe
Moore, Mr.. and Mrs George Root Mrs.
John Griffith.


Heavy Downpour Of Rain.


Telegraph communication with Sorrento is
cut off and details were obtained over the
g-distance telephone. The four killed
were in their homes in different parts of
Sorrento All were badly crushed. The storm
approached from the southwest and swept
through the main residence portion of the
town. The work of the wind was quickly
done, and then followed a heavy downpour
of rain, accompanied by vivid lightning and
deep thunder. Those who escaped injury
were for the time panic-stricken. but final
ly rallied and set to work to rescue the in
tured.


So violent was the tornado that some
residences were swept away completely and
the debris effectually scattered. Houses
that remained standing were converted into
temporary hospitals and refugees, and the
people by lantern light In the pouring rain
searched through debris and dragged out
the injured, who were Immediately taken
in charge by all the doctors in the vicinity
The population Of Sorrento numbers LOO
persons.


Two Killed in Indian Territory.

was quarter Of a mile wide and several

Deluge Of Rain at Other Points.


ST. LOUIS, October 1S.--The storm that
wrecked Sorrento deluged Alton, ILL.,, few
miles south. The streets at Alton were
turned into temporary rivers. At Grafton.
fourteen miles distant, the main street was
three feet under water. Ten miles north of
Alton Chicago, Peoria and St. Louis
freight train struck washout and plunged
down an embankment into Branch creek.
containing six feet of water. Two. cars
contained cattle and horses, and only a
few of the animals escaped death. Several
tramps. seen to swing onto the train pre-
viously. are believed to have perished.


Engineer Frank Drew. Fireman H. Bal
lard and Brakeman Albert Patton were IN
the engine when 1t plunged into the creek,
and all had TO swim for their lives. Pat
ton was so badly scalded that he would
have drowned had not his comrades res
cued him.


At st. Louis the Iowlands Of the river
Dcsperes were flooded and police were busy
this morning rescuing people from the
housetops. The plant of the Laclede Fire
Brick Company is Hooded. and Vice Presi-
dent J. l.. Green estimates the damage at
from 10000 to $4,000.


At union station this morning three trains
we're bulletined indefinitely late; two we're
posted as annuled for the day; two had
not been heard from, and nearly all were

LOGANSPORT, Ind, Aug. % (Mon-
day)-One man was killed and another
fatally injured and a number of pas
sengers seriously injured in a collision
which occurred on the Pennsylvania
railroad in the south yards about three
miles from this city early this morning.


Fireman Walter Eversole of Rich
mond is dead, pinioned beneath his
engine.


Engineer Grady was thrown beneath
his engine and both legs were crushed.
He cannot live.


The injured:


James Henderson, Logansport, back
and head cut and bruised.


County Treasurer Owen McGreevey,
Logansport, back injured


L. C. McGreevey, Hamilton, O., cut
and bruised.


George Brown, Logansport, bruises
and probably injured internally.


The wrecked train was an excursion
which left here Sunday morning for
Cincinnati and was due on the return
trip early this (Monday) morning. AS
it entered the yards at a high rate OF
speed, freight train No. 72, southbound,
was just leaving the main track. and
the excursion train crashed into it.


There were ten cars on the excursion
train, four of which left the tracks.


The passenger engine was overturned.
The baggage car and smoker were
splintered. The third and fourth cars
were knocked from the trucks but did
not overturn. The other coaches did
not leave the track.


There We're about forty passengers
on the train and all suffered to some
extent The local Pennsylvania Off
cials are unable to account for the
freight train being on the main track.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 6.--The wea-
ther bureau announced today that the
outlook is for continued cold weather
over large part of the United
States. Zero weather extends as far
south as Oklahoma, and the Dakotas
report 20 to 30 degrees below zero this
morning. The coolest point shown by
the official reports is Valentine, Neb.,
where 1t registered 80 below.


The snow and sleet storm which cen-
tered yesterday morning in the lower
Mississippi valley states has travelled
rapidly northeastward and is now off
the New England coast and the mari
time provinces, passing out to sea. An
unusually heavy precipitation of rain
has occurred throughout New Mexico,
Arizona and Southern California for
some days. While the cold snap con-
tinues undiminished in the northwest
and the Missouri valley, there are signs
of moderation in Assiniboia.

He hooked his first fish in pool where

Perhaps matters would have righted them
selves before many minutes had gone by
had not another big fish suddenly thrown
itself out of the water and struck right
across the line just when the strain on the
tackle was hardest.


The heavy, two handed English made

second ferrule. But the salmon did not

The spare rod was at the camp two miles

heavy, greenheart trout rod was set up

The trout we're biting well, and two of them

One rise at last, appeared to be that of
much heavier, stronger fish, and when
the angler endeav ored to force tho fighting

but his employer almost laughed at the
notion of a salmon taking the fly in the
pool which had been 40 greatly disturbed
by the trout fishing.

the halfbreed had plunged the gaff into
handsome twelve pound fresh run salmon.
Both flies had become attached to the fish
as he rose, one in the upper lip, the other
around his body. which accounted for his
being taken so easily.

Pittsburg May 16.-A railroad collision for

road, which is owned by the Westinghouse in
terests. In addition to the 800 delegates there

A train composed of fifty steel cars which had
just been received from the works was divided
into three parts. TWO Of these parts were left
standing on the track, a space of about fifty
yards dividing them. The third section, to
which the engine was attached, was then drawn
down the tracks a distance of two miles. The
engineer pulled the throttle wide open and
Jumped oft and the section of the train crashed
into the stationary cars while running at
speed Of forty miles hour There a
culver the three sections united automatically
and then settled down on the tracks without
any damage having been done The cars and
the engine were equipped with friction draft
gears which absorbed the strain.

The great attraction for several
thousand people of Los Angeles and the
coast cities Sunday in the harbor at
San Pedro was the presence Of German
warship Fake.


The Fake is a thoroughly equipped
and well manned sea warrior of the
small cruiser type, about the build of
the third class cruisers of the American
navy.


The Fake, in command of Capt. Am
mann, cast anchor inside the break
water at San Pedro on Saturday morn
Ing, Immediately upon arriving from
San Francisco, where the ship has been
at anchor for six weeks. The stay in
the harbor will terminate on Wednes-
day, when the Fake will steam away
for San Diego and Panama, where half
the crew will be changed, the other half
taking the cars at Panama for Colon,
whence they will board mail steamer
for Germany. The crew will be rein
forced by sailors from Kiel, who will
board the ship for the remainder of
the cruise in foreign waters.


Although the notice was brief, so
great was the desire of fellow country
men to tread the decks of the German
warship that all of the launches in the
San Pedro harbor were required to
transport the crowds to the ship.
Launch after launch loaded to the
guards cut through the water, begin
ming early in the forenoon and still
more were coming at o'clock. The
boat was thronged from stem to stern
and all were cordially received by the
officers, sailors and marines, everybody
being shown the first and secondary
batteries, the rifles, the engines in the
hold and the electric equipment.

The fire boys at engine house number
IA, Central avenue and East Thirty
fourth street, have just experienced
new sensations not exactly in the line
of fire fighting, but even more stren-
uous and painful than the ordinary fire
experience. They have been fighting
bees, or rather they started in with that
determination, but retired ingloriously
defeated until they grew convalescent
from the torpedo" attacks of the en-
emy and started on new tack, that of
smoking the bees into submission.


"They we're sulky set and their fir
ing line was mighty sharp. They gave
us boys the kind of sharpshooting that
caused our jaws to swell up in big
shape" said Lieutenant Strohm the
other day.


"And one of the little imps stuck his
implement of defense square into my
Adams APPLE" spontaneously burst
out one of the boys, as he placed his
fingers under his chin.


A large swarm of bees moved in be-
tween the outer wall and the plaster
ing Of the engine house, about two
years ago. The fire boys had been wat
ching the movements of the busy little
bee, improving each shining hour, gath
ering honey every day from every open
ing flower, meantime nursing their
fondest hopes, which later developed
into sore bumps, in anticipation of
prolonged feasts Of hot biscuit and
fresh honey.


Thinking the time was ripe to make
strike, few days ago they took their
little ak and attacked the side of the
building in the approved style of fire
fighters in reaching smoldering fire.
But instead of the regulation smoke
and flame they received special point
ers' of a different nature when the
bees presented their bills" which was
very early and often.


But the boys persevered with the de-
termination that if they could endure
fire and water, they could conquer
few spiteful bees for the sake of the
honors and the honey. When one of
the ax-men would become weary"
and wanted a rest another brave would
fill his place until he in turn became
"wearied" And so it continued for two
days, excepting the intervening night
of agonizing dreams and fitful maps of
disturbed slumbers.


At last the boys produced their own
smoke and compelled their little enc
mics to capitulate, 'interning" them in
a hive. After the bees had recovered
from the smoke they seemed confused
The boys, noting this state of affairs,
called in an expert bee man from the
country, who placed the hive right side
up with care, administered soothing
syrup and the bees were all right.


The boys were much disappointed
upon opening the honey trough, for the
ton of honey they expected as a re-
ward for their labors did not mater
alize by 1895 1-2 pounds.

BRIGHTON. Colo, April 8-Because
the County Commissioners of Adams
County did not honor a requisition for
filing cabinet issued by County Judge
Gutheil, they were fined $50 each and
ordered to Jail by the Judge yesterday.
John Benbow. Edward Fitzpatrick and
Frank Purse are the Commissioners.


There has been friction between the
Commissioners and the Judge. A few
weeks ago the court decided that it
needed a filing cabinet The Commits
sioners were asked for it, but failed to
realize the Importance of the request.
Yesterday morning the Judge issued
citations requiring them to show rea-
son for their action. The Sheriff found
the Commissioners in consultation con
cerning another matter The hour for
appearance not having been specified,
they did not go Immediately to the
courtroom.


After luncheon the Judge issued
attachments for contempt against
the Commissioners, and these were
served. The court fined them
$50 each. County Attorney Pierce
gave notice of appeal The court re-
fused to recognize the motion. and an
application for a writ of supersedeas
was suggested, but on account of the
absence of the court stenographer no
record of the trial was kept and papers
could not be prepared. Finally the
Commissioners apologized, and the
Judge remitted the fines during good
behavior. He got the file.

Essen. Prussia. Jan. 26-The coal mine owners
took a decision to-day that probably will result in
settlement of the strike They determined to in
form the government that they would accept any
Judgment parliamentary commission might render
after inquiry into the grievances of the miners
and that the owners would Immediately remove the
grievances.


The resolution embodying this decision, which
binds all the members of the coal syndicate. sug-
gested that the Interior Departments commission
already at work be authorized by the Prussian Diet
10 act for the Diet. The resolution also affirmed
that the attitude of the mine had been mis-
understood and that this proposition was only
repetition OF what was offered by the Interior De-
partment representatives, January IA.


Powerful political influence has been working
toward bringing the members of the coal syndicate
to to-day's decision. The Emperor has himself
talked with three four persons concerned, and
has given his personal opinion that the employers
ought to take such attitude as to make a COM
promise possible.


News of the Mine Owners Association action
reached the Boerse before the closing and strength
ened the market.

with cargo of oysters

wind pulled, snorted. piped up and hit her.
Now there was channel two hundred
feet wide and deadly shoals on each hand
unseen but not unheard, for ever and
again. the old sloop tore through the
seas half buried to leeward. their BOOM
ings Numbered on either side.


Through the blindness she slashed, now

The Run for Harbor.

water fifteen miles away to the west. in a
storm which drove so thickly that from
the helm it was impossible to see more
than vague shadowy something which
was the vessels tlbSai.


Now every wave that ran at her was
bigger than she was. She shook them off

shifting OF activity from one quarter Of the

Prominent Subjects.


The most prominent subjects for at

the progress of the peace negotiations at

The weekly weather bulletin of the Agrt-

The commodity markets today moved ir-

scant influence in the dealings in securities.


London Continued Firm.


The London stock market continued very
firm in nearly all of It's departments. The
cheerful speculative sentiment prevailing
there was based upon the very easy none
tary situation and the optimistic views with
regard to the outcome of the Portsmouth
peace negotiations. Foreign houses were
more active in the local market than they
have been for many days past. and their
purchases were estimated at upward OF
5000 shares, fairly well distributed among

This buying contributed a great deal to
the strength which the market displayed at
the opening of business, and upon its con-
clusion the trading quieted down and de-
veioped the uncertain tone already men,

Industrials Prominent.


AS noted above, the Industrial stocks
were particularly prominent in the deal
ings, furnishing most of the more extern
sve advances scored, and showing for the

tonal Lead and American Smelling. The
last-named stock moved irregularly in the
early dealings, but subsequently rose
smartly upon renewed discussion of the
prospects for the declaration of an in
creased dividend.


The Copper Strength.


The continued strength of copper metal

gamated Copper shares.


The United States Steel stocks. while ac-

No well-detined and sustained tone ac-

list Transactions there also were unat-

most general character.

text:
How to improve the condition of it's
women is one of the greatest problems
which faces India. That their lot has been
a hard one; that they have not been given
a fair chance in life that the natives of
India can never rise to high position
among the nations until their women have
been elevated, is being more and more COM
monty admitted.


With the progress of education and the
growth of the Christian community, Indian
women are slowly coming to understand
that many spheres of activity and useful
ness which hitherto have been closed to
them are as appropriate for them as for
their husbands and brothers. For the pres
ent the Christian community must lead in
ali these movements. The Marathi Mission
of the American board, working in the
Bombay presidency. has now fairly de-
veloped several industries for girls. The
most important are weaving with hand
looms, rug making, lace embroidery and
art needlework. The objections to the first
and second of these are that the profits are
small and that they require machinery and
equipments which prevent their being de-
veloped except in factories. In India. much
more than in the United States, factories
are unsafe places for girls. The third and
fourth industries are most appropriate for
Indian young women. They can be de-
geloped IN private homes anywhere else;
they require only small and inexpensive
outfit; they offer large scope for skill, in
telligence and taste. and also bring fair
profits.

Plants sleep much the same as ami
mails. Their sleep is quite real, and its
reality can be shown. Perhaps the best
marked form of slumber in the vege-
table world is that of the great winter
rest when so many species retire alto
gether under the sheltering soil, and
there lie dormant, side by side with the
slumbering animals. How does the long
winter rest of animals differ, after all.
from the winter rest of the crocus or
the hyacinth, which withdraw all the
living material from their leaves in
autumn and bury themselves inches
deep in the soil in the shape of bulb
till February rains or April suns tempt
leaves and flowers out again? The
whole vast class of Dubious and tuber-
Gus plants, indeed-the lilies, orchids,
daffodils, narcissi, tulips, squills, blue
bells and snowdrops-are they not just
alternating creatures, which retire un-
derground in autumn with the slugs
and the queen wasps, to reappear III


spring about the same time with the
return to upper air of the moles, the
tortoises and the fritillary butterflies?

RUSSIAN HEADQUARTERS Huan
Mountain, March 1.--After an all night
battle the Russian forces which seized
the railroad bridge across the Shakhe
river retired after having DESTROYED the
Japanese fortifications at the further
end of the bridge and thrown the Jap
anese forces into CONSERVATION. The
Japanese losses were heavy.


The attack on the bridge began at 8
o'clock Tuesday evening. Under cover
of heavy bombardment Russian
chasseurs dashed forward and crossed
the bridge, drove back the defenders
and occupied the further end OF the
bridge. There the chasseurs threw up
hasty entrenchments and soon drove
the Japanese from their defenses at
the head of the bridge. An hour later
the chasseurs rushed across the bridge
and seized and fortified thicket oppo-
site, overcoming a number of wire en-
tanglements and blowing up the Jap
anese redoubts. An artillery company
kent up the bombardment and sue
ceeded In demolishing the Japanese
searchlights.


Desperate Struggle in the Dark


A stubborn fight in the darkness be-
gan, the gloom being but slightly dis
PEELED by the pale light of the stars
and the reflection from fires kindled by
the explosion of shells. The Japanese
brought up their quiokfire guns and
forced the Russians to abandon the
thicket, from which position the Jap
anese proceeded 10 lombard the regi-
ments holding the head of the bridge.
The night was desperate and at close
quarters. The Japanese rushed up
heavy columns of reinforcements and
charged repeatedly across the river.

Borden had gone into the Ice box

How careless of some one" said

ming the door shut and turning the
catch. The noise drowned the yell of

his wife did not hear, and walked
leisurely away while the captive beat a

Gradually the intense cold chilled the

tubs of lard and butter to keep himself
from freezing. Then the lack of mir
affected him, and for an hour between
gasps he battled for breath and

oh, better that her battered hulk
