Duck hunters are now having good sport
on the Potomac below Alexandria, the long
expected birds having arrived in large num-
ber within the past forty-eight hours. The
ducks came after the heavy northwest blow
and the cool weather that followed it Wed
nesday last and are now on their feeding
grounds on the flats Capt. George Cook of
the Potomac Dredging Company reports
having seen several large focks of ducks
yesterday that must have numbered several
thousand birds. AS far as he could see
there were very few crow ducks in the
focks, but mallard shutters and dippers
were numerous. There were no canvas
backs seen. Several hunters were out after
the birds yesterday. and all secured good
bags, but the birds are shy and hard to ap-
proach. The movements of the ducks are
very erratic. Today there will be thou
sands of them feeding on the river and by
tomorrow every one of them win have dis
appeared, only to reappear as suddenly as
they left Rabbits and other game are re-
ported plentiful this season In the counties
along the Potomac. and hunters are leaving
here daily for river points to try their luck
after the rabbits. squirrels and birds.

the National Theater last night. Elaborate
scenic effects, splendid costuming and all
possible accessories to charm the senses,
make the production notable. The Rogers
Brothers are once more the Rogers
Brothers-and there is hardly anything else
TO say. A good many persons have been
heard to register the opinion that the
Rogers Brothers are not funny. These
critics constitute about the most foolishly
receptive portion of the audience when the
time comes. The Brothers still talk down
each others threats, wreck the English
language every minute, sing songs foolish
beyond the dreams of frivolity, and crack
jokcs-some of them good. The company
this year is large and the chorus particular
ly well trained. The dances and ensembles
were enthusiastically encored by the large
audience. Josephine Cohan formerly one
of the -Four Cohans,' made the hit of the
production in the song and dance, The
Village Maid Miss Conan didn't have
enough to do, however. Bessie de Vote, who
can smile naturally for three hours a
stretch, was extremely capable in the SOU
brette role, and Dorothy Hunting's songs
were well received. The other members of
the cast We're capable. The music by Max
Hoffman was above the average. He still
retains the old trick of playing the popular
airs OF the piece between the acts ana as
usual the gallery had great sport whistling
the Silver Nile and The Village Maid
When Maurice Levy welded the baton for
the Rogers Brothers this part of the even
ings fun became important additions to
the stage attraction and Mr.. Hoffman has
wisely concluded to follow the methods of
his predecessor. The training of the chorus
was so remarkable to call forth un-
usual praise. Several seasons back it was
considered quite a feat to have half a
dozen women go through intricate dancing
steps to music while last night the entire
Rogers Brothers chorus executed steps
that would have earned applause for a solo
dancer. Everybody on the stage appeared
to enter into the fun with animation and
energy. The audience was unusually large.

LONDON, May 6-The stock exchange
has experienced another dull and tiresome
week. Brokers say there has been a better
feeling in most directions and a certain de-
gree of frmness, but the quotation tables
hardly bear this out, for minus. signs are
pretty general, with the exception of the
foreign department.


The same old causes apparently dominate
the market, namely, the timidity of specu-
lators because of the uncertainty attach
Ing to the situation in the far east the
overloaded bull account and the moderate
stringency in the money market


Ease, which was expected in the money
market after the turn Of the quarter, has
not yet manifested itself Heavy issues of
exchequer bonds and the floating of new
securities have had the effect of keeping
loanable funds somewhat scarce.


The talk now is that there will be an i'm
provement in about ten days, based partly
on the expectation that the government will
pay off treasury bills and that there will be
a heavy influx of money from the provinces

has fallen once more below 80, other gilt
edged stocks also dropping. Home rails con-
tinued their downward course, practically
all of them closing under last Saturdays
prices.


American rails followed the New York
market pretty closely and the closing prices
exhibit number of heavy shrinkages.


There has been a little continental buying
of mines, but not enough favOrably to at
feet the market.


Foreigns have shown fair amount of

neighbor who had been summoned to the
house by the woman's grandchild. When

rocking chair taking a nap. Upon her re-
turn to the house she was still sitting there
and the child was unable to arouse her.

was dead the police were summoned and

After waiting for three hours the visitors left

Sada Yacco, the charming little Jap
anese actress, is a great favorite in
Paris. She is, moreover, exceedingly

Mistress Sada was invited to take

which was presented to the fascinating
Oriental by the august donor himself.


smile was his reward-that beam
ing, childlike smile, which only a pretty
Japanese girl can properly achieve.
Sada Yacco recognized the gentleman's
good intentions and gave him full
credit for them. but she is as practical
as she is grateful. and this is what she
said:


VERY sorry Very sorry. Not take
vase to Japan. Too far. Get broken.
Take money. Very sorry"


While the onlookers gasped she
beamed on the president all over again,
sweetly, serenely unconscious that she
had done anything out of the ordinary.
And she got the money.

NEW YORK, June 9.--After sobbing all
night in her berth pretty young Jewess
whose last name was Liftner jumped over
board as the steamship Hartford came
through Hell Gate this morning at 7
O'Clock. She was seen bobbing about in
the waves astern, but before the boat could
be put about she had sunk. The body was
not recovered


The Hartford, which belongs to the New
York and Hartford Transportation Com
pany, brought the news of the suicide
when she docked today. Miss Liftner went
aboard a few minutes before the boat left
Hartford yesterday afternoon at 8 o'clock
There were signs Of tears on her face then,
the purser noticed, and from what others
say she must have been weeping almost
steadily until she sank her troubles in the
waters of the sound.


She did not appear to be over eighteen
years old, and was decidedly good look
ing, with dark hair and eyes and oval olive
skinned face.


On the deck where she had been seen
last her belongings were lying. They in
cluded a cheap umbrella a bundle contain
ing black skirt and white shirt waist
and small new hand bag. In the hand
bag was a little pocketbook, and In this
Captain Bacon, the master of the ship,
found $1.56 and two cards.

VLADIVOSTOK, June ia series

OF the Associated Press has had with
naval officers who survived the battle
Of the Sea of Japan has developed a
most sensational story of the causes
Of the Russian disaster first of all
and the complete Generalization which
followed the sinking Of the flagship
Kniaz Souvaroff and the wounding of

jestvensky only once after the juno
ture of their squadron, and then only

All the stories of extensive target
practice in Madagascar, it seems, were
false. During the entire voyage there
practically was no training in gunnery
worthy of the name and the big gun
practice was confined to three shots per
vessel. Ugly stories are told Of the
happenings at Madagascar. Some Of
the crews certainly were unframed in
gunnery and, exhausted by the eight
months voyage under trying moral and
physical conditions, were no match for
the veteran Japanese, whose marks
manship was wonderful. They coll
centrated their fire on one ship until
she was placed out of action and then
on another, thus successively sinking
the Oslagia, Alexander III and Kniaz
Souvaroff.


Grave Structural Defects


Some ships developed deplorable
structural defects. The Oslabia sank
without having a single hole below the
water line. Heavy seas entered the
vessel above the water line and the
water tight compartments, which were
changed several times during the voy-
been calculated for and burst, flooding
and keeling the vessel over until she
turned turtle.


Lack of homeogenity among the ships
harmony. The Vladimir Monomach,
Admiral Oushakoff and Admiral Sc
niavin had to lag behind, thus becom-
ing easy victims. Finally. the ammuni-
tod na Arcf
days fighting.


Even the very morning of the battle,
while the buzzing of the wireless in
struments on the Russian ships showed
that the japanese scouts were commu-
nicating his dispositions to Admiral
Togo, Admiral Rojestvensky continued
his careless maneuvering, and when the
Japanese actually appeared the Rus
slams were caught in an impossible
formation and were attacked on three
fronts. Rojestvensky's position was
cramped and his transports were badly
placed and caused confusion, so that
while the Japanese were raining pro-
jectiles even from machine guns on the
Russian ships the latter were huddled
together, blanketing each others fire.


Mines and Torpedoes Work Havoc


Only the leaders of the columns could
bring their guns to bear, and those the
unframed gunners fired wildly. The
mines and floating torpedoes sown in
the paths of the Russian divisions add
ed to the confusion. The Borodino, Ad-
miral Nakimoff and Vavarin fell VIC
Tins to these distractions.


1t is a heartrending narrative that
Russia and the world should know. The
sailors and officers were not altogether
to blame, for the main fault lay else
where. There were many heroes among
the Russians. Capt. Berkh of the Os-
labia committed suicide on her bridge
as the ship sank rather than save him
self. There were thousands of other
heroes whose names the world will new
er know.

CHICAGO, November Clash payments
of wages in Indiana harbor frightened the
employees of the big factories there so
greatly last week that they started a run
on the Indiana Harbor State Bank. The
financial storm ragged for three days, and
the tempest was quieted solely by the sight
of piles of currency and gold which the
bank officials placed in view OF the ignorant
foreigners who were clamoring for their
money. The run at last was checked, and
nearly all the money that was drawn out
has been redeposited. The anomalous fright
resulted from the fact that the inter-
national and Steel Company at the end Of
the previous week, on the regular pay day,
paid in cash instead of following its old
custom of giving the employees checks
drawn on the bank. This led to the con-
clusion that something was wrong with
the bank and the run ensued.

WEST NEWTON, Pa, Oct. 1.-"What
are you doing around here?" thun-
dered John Williams, wealthy farmer
near here, when he saw George Keck,
formerly one of his hands, drive up 10
his gate.


"I've come for my wife," said Keck.


Your what? You haven't any wife
around here" said the farmer.


"Oh, yes, I have" answered Keck.
your Katie is my wife, and I've come
to take her with me-"


Katie, the 20-year-old daughter of the
farmer, and the belle of the neighbor-
hood, recently returned from school,
stepped forward and admitted that she
and Keck had slipped away from the
parental home three months ago and
been married.


Williams rushed to the corn crib and
took down the old family shotgun. He
blazed away, and there was a scream
from Katie. Some of the shot struck
her right arm. Covering Keck with
the remaining barrel Williams locked
Katie up in the smokehouse and drove
Keck from the place.


The next morning Keck returned.
He brought back a dozen of his
friends, all armed. Katie was still
locked up in the smokehouse, and her
mother was with her. Williams was
soon overpowered and the two women
were set free. Katie said she would
accompany her husband, and her
mother decided that where Katie went
she also would go.


The party drove away leaving Will
liams in a rage. He threatens to dis
own both his daughter and his wife.
Keck is twice as old as Katie and has
always been a poor farmland. His
bride was to be sole heir to her fathers
big fortune.

Eleanor was born in Southern Texas

impressions were those Of the balmy
south and the zephyrs that tell of the
"sunshine and the palm trees and the
tinkly temple bells" became dear and
associations Of her infancy. Her early
life was peaceful and she was content
with existence.


! .'Then there came a change, as all

knew no real hardship. Her guardian
ter, decided to give his W gard to A
son avenue N, Minneapolis, and the

From the day Of her arrival in Min

satisfaction, but did not complain. She
vas was Il: treated kindly, but the Hocum
charge and her despondency did not
please them. When the cool nights
came the little orphan shivered and
skunk away by herself into the warmest
corner she could find, and was often

| Inc H0cum'S hnally gave up trying

The day of leaving came. Eleanor

a happy bark. Eleanor, a great dane

Evidence came to light in Chicago yester.
day showing that the professional labor


'sluggers" maintain a victims hospital"

jury. which just adjourned, had strong
hint of the existence OF such place. where

killed, but out of the mutterfngs and half

der. express messenger and veteran of the

Knocked down on the street by three

rs was stripped, Wilder was kept for three
weeks. Every day and night his tormen-
tors would visit him, prick him with brad-
avis, burn his feet with matches and his

over his body are burns inflicted by lighted
candles.


His condition is extremely critical today.
and he will probably die without being able
to throw any further light upon his case,
denounced by the authorities as the most
outrageous since the dark ages. Tho police
believe that in his case they have clew to
the mysteries connected with many deaths,

bodies of men bearing marks of torture.

held prisoner and tortured to make him

pected of maintaining their victims hos

The Islands of the Everglades are covered
with luxuriant virgin forests The liveoaks
and the bays are present in large numbers,
interspersed with wild cucumbers, wild
lemon and wild orange. The papaya, the
custard apple and the prickly ash are of
very frequent occurrence, and here and
there governed by the size and elevation OF
the islands, are the cabbage palmetto and
the pine. Wild rubber trees are also found
in some localities, growing to enormous
size. Throughout the region there is
phenomenal growth of vines. The morning
glory and honeysuckle attain great size
and almost everywhere. The wild fig,
which fastens Itself about massive trunk
of liveoak or bay, lives its cannibal life
til the supporting tree trunk has been de-
stroyed. Wherever the land is dry enough
the coontie plant hourshes. This plant is
really the Florida arrowroot. 1t is the
mainstay of the Seminole. From its root
he extracts -four ard starch, both of which
are delicate and digestible.


There is a remarkable variety and pro-
fusion of wild flowers. Water lilies and
spider lilies abound. Orchids found IN
great numbers and are of great beauty.
On many OF the islands grow giant ferns,
the fronds of which measure ten feet in
length


The shores of the streams by which the
Glades are entered are covered with rank





tree grows all about the edge of the
Glades, producing blue fruit on the eastern
edge and white fruit toward the west. The
fora of the whole region is unique and UNI
studied, and contains, no doubt, scores of
plants unknown and unclassified


The Everglades are not sportsman's
paradise, in the usual sense of the term,
Nevertheless. animal life is fairly abundant
in that portion of the area where the
larger islands lie. Deer are found on both
the eastern and western edges and now
and then bear is seen. The panther has
not entirely disappeared, an occasional one
finding its way into the explorers camp.
Offers are plentiful. and the Seminoes,
who hunt both the otter and the alligator
for their skins, derive considerable rev.
enue from otter trapping. The alligator is
often SEEN and his gentle roar is by no
means unmusical On the Soutfeas stern
edge the crocodile (Crocodilus Ameicus) Is
found in small numbers. though his more
favorite haunts among the mangrove
Businesses between the Glades and the

sensational story of the causes of the Rus

mony. The Vladimir Monomach, Admiral
Oushakoff and Admiral Seniavn had to lag

tins

vering, and when the Japanese actually ap-

This does not mean that long-dra wn out

of the two sides. This is bloodless war
a merry war with roses and other flowers
as the fragrant and harmless weapons


In the French town of Mention. on the
Mediterranean sea, flowers grow in great
abundance, and every spring the people
have a flower festival in which large num-
ber5 take part.


Along the sea front there Is a broad.
smooth road fringed with palm trees and
on one side a beautiful park. Just before
the holiday wooden stands. with rows of
seats. are built along the road. These are
richly decorated with cheese cloth in red.
white and blue. Painted flag poles are put
up at short Intervals, and from these wave
not only the French flag, but flags of many
other nations, making the scene one of
great beauty.


When the day comes everybody wears the
gayest possible costume. Those who have
carriages take part in the parade; others fill
the long banks of seats in the stands. But
everybody carries flowers. The decoration
of the carriages is competition. Hand
some banners are presented to the persons
whose decoration the judges decide to be
the prettiest. Even the wheels are fes-
TONED until they look like solid disks OF
flowers.


AS the line OF carriages iiIoNto the
Gus bands play and the people applaud this
pretty design or that. Clapping and cheer
ing are heard all along the way. Every
one is in good humor. The judges carefully
inspect each carriage and decide which ones
deserve prizes.


When the procession has passed the whole
line of spectators it turns around and comes
back Then the fun begins. Now comes the
war-bateille de fleurs the French call 1t.
The people in the stands peit those IN the
carriages with bouquets. while the ocou-
pants of the carriages return the volley5
with laugh and shout. The oands pay
lively airs or military tunes while the battle
RACES like merry game of SNOWFALL. The
road is soon carpeted with violets, roses,
carnations and lilies.


Finally the procession returns again and
the Judges announce the winners and award
the prizes. This festival is regular yearly
occasion in Mention. The people there would
as soon think of letting it pass unnoticed
as we Americans would pass by the Fourth
of July.

Millions of flies have invaded the Cardiff
docks district. and have so infested the
principal thoroughfares that pedestrian
traffic has been diverted into other streets.

eatesmen at the pier head were attacked

houses The shopkeepers complain bitterly

warehouses are seriously interrupted in
their work From their appearance the
flies belong TO a foreign species. Unlike
the British fly. they have long bodies. crawl
very slowly and bite badly They first
made their appearance on Sunday. The
sanitary authorities discredit the report

Directly in my path stood ancient
swamp white oak. the greatest tree, 1
think, that / have ever seen. 1t was not
the highest, nor the largest around. per-
haps, but individually. spiritually, the
greatest. Hoary. followed and broken
limbed. his huge bole seemed encircled with
the centuries. and in this green and griz-
zled top all the winds of heaven had some
time come


One could worship in the presence of such
a tree easily as in the shadow of n
vast cathedral. Indeed. what is there built
with hands that has the dignity. the maj
esty, the divinity of life? And what life
was herei Life whose beginnings lay 60
far back that / could more reckon the
years than l could count the atoms 1t had
builded into this majestic form.


Looking down upon him from twice his
height doomed tulip poplar, clean, boiled

gold with blossoms. 1t was a respondent
thing beside the oak, yet how Enthusiastically
the gnarled old monarch wore the crown!

height, and as for blossoms-nature knows
the beauty of strength and inward majesty
and has pinned no boutonniere upon the
oak.

scow sloop Detroit originally purchased
by San Diego enthusiasts to defend the
Upton cup was ignominiously defeated
by the staunch old Venus. Herb Pease's
cruising sloop.


With choppy sea running off Ocean
Park yesterday the eastern scow was
outfooted and outsailed and literally
never had a chance under the handicap
of the prevailing weather conditions to
delight her new owners by winning the
first race sailed under the colors of the
Terminal Island club.


The Venus found the weather to her
liking and while George Folsom's Mis-
chief was always up in the going the

Erkenbrecher and Jenkins remarked on
the pernicious whims of fate and for

mill pond sea before consenting to sus-
tain her fleet reputation.


The Ocean Park Country club cup
was offered as trophy for an unre-
stricted class race three years ago, the
stipulation being made that the annual
event should be sailed off the beach
town. With the hurried purchase of
, the Detroit, mainly, of course, for the

incidentally the Ocean Park bauble,

owners Of the Mischief and the Marie,
for they pictured themselves relegated
to poor second place by the advent Of
the Detroit town scow.


But yesterdays race worked a marked
change In the mental attitude of the
masters of the aforementioned craft
but particularly so to Herbert Pease
and his crew of heArties.


The race, which resulted in a de-
cisive victory for the Venus yesterday
was sailed over an equilateral triangle
two miles to each leg and twice around
the first leg to windward.


In the first leg the Detroit Rugged
the beach, the Venus and Mischief lay
ing course well out in the channel.
The Detroit assumed the lead for the
first half mile, but in rounding the first
mark the Venus and Marie had prom

beat to the outer mark the Detroit held

line the Venus showed clean pair of
heels to the remainder of the fleet. The
Pease boat dropped her mudhook of
the Venice pier. while the Detroit ana
Mischief struggled over the line in the
order named.

The residents Of Baden, Ocean View.
Colma and adjoining towns are much
wrought UP over the heavy blasting
that is being done by the Southern Pa
cifc Company In the construction of its
new cutoff about five miles from Ba-
. den. The citizens firmly believe that
the blasts are responsible for many Of
the numerous shake-ups felt recently.
For nearly two months blasts have
been going off night and day at short
intervals. Some of them are small and
explode without annoying, while others
are as heavy as it is possible to make
them. and when they explode the citi-
zens OF the adjoining districts say the
whole country for miles around Quivers
and Quakes just like an earthquake.


The officials Of the company and the
contractors who are working on the
new road deny that the blasts are felt
In the vicinity. They admit that some
heavy charges of dynamite have been
set off since the work began, but add
that the explosions were never felt and
that it would be impossible for the
shock to effect the district miles away.


The last heavy blast was set of on
New Years day. Late In the afternoon
thirty tons Of dynamite were exploded.
and the entire side of huge, rocky hill
fully 300 feet long was blown away and
its fragments were scattered far and
near. A saloon man in the vicinity says
his beer kegs were hurled from their
positions and his saloon was nearly
wrecked. The people Of Baden were
terrified when they felt the earth shak-
ing.


Blasting has been going on steadily
at two points along the old road that
leads from Baden to South San Fran
cisco. The earth has been loosened all
along the line and two mammoth steam
shovels are at work clearing away the
rock and dirt that has become loosened
by the blasts. Work on the new tunnel
near South San Francisco will begin In
a few days. and it is probable that
some more heavy blasting Will be done
there.


Strange to say, the residents who are
complaining about the blasts never
hear a report when they feel the shook
All the reports have been smothered.
for the reason that the dynamite works
down and the rock and clay are loos-
ened from beneath. The heaviest Of
these blasts have torn away entire sec
tions OF ground, while the work accom-
plished by the light blasts Is hardly no
ticeable.


The people who reside in Belmont and
other towns farther down say they
never experienced any shocks when the
Baden folks complained Of quaking
earth. Experts say the rock and clay

A detachment of six men was carrying
dispatches from a command near Red river
to Camp Supply. OF the six two were
scouts. Amos Chapman and William Dixon
The others We're cavalrymen. Far from
any refuge they were surrounded by nearly
200 Indians. They sought shelter in a bus
falo wallow and prepared to hold their
ground. The attack came at 6 O'Clock In
the morning, and the long, long day
stretched before them. In the first rush
vate Smith mortally. The other hurts were
severe.


They were hemmed in on all sides in an
open plain, and were outnumbered almost
twenty to one. One of the scouts, while
severe fire was being poured in at them at
close range, succeeded in throwing up a
scanty intrenchment with his bowie knife
and his bare hands His comrades held the
Kfowas and Comanches off until this little
help was ready as refuge and they moved
into the trench, the wounded walking with
brave and painful effort.


Although private Smith was wounded I'M
to death. he sat upright in the trench to
conceal his crippled condition from the foe.
From early morning until night this hand
full Of Ave men was under an almost con-
slant fire, often at such short range that
they could bring their pistols into play
Thus they fought for their own lives and
defended their dying comrade, without food
and for drink only little muddy rain water
mixed with their own blood. They killed
more than dozen Indians and wounded
above score.


Relief came that night, but 1t was thirty
six hours after the first attack before
medical aid and food could be given them
at the nearest post. Private Smith died be-
fore camp was reached. Every man was
wounded Scout Chapman severely and
Scout Dixon several times, but not dam
gerously. This band of four soldiers and
two scouts were of those who had been
fighting and marching for weeks amid the
most dreadful privations. They were worn
to skin and bone, but their souls were as
''big as all outdoors" and they finched at
no odds under heaven. And by such men
as these was this nation made.

been working at the Schuylkiil Arsenal for the

inspectors to the officers in charge of the arsenal

maments has ceased, and therefore the
reinforcements were sent back to their

SAN BERNARDINo, July S.-Mrs.
Charles Cooley of East Cotton left her
home last Saturday to visit her per-

safely, but day or so afterward left
and has dropped completely out Of
sight.

sibly the disappearance Of the couple

ley finds his brother he will also find

the fact that they both disappeared on
the same day and nothing has been
heard of either.

at her home with no one to care for
them except the husband, who is nearly
wild with grief over his wife's dis
appearance.

Geneva Correspondent of the London Express


Two young Italians. named Guetta and
Sorato, both in their teens, and living In a
little village near Bellinzona, fell in love
with the same girl, who is said to have
liked both suitors equally WELL


The young men. after many serious quar-
rels, decided on a very original plan to
settle the dispute. Informing their parents
that they were going on an excursion to
the mountains, they set out for the Splu-
gen Pass, which is notorious for its ava
lanches at this time of the year.
Z Choosing the most exposed slope, they
agreed that each should stand for two
hours every day (between 9 and IL am.
the most dangerous time) In the path of the
avalanche and allow fate to decide their
destiny.


For three mornings these conditions were
carried out. but nothing serious happened.
though several avalanches came down the
slope, but not near the foolhardy youths.


On the fourth day an enormous avalanche
passed near Guetta, who was knocked
down by the rush Of air, but not hurt.


AS the young men had no more food left,
they returned to the village to procure
some. but the authorities got wind of the
affair and threatened them with imprison-
ment- The youths then decided to draw
lots for the girl. and Sorato won. Guetta
left the village and the young couple were
married.

PHILADELPHIA. Pa, November 20
TIE Inquirer tomorrow will say:


Secret service agents have been working
at the Schuylkil arsenal for the past week
investigating charges Of collusion between
the officials and the contractors. and as a
result of their endeavurs arrests may be
made at any hour.


1.-The secret service operatives were set
in motion at the direction OF President
Roosevelt himself. whose instructions were
that the local bureau should be free to call
upon the Washington branch should any as
slstance be needed.


THE investigation has been broad ana
extensive enough to cover every depart
ment every official and every employe In
that important military depot.


While the board of inquiry, composed
of Ma jors Galbreth. Greble aud Baxter, mas
been working openly, examining witnesses
from every department, the government de-
tectives have been gathering evidence III
their own way.


THE object has been to determine just
what officials seemed most anxious to nave
the contractors get the work that nad pre-
viously been done by the widows 81 Old SOL
diers; to determine whether they mad any
motive for favoring contractors or whether
they were honestly anxious to secure
cheaper work.


THE secret service people know positively
that after the work was done by contrae-
tors inferior goods were passed and inferior
workmanship was marked with the stamp
of approval. They also know that the
blame of all this has recently been shifted
by the division inspectors to the officers in
charge of the arsenal. These inspectors
have made some grave charges against
their superors and the charges have been
fully investigated.


The War Department at Washington has
decided on certain reforms for the arsenal,
which is regarded as the most important
military depot in the east, and it is in line
with this resolve that the board of inquiry
started its investigation, and upon it's rec
concentrations that Col. Pope transferred

PHOENIX. Ariz., Aug. N.-Phoenix and
vicinity last night experienced the most
destructive electric storm of years, which
was accompanied by heavy fall of rain.
The lightning struck at various points
within the city, though there was no loss
of life The principal damage was to the
electric lines of the city. Six hundred
telephones were put out of operation, and
the city lighting plant and power COM
pany was considerably damaged. There
were no electric lights last night, and all
circuits have not yet been repaired. The
electric equipment of the cars of the
street railway was burned out. and the
system running through the center Of the
town did not resume operations until this
evening. The fire-alarm system was also
badly disturbed, and 1t required all day
to recair it.


During the first part of the storm a
high wind did some damage. An awning
in front Of Wakelins wholesale house
was torn down and heavy plateglass win
dows, valued at $780, were smashed.
Chimneys were blown from residences
and there were other slight property
losses.

Ethel Lingo and Winifred Vosler, two
young women eighteen and nineteen
years of age respectively, narrowly es-
capped being killed by an automobile at
the junction of Main street and Mani
tou avenue Sunday evening.


The two girls were crossing the
street when they were suddenly run
down by the machine, which was going
at high rate of speed.


The automobile struck Miss Lingo,
knocking her down and dragging her
for over twenty-five feet before it was
finally brought to halt.


When the machine was finally stop
ped, and Miss Lingo disengaged from
the wheels, it was found that she suf-
fered no further injuries than badly
bruised shoulder and slight bruises
about the head. That she was not
killed outright was little short Of a
miracle, as those who saw the accident
say the girl was dashed to the ground
many time during her perilous trip.


The chauffeur of the machine took
Miss Lingo to the Naomi hospital,
where her injuries were treated.


Miss Lingo says that she does not
blame the chauffeur for the accident,
as she stepped directly in front of the
machine before she saw it.

DETROIT, Mich, June 6.-ReportS To-Day
from the state say that the rain and wind
storm which was general all over the lower
part of Michigan yesterday afternoon and
last nigh. was the most severe in many
years In addition to the loss of life re-
ported last night in Sanilac and Tuscola
counties, where the storm assumed cyclone
proportions, heavy property loss is reported
in all directions. Streams are flooded and
out of their banks, and in western Michl-
gan railroads are seriously delayed Thirty
washouts were reported today on the Pere
Marquette system, and the Grand Trunk
reported eleven.


At Grand Rapids the rainfall was almost
a cloudburst. On the west side districts
were flooded that were not affected by the
great flood of 1904. Water ran through
some west side streets four feet deep, mood
ing many houses.


About 500 homes were surrounded by
water. A number of manufacturing plants
were compelled to close for the day, their
first floors being two and three feet under
water. No trains arrived or departed from
the city during the early part of the day.
Washouts Caused Railway Accidents.


IONA, Mich, June 6.-Washouts caused
by last nights terrific rain have caused two
railroad accidents near here, one on the
Pere Marquette and one on the Detroit.



men were killed in the Pere Marquette
accident and four members of the train
crew were injured in the Detroit, Grand
Haven and Milwaukee accident.


A Pere Marquette train ran into wash
out near the state reformatory, and the en-
CINE was derailed and tipped over Engi-
neer w. Alvord and Fireman H. Payne of
Ionia were killed and Brakemen Coffee and
Neatly were slightly injured.


Detroit, Grand Haven and Milwaukee
westbound train No. IL, from Detroit, also
ran into a washout at Tibbits creek last
night and the engine and one car We're de-
rallied. Engineer Johnson Mail Clerk
Evans, Baggageman Tolles and the fireman
were injured, but, 1t is said, not seriously.


Three Grand Trunk bridges are washed
out in Ottawa county, where the streams
are running over their banks. At Lowell
the dam and bridge across Grand river
We're washed out, with two buildings that
stood on the bank. At Ionia the Grand
river is many feet over its banks and
thousands of dollars damage has been done
by the high water.


The Springbrook mill, two miles above
Lowell on the Grand Trunk, was washed
out At Lansing the precipitation was 4s0
inches, and the Grand river rose seven feet,
flooding cellars in the west side of the city
and Easements in the business section. The
storm damage at Hart, in Oneana county,
is estimated at $30O


In Detroit the precipitation was 294
inches yesterday afternoon and last night,
the heaviest fall In thirteen years. Nearly
boat in Grand Haven from Chicago and
Milwaukee were unable to proceed this
forenoon as the washouts had tied I'D the
railroads.

TACOMA, June 15.-After hard and
exciting chase through stormy waters
Neah Bay Indians yesterday captured a
whale ten miles off Cape Flattery. The
tug Wyanda was engaged to tow the
monster to Neah Bay harbor, where a
great feast of blubber and oil is now in
progress.


When the Wyanda arrived on the
scene six canoes filled with Indians
were being jerked about furiously by
the angered leviathan. Much excitement
prevailed, as the chase had been a long
one and there was danger for hours
that the boats would be swamped by
heavy seas and the antics of the whale
The Indians displayed great dexterity
in handling their frail canoes in nasty
sea while following the line attached
to the maddened whale.

SAN FRANCISCO, Dec. 2.LThe
steamer Roanoke, which was disabled

and for the safety OF which some anxi-
ETY. was felt, arrived here safely this
afternoon with her passengers all
well. When the Roanoke struck OH the
bar she lost her stern post and rud-
der. The hull of the vessel was not
injured. On Tuesday and Wednesday
last while coming down the coast the
Roanoke met heavy weather and
strong winds.


The Roanoke was crossing the Hum
boldt bar at o'clock Monday after
noon when a huge sea slapped across
her stern and carried away rudder and
rudder post. Fortunately the tide was
ebbing, and by the judicious use of the
head sails Capt. Durham was able to
work his vessel out through the south
channel into the open sea.


The sea which smashed the rudder
was followed by others which swept the
coasters decks,


The passengers were herded in the
saloon. The Roanoke was drawing nine
teen feet. There was but twenty feet
of depth in the south channel and sew
eral times the steamer bumped the bot
tom. But she got clear all right and
stood off shore. where she was Joined





Capt. Durham decided that he could
make San Francisco under jury rudder,
and the next morning a temporary
steering apparatus was rigged.


1t served until evening when a heavy
southeaster came along. one of the
first seas put the jury rudder out of
commission but with foresail. jib and
stay sail the captain managed to keep
the Roanoke from wallowing too deep
ly in the trough of the sea.


Another jury rudder was rugged, but
that followed the first and after that
the Roanoke's course was governed by
u drag rudder made of an anchor bal
lasted boom astern.


Head winds were encountered and
three or four knots an hour was the
best that could be got out Of the Ro-
anoke. She never was out of sight of
land and until Thanksgiving day was
in view of Mendocno light.


'"The only real panic we had" said
the passengers, was on Thanksgiving
DAY, when we found we would get no
turkey for dinner. The corn beef has
proved to be all right. though, and

pected as reduced to pretty simple
fare, and it was necessary to breach

STANFORD UNIVERSITY, March
21.-It was nearly 2 o'clock this aft
ernoon when the private funeral train
bearing the body of Mrs. Stanford ar
rived at Menlo Park. The coffin was
Immediately placed in the awaiting
hearse. Then the little procession of
friends moved slowly out on the coun-
ty road TO the home on the Palo Alto
estate. There the body was taken from
the hearse and laid in the main room
Of the Stanford mansion. The rela-
tives, friends and student representa-
tives who had accompanied the re-
mains from San Francisco passed in
single file through the room and looked
for moment at the closed coffin. Then
they passed out of the house and drove
away, leaving the body of Mrs. STAN
ford in charge of Charles G. Lathrop,
brother of the dead woman.


Miss Bertha Berner did not follow
the funeral procession to the Stan
ford mansion. but, accompanied by
Mountford Wilson, she was driven d.
rect to her home in the foothills back
of the university. In her lap she car
ried a basket of fresh tropical fruit,
brought all the way from Honolulu.
Mr.. Wilson helped Miss Berner from
TIE Carriage anu IISn hurried 10 cdIcn
the return train for San Francisco.


There was no demonstration at the
station when the funeral train pulled
into the Menlo Park depot. The crowds
were at Palo Alto, where, since 10
o'clock in the morning, they had been
patiently waiting for the arrival of the
body. Foreseeing this, arrangements
had been made to have the body taken
from the cars at Menlo Park and
when at last the train stopped at Palo
Alto the tired throng gazed disap-
pointed at the empty coaches.


EMPLOYEES GATHER.


At the Menlo Park station there
were gathered about fifty persons
! Many of these were the old employees
of the stock farm, who had been told
where the body would be removed AS
the coffin was lifted from the door of
the car the company stood with bowed
heads, their hats clutched in their
hands, many of them with tears run
ming down their wrinkled cheeks. Some
difficulty was experienced in raising
the coffin into the hearse, and when
these hardy employees saw the trouble
they stepped forward with one accord
and helped carry the bier each man
anxious to do some little service for
his dead mistress.


The servant who took the death of





Charley Wooster, the aged coachman
For forty years he has been in the
Stanford service, coming out from New
York with them in the early days
He sat on the box Of the same car
riage in which he had driven his mis-
tress to the station on the fatal day
that she sailed for Hawaii. The old
driver was weeping when the train
came In, and although he tried his best
to hide his emotion, when the coffin
was lifted into the hearse his large
frame shook with sobbing. He would
not drive the hearse, but he followed
close behind with the carriage Of Mr.
and Mrs. Lathrop.


Detective Gibson was the first man
to alight from the funeral train at
Menlo Park. He was on the steps be-
fore the cars stopped, and he hurried
forward to the baggage car, where
the coffin had been placed Close be-
hind him was Detective COLUMBIAN,
These two stood beside the coffin as
it was taken from the train. Presi-
dent David Starr Jordan and Timothy
Hopkins came next, both looking tired
and worn. Then followed the funeral
escort, composed of representatives
from the faculty. alumni and students
of the university.

den departure is attributed to the oily
condition of the. water in the upper

preventing them from flying. The

tically helpless. The late southwest
winds have caused the oil which is dis.

ocean.

covered with oil have gone in search

not return to Richardson's Bay for
many moons. The oil-covered birds,
helpless to search for food, will perish
in a few days.

BALTIMORE, Sept. 20.-The mar
riage ceremony of Morris Lovenstein
and Miss Blanche Pollock at the Nc
Cullough street synagogue last night
was interrupted for over an hour by
the absentminded bridegroom, who
dressed for the nuptials and then left
the wedding ring on a bureau in his
room.


The ceremony had proceeded to a
point where the rabbi asked for the
ring.


Lovenstein hurriedly looked through
his pockets. The ring was not there.
Palefaced he glanced around, helpless.
The bride was visibly embarrassed.
The rabbi was in despair.


IT'S home" faltered the bridegroom.


Go and get it," ordered the rabbi,
and the bride seconded the order.


Lovenstein rushed away, and an hour
later returned, breathlessly, with the
little band of gold. The ceremony
proceeded and the pair were made man
and wife.

CHICAGO, February 17.-Twelve mer
were held up by six armed robbers in the
office Of Max Mildenberg, proprietor of the
electric light and gasoline delivery, ely
bourne place and Hawthorne street. The
highwaymen fired several shots as they
entered, -woundng two persons. They
knocked another unconscious with a blow
from a revolver. They then took more
than $500 and escaped


There were only four men in the office
when the ROBBERS entered.


F. Mildenberg, brother Of the proprietor,
and Julius Bensev, the clerk, were balanc-
ing the books, while Richard Hayes and
James Fay, foremen of the drivers, were
making their daily reports.


Fired Without Warning.


Without warning. the six robbers ap-
peared and began firing. Bensev and MIL
denberg dropped to the floor to escape the
flying bullets, but the two foremen were
struck and slightly wounded. After the
shooting the robbers ordered the four men
to hold up their hands.


At this point eight of the drivers and
filters who were in barn at the rear
hearing the shooting, ran into the office
Revolvers were pointed at them, and they
were told to Zine up" against the wall





While the two robbers kept the victims
In subsection the other four took Bensey,
the clerk, into the inner office and ordered
him to open the safe.


Robbed Safe of $500.


He complied and they removed the con-
tents, amounting to $500, the entire pro-
ceeds of the days sales.


An inner compartment remained locked,
which contained only the private papers
Of the proprietor. Bensey was commanded
to open this, and when he said he could
not, two of the robbers struck him sew
eral blows with their revolvers, making
him unconscious. Then they carried him to
the outer Office, where they forced the
twelve to lie face downward on the floor
until they could be searched.


When they secured all the plumber they
could find the robbers ran out. Two patrol
wagons crowded with police were sent to
the scene, and the neighborhood was
searched, but no trace of the men could
be found.

Had II not been for the cool heads among the
passengers the ferryboat Virginia of the
Grand-st. line. Brooklyn. and the Long Island
Railroad boat. Long Branch, when the two came
together OF Grand-st. yesterday, there would have
been panic and possible loss of life. When the
boats came together both loaded fore and
aft with crowds bound for Brooklyn and Long
Island City.


Both boats left the slips at the same time. The
Grand-st. boat had the north berth, and it was
necessary for the Long Branch TO its course.
Usually the boat for Long Island City waits for the
Brooklyn boat to get we'll It's way, and then
crosses astern Yesterday, the passengers saw
the accident, the Long Branch failed to lay to
until the Virginia had cleared Instead. the pilot
turned the boats nose sharply upstream. Just as
Virginia came out.


In instant the passengers realized the danger
Those the Long Branch rushed over to the star
board side of the boat to be as far away
possible when the crash came This caused the
boat to list heavily, and it in this position when
the of the Virginia bored it's way into the port
paddle wheel. For minute the two boats held
by the wreckage. drifted along together Then the
Virginia, which had been but slightly damaged
backed away from the Long Island City boat


For a minute the passengers in a state
that threatened serious panic. The captains deck
hands and the cooler heads quickly reassured the
frightened ones, however. and in a short time the
danger had passed, although there were many who
were hysterical and cried to be taken from the
boats Nearly every one in the mean time had been
provided with life preserver.


After the crews had made hurried examination
of the damage to the two boats both went on
reached Long Island City. None of the crews would
say which pilot was to blame for the collision.

LONDON, April 29-There has been con-
siderable depression in the stock markets
this week, and practically all the quoted
stocks closed lower today than week ago


In assigning cause for the depression most
persons attach considerable Importance to
the political uneasiness that prevails In
connection with the war in the far east
and the Franco-German situation In refer
ence to Morocco. The break in the Ameri-
can New York has, however, been perhaps
an even more influential factor, for specu-
lative activity has centered in that market
for several months.


Back of all, however, is the old trouble OF
"indigestion' There is no doubt that the
bull account is tremendously overloaded.


1t is supposed that a big Japanese naval
victory would help the market by inducing
speculation and investment buying that
would relieve the overloaded bulls. Another
view is that the market would be a mod
crate and progressive decline in prices all
along the line, until the market is brought
into what is called a healthy state.

ment has actually been started and call at
tention to the fact that there are not much
more than dozen plus signs in the quo
tation table in which this weeks prices are

one-quarter to two. Mines have been let

seize such clothing as was near their
beds and fee to the street. The fire.
men carried out one man, having
found him in hallway overcome with
smoke. He quickly revived.

with clothing. 1t was necessary to
sound second alarm summoning
four additional engine companies be-
fore the firemen could check the
spread of the flames and prevent the

Warsaw, May 25.-The Jewish disturbances
which broke out last night continued all day to-
oay and were still in progress late tonight.
hlght persons have already been killed and one
hundred wounded, nineteen seriously. The
damage to property has been considerable.
Ihere has been no piIlaging. but the destruction
OF the furniture in the various houses has been
absolute


The mob, armed with axes. smashed the doors
ana windows and brought the furniture out on
the Streets where they broke 1t into small
pieces. The owners of the furniture. in attempt
ing to defend their belongings, were attacked.
beaten and even killed. Knives and revolvers
were used freely and many persons were ter
ribly injured


The authorities took no steps to prevent the
riots until late tonight when the Cossacks fired
on the crowds at two points wounding four
persons


The correspondent of The Associated Press
spent several hours in the disturbed district
Dut did not see a single active policeman. In
course Of the day patrols occasionally appeared
but they regarded the proceedings merely as
spectators


The character Of the disturbances Is unprece-
dented. The whole affair is conflict between
the respectable Jewish socialist classes and the
disreputable Jewish element. There are con-
hicting stories as to the origin of the trouble.
One report is to the effect that the respectable
Jews. tired of hearing the members of their
race called by opprobrous names, decided as
the police were receiving brides for protecting
disorderly houses and persons, to take the mat
ter into their own hands. Another report has 1t
that Jewish roughs, in the guise Of members
OF the Bund were Ievy1ng blackmail upon shop
keepers, thus engaging the socialists. In any
casa. the socialists seemingly determined on
crusade against the undesira bic persons Of their
own race. with the result that crowds Of men
and boys systematically destroying the dis
reputable houses.


Extraordinary scenes were witnessed late to-
night when the crowds visited the better quar-
ter OF the city and demolished apartments filed
with costly effects Wardrobes pianos and mir
rors were thrown out of the windows- The mob
in the streets left open spaces for the falling
articles and then completed the work of de-
struction In one place a quantity Of valuable
1ewelry was taken out and deliberately smashed
with stones.


The whole affair was carefully organized. The
leaders were supplied with the addresses Of the
owners OF disreputable houses, and scarcely a
single resort in Warsaw escaped destruction

juries disagreeing, sailed for Liverpool
to-day on the White Star liner Majestic.

name, using that of Mrs. Jacob Becker"
John B. Millin, formerly Young's racing
partner, accompanied her, sailing under
the name of John Becker" Millin per-
sistently attempted to hide his identity
under the name of Becker, but was posi-
lively identified by detectives who were
on the pier.

mourning and carrying a large and hand
some bouquet Of roses. She then came
into sight of Mr.. Becker and waved
her adieux to her brother-in-law and sis
ter, who were on the pier. Just as the
vessel slowly backed out she tossed the
bouquet She seemed very happy and
waved her handkerchief to those on the
pier until the vessel was far out in the
stream.

law admitted that the couple were Mrs.
Young and Mllin and said that Mrs.
Young was making the trip for her
health Friends here believe the two have
been secretly married.

By Associated Press.


NEW CHWANG, March 8, via Tien-
tsin.-With Japanese flags flying, a
band of Chinese bandits today be-
headed two young Russians, who were
alleged to be spies, at Sinmintin. The
first one executed was evidently an
officer, but he was wearing a Chinese
overcoat. He kneeled without a muir
mur while his companion watched the
death stroke. The second captive was
clothed in Chinese clothing throughout
He whimpered for moment, but re-
gained his nerve and struggled fiercely.
He was thrown and killed while long
trumpets fanfared. The chief of the
bandits was mild-mannered old man
wearing a Japanese sword. He watched
the execution unmoved. "They are
Spies" he said, land we should kill
them. Besides, it is difficult to trans
port them"


Last Monday night the bandits sur
prised a small body of Russian scouts
and killed twenty-five, besides captur-
ing the two that were beheaded. To-
day the whole band, consisting of 200
cavalry and 100 infantry, formed a
great circle on the outskirts of Sinmin-
tin. The bronzed and stern featured
Chinese dismounted and held their
gayly trapped and shaggy ponies. The
men were armed to the teeth with long
rifles and Mauser pistols. The infantry
were mostly turbaned, but many wore
Russian caps.


The Russian captives were brought
to the center of the circle with a flour
ish of trumpets. They were stripped
and their arms were bound together
behind their bodies. They were turned
over to a six-foot-high executioner,,
who smilingly drew his red-sheathed
sword and wiped the blade on the
clothing of the corpses.


When the executions were finished
the corpses were left lying on the sun
lit road. Bugles were sounded and the
bandit cavalry swung into their sad
dies, while the infantry fell into line
and departed from the scene of exc
cution.

ished stone.

perched on a brass pedestal. Around the
outer walls were the laurel entwined names
of all the other states and territories.

SAN JOSE. Cal. July 1s.-with wo-
men fainting and men sobbing, brave
and popular Daniel Maloney, who has
made numerous public ascensions with
Professor Montgomery's famous aero
plane, fell 5000 feet to his death at
Santa Clara this morning.


Prof. Montgomery had announced an
ascension this morning from the
grounds of Santa Clara college in
honor of the League Of the Cross ca
diets, who are holding their annual en-
campment in that town. The announce
ment attracted probably 1000 people,
who shortly after 10 o'clock watched
with absorbing interest the airy ma
chine as it shot up from the college
garden attached to a huge balloon and
with Maloney firmly seated in his usual
position.


At a height Of 1000 feet Maloney cut
loose and began maneuvering the aero
plane. He circled gracefully about for
some minutes, having the machine ap-
parently under perfect control Then
he essayed a deep dip. Suddenly the
machine swerved, hesitated, and then
turned completely over.


1t righted itself, sank down a con-
siderable distance and turned over
again. Maloney was clinging desper-
ately to his seat and evidently endeav-
oring to gain his control. But all his
efforts were vain. Again the aero
plane turned in the air, and this time
the wings came together and the man
and the machine plunged straight
downward, while the Mortified specta-
tors gazed helplessly upward.


For distance of probably thousand
feet the aeronaut fell, still clinging to
his machine. Both alighted in the rear
of the tannery Amid shrieks and
groans, many of the spectators rushed
to the scene. while others turned away,
weeping. A number of cadets first
reached the unconscious man. and
picking him up they conveyed him to
the college hospital.


His head was fractured and blood
was flowing from his ears and mouth
He expired within a short time.


The aeroplane, which was constructed
of the toughest oak procurable was
ground into small fragments.

The vogue of the illustrated souvenir pos

visitors in out-of-the- way places has be-
come all but universal mania. The Bos-
ton post office reports handling 25COO Of
these yellow imps in a single day. The
so-called comic valentine once tainted the
postmans bag. It's influence, however,
lasted but for a day. while the souvenir
postal card ceaseth not day nor night to
cry for destroyer.


From one point of view, the growing pop
uiarity of these postal cards but evidences
anew the danger with which modern
mechanism is continually encompasslng the
older handicraft arts. The printed book
has driven out the illustrated missal. THE
uuarter-sawed oak of Kalamazoo has dis
placed Chippendale and Sheraton. And at
last the Illustrated postal. with cheap
ready made sentiment and It's chrome lith-
ograph threatens the letter of friendship,
travel and description. This residuary field
of the epistolary art was long supposed to
be safe from the inroads of the printing
press. Political intelligence such as fills
Horace Walpole's six stout volumes of pri-
waite letters has for over a entury been
disseminated in the newspapers. Scientific
news has long since found similar media
of publicity. But the intimate unbosoming
of friend to friend at distance had held
atNbay all the devices of modern machinery
until the advent of this substitute for
real letter.

mission for her to land. The matter

Washington, but no action had been
taken when the woman suddenly gave

A squaw left her two boys to care for her
papoose while she worked inside the tent
She did not notice what the boys were
doing with the papoose until 1t began to
cry. The squaw was unable to find the
miscreants, until their distant voices told
her they were down by the river Not COM
ing when she called them, the squaw found
that they were 5unwillingly disobedient
Their feet were stuck fast in the wet clay
of the river bank With great difficulty she
got them back to the tent Then they all
laughed at their footprints in the clay for
deep holes remained wherever they had
stepped.


The band of Indians left camp before gun
rise the next morning. The squaw with her
boys and papooSe were soon far away.
During the hot summer that soon followed
the same band returned to the river they had
left. The two little. boys ran down to the
river bank. No rain had fallen since their
last visit and they easily found their foot
prints in the clay: These had dried until
they were as hard as stone. They called
their mother to look at the holes. She took
some clay In her hands, wet 1t in the river,
then shaped 1t like the hollow stone she
used for cooking. She dried 1t in the sun.
and when 1t was hard proudly showed her
dish to the old chief. He then ordered
all the squaws to go and do likewise but
they all soon realized that their dishes
would not hold water, and broke easily.


One day a squaw wanted to save some
fire. which was very hard to get. Not hav-
Ing anything to keep 1t in, she seized one
of the clay dishes which had been abandon
ed as useless. The hot Goals baked the
dish, and she later discovered that it would
not break.


Wonder Of wonders 1t also held water!
Calling the chief and the other squaws
around her, the Indians realized that they
had learned how to make clay dishes in
the right way.

NEW YORK, March 11.-Realizing
that their fight against the INTERIOR
ough company has been lost, the old
employees of the subway and elevated
railways today crowded the offices OF
the company, seeking their former po-
sitions. Some 5000 men applied for re-
instatement, but not more than 500
were accepted, the officials claiming to
be satisfied with the men who had
enabled them to break the strike, and
announcing that in future the rules
as to sobriety would be more strictly
adhered to.


All applicants were notified that they
would have to pass the physical ex-
animation and go to work as new men,
which means that those who went on
strike would lose their seniority and
the increased pay that they had won
for length of service. Messrs. Jencks
and Pepper, the strike leaders, ad-
mitted that the strike had been lost
and advised the men to get back their
positions If they could. AS for them
selves, the officers said that they
would not again work for the company.


Mr. Jencks held the press responsible
for the result, contending that the
papers had aroused hostile sentiment.
The strikers bitterly denounce their
leaders, saying that the men were de-
ceived by them.

BY Associated Press.


NEW YORK, Aug. 22.-The steamer
Athos, seventeen days late, with eight
passengers, a cargo Of rotten bananas,
and the bones of half eaten sharks on
board to Indicate the perils Of her
voyage, arrived off Scotland lightship
last night.


On July the Donald Steamship com.
pany's steamer Athos left Port An
tonic, Jamaica, for New York, six
days voyage, with provisions in plenty
for this short period. Three hours out
of port an eccentric rod on the engine
broke, and from that hour until last
Sunday, proceeding sometimes only an
hour day under her own steam, the
Athos drifted at the mercy Of storms,
in constant danger of famine, without
drinking water and receiving supplies
from time to time off passing vessels
until, on August 20, the disabled
steamer gave up and signaled the
steamer Altai for tow. This steamer
brought the Athos to New York.


The trouble was with the engine.
From July 30 to August one to two
breaks daily were recorded The log
shows that the delay was only thirty
minutes long on August s. Two days
corded. Cinnamon on board attempted
to eat the sharks, but the meat made
them i'll and the fish were thrown into
the sea.


On August the disabled steamer
sighted the Adirondack and signaled
"All well on board" but on the 10th
the last tank of water was opened and
was found to be tainted with the Juice
of rottlng bananas. Some dolphin were
caught two days later, and on August
13 the incipient famine was further re-
lieved by the steamer Montevideo,
which supplied provisions.


For nearly week, between August
10 and August II, the engines shaft
was useless and not only was the
steamer forced to drift about while re-
pairs were under way, but for two days
of this period a great storm and high
seas broke over the helpless steamship.
flange broke and the Athos abandoned
an attempt to reach New York under
her own steam, after twenty days of
continuous accidents. 1t was decided
to accept the offer of tow. This did
not come for two days, during which a
second food famine was averted by the
steamer Vera, which came alongside
the Athos, supplying eatables and
drinkables. Worse though even than
the dangers Of the sea and famine, the
passengers say, was the odor Of the
decayed banana cargo.


At Scotland lightship last night the
tow line broke, as last chapter in her
long series of accidents, and the Athos
could not repair the broken line in the
dark but anchored for the night, while
the Altai brought her passengers to
quarantine. Today tugs were sent out
to bring the Athos into port.


Passengers Of the Athos on landing
today reported that the famine caused
small mutinies among the ships crew
of eighteen Cinnamon. Trouble first
started among the coolies over the
dearth Of tobacco and rice. A negro
helper was stabbed during one of the
fights but the officers and passengers
were not seriously menaced. At one
time the only water to be had was
ocean brine which had been boiled and
condensed. One swallow a day to each
person was all this process furnished.

NEW YORK, August 12.-John Hartigan,
laborer, was blown into the air with a
geyser of steam, which rose Ave stories high
from an exploding steam pipe ten feet be-
low the pavement of Vesey street today
Other workmen were severely burned and
the lives Of passersby were endangered.


The explosion occurred from a leak In a
six-inch steam pipe at the bottom of a ten
foot excavation, where Hartigan was dig
ging. He was the only man at the bottom
of the pit when the pipe burst. Along with
quantities of gravel and scantlings. which
rose with the first jet Of steam. and rained
down over the street, Hartigan's form was
plainly seen.


Lay in the scalding Steam.


He was blown completely out of the hole
and fell against hydrant with force that
broke his right leg. For five minutes he
lay in the scalding steam. while passersby
hid from the falling debris and hot steam
in nearby stores. Hartigan was finally res
cued by two felow-workmen, Thomas
O'Mara and Max Engel. who were at the
edge of the excavation when the explosion
occurred. and both of whom were painfully
burned. They ran from the hole until the
worst Of the explosion was over


Hartigan was taken unconscious to the
hospital, and revived by StimulantS, after
which he received the last sacrament.


The steam geyser spouted for several min
utes before the supply valve closed.


Hartigan died about two hours after be-
ing taken to the hospital.

ST. PETERSBURG, Aug. From a
member of the imperial encourage, the
Associated Press learns an interesting
fact. showing how quietly preparations
were made for the meeting between
Emperor Nicholas and Emperor Will
liam.


Though the German emperor had
been exchanging kilograms with EN-
peror Nicholas for three days before
the meeting, the party on the imperial
yacht Hohenzollern were unenlightened
as to their nature and retired on Satur-
day evening in ignorance of the forth
coming event. During the night EN-
peror William personally ordered the
course of the yacht to be changed to
the eastward. When the surprised
guests noted the new direction of the
Hohenzollern in the morning, Emperor
William jovially broke the news that he
would dine with the Russian emperor
that evening. Dinner was prepared on
the Polar Star, the Russian imperial
yacht, but the Hohenzollern failed to
arrive in time, and finally Emperor
Nicholas and his party dined without
the expected guests.


When the Hohenzollern did arrive and
the German emperor and his suite had
boarded the Polar Star, Emperor Mich
olas greeted him, saying: Thou art
too late. We have already dined,"
using the familiar German thou"
Emperor William replied laughingly
and the incident gave the keynote to
the informality which marked the meet
ing of the sovereigns and their suites
throughout.

ST. PETERSBURG, Feb. 18.-At the
moment a few old Eastern coins are in
finitely more valuable to the Czar than
all the gold in the Siberian mines,
which are his. For Nicholas firmly be-
lieves that these coins are blessed
amulets, which protect him from all
harm. and most particularly from death
at an assassin's hands.


Never is the Car without the coins.
He has more confidence in them than
in his soldiers bayonets to safeguard
him when he goes among his people.
The silver pieces jingled in his pocket
during the ceremony of blessing the
waters Of the Neva, when was fired the
charge of grapeshot which might have
wiped out the whole Romanof dynasty
-Czar, Czarina, Grand Dukes and all.
In the shower of bullets his Majesty
displayed the greatest sangfroid.


The head of the Greek church OBJ
tained the coins from Bernhard Tut
nauer. a Jew, who lives at Radautz,
town in the Austrian crownland Buko-
vina. Three years ago wonder-work-



nauer's guest. Departing, the rabbi re-
warded the hospitality shown him with
the coins. saying:


My son, although these pieces may
seem a poor gift, they will protect those
far greater than you in time Of dan
GER


Lately, for three nights in succession,
the vision Of Alexander III, the Cars
father, appeared to Tutnauer and told
him the rabbits coins would shield any
one who wears a crown from a violent
death. Tutnauer sent the coins to the
Russian Charge d'Affaires at Vienna
with a message which vividly described
his triple dream.


Much impressed, the Charge forward
ed the coins to his Majesty, who, most
gratefully, acknowledged their receipt.
The few faithful who surround him re-
joice that the coins have lent him con-
fidence. They do not seek to disabuse
him of his belief in their protecting
power


Before the Czar put the coins in his
pocket they had been tested at the
Imperial Laboratory for any insidious
poison that might lurk in them.


So the superstition which enthrals
the Gar as completely as the lowliest
Of his moujiks has manifested itself
again. Now he is reconciled to the loss
of Zenobia Golaczyi the beautiful little
woman from Poltava, the charming
mystic who conJured pictures for him
on a screen. The dreamy prophecies
interpreted the meaning of the dull,
confused, waving masses of light she
summoned to please herself and her
imperial patron Her seances gave
him hope; she showed him the shad-
owy Japanese fleeing before dazzling
Cossacks.


UnluckiIy for herself, the Golaczy
was not content to deal alone with the
Cars fears and hopes. She promised
TO tell him what the Grand Dukes
were plotting. what his Ministers were

If all goes well we shall be able in less

When the French found a year ago that.
with their picked camels trained to the
habit of fast travel. they could cross the
desert in one-third the time consumed by
every explorer who had made the journey
they decided that the time was ripe to
build telegraph line across the desert The
governor general Of Algeria said II was
a good idea, the French minister of colonies
agreed with him and the work began


They have stretched the wire from the
Mediterranean across the sandy waste down
to the Tuat oases, region that few
years ago had no use for white men and
would cheerfully kill any Christian who
should venture within reach. The French
are just now selecting the route south to
the Ahaggar mountains, where the bandit
Tuaregs live when at home.

YoNxERs. July 30.-An excursion party
on two barges towed by q tug came peril
ously near being dashed on the rocks at
North Yonkers this evening during storm.


The quick work Of the Joseph Peene, sr..
a Yonkers tugboat, which went to the
rescue, alone prevented the disaster.


The excursion was under the management
Of THE Two Sergeants, Hoboken organi-
zation. They had the tug Neptune and two
barges of the Meyers Navigation Company.
1t was after O'Clock when they cast on
from Rverview Grove. opposite Yonkers.
Soon the engine on the tug stopped sud-
denly. Every effort to start it was futile.
Meantime the two barges and the tug drifted
toward the Yonkers shore. The captain
whistled for help and many small river
craft responded.


James Cunningham Of ls2 West Four
teenth street and B. Plumacher of,sA East
Fifty-ninth street, New York. with party
were among the first to reach the barges,
and they were asked to speed to Yonkers
for a tug. which they did. Small river
boats took large number Of people from
the barges and landed them at Yonkers.
where they took the train for home.


The Peene made fast to the barges
and pulled them out into the river when
they were within 100 yards Of the rocks.
After over an hours drifting the engine Of
the Neptune was repaired, and the ex-
cursion proceeded to New York.


The captain Of the tug refused to give
his name or to say what caused the accident.
People on the barges declared that the
hawser broke and, becoming entangled In
the propeller disabled the engine.

NEW YORK, Feb. 5.-Ice foes COM
pletely filled New York harbor today,
rendering the passage of vessels into
and out of the port slow and difficult
In the Narrows the ice pack was so
dense that even the powerful trans
atlantic liners had trouble in forcing
passage. One of the serious results
of the presence of vast foes in the
lower bay during the past four days
has been the breaking and carrying
away of vast numbers of spar and can
buoys in the various ship channels
Captains of coastwise steamers and
Sandy Hook pilots have reported a
| number of narrow escapes from
grounding caused by the displacement
of buoys. Capt. Shepard of the light
house board said that the displace-
ment of .buoys by ice during the week
was unprecedented in the history of
the department, and that the condi-
tions of navigation into and out of the
port are the most dangerous that have
ever existed.


All the steamers of the Sound fleet
arrived safely today, although several
hours late. Their captains reported
that heavy ice was encountered
throughout the Sound and that naviga-
tion was barely possible. On several
occasions the fleet of New Yorl-b bound
steamers was compelled to unite and
attack the ice in wedge formation.
Owing to change in the wind the
North and East rivers were compare
lively clear of ice during the day, and
the ferries were operated with little
interruption.

YULE BY THE INGLE.
Like hopes faint-faltering from the lip
The last leaves drop from off the briar;
Where now the shriveled, ashen hip
Shows once the red rose lit it's fire: : @
But by my genial ingle CLOVIS


Her cheek-the summers fairest rose!
The garden copse is reft Of song;
No meadow choir sulutes the sun;
The wan night long, the white day long,
Pale Silence keeps its orison;
But where my ingle sheds its cheer


Her voice-sweet autumn's own hear!
The branches writhe against vault
With tattered vapory streamers strewn,
Where outcast winds make mad assault,
Blurring the vespers of the moon;


But by my ingle, in her eyes,


see spring hyacinthine skies!
So all the year meets at the Yule,
Transmitted by Loves wonder art;
His glass, as doth magic pool,
Make rime and bloom seem one at heart;


Yule by my ingle means for me


The crown of LIES felicity!
Clinton Scoliard, in December Smart Set.

Farrell and his daughters left Plymouth

Train Near NEUTRALITY-SUSPICIOUS. Boss

HARRISBURG, Pa, July s.-One hundred
pounds Of Contractor a. 8. Krbaugh's
rock powder exploded this morning, directly
across the Susquehanna road from the scene
Of the big wreck Of May IL, when . carload
Of the same contractors explosive blew
up Pennsylvania Railroad express train
and killed twenty-three passengers. The
explosion Of to-day killed eight and injured
two. All the victims were employees Of
Kerbaugh and were at work on new
Pennsylvania freight line across the river
from South Harrisburg.


The dead are: James Wiseman; shooter
boss. Of ss Front avenue, Buffalo, N Y;
Arthur Green and Robert Thompson,
negro steam drillers; Frank Mulluch,
Slav. and three Italians and a Slav who
were known only by numbers. The injured
are William Reed and G. C. Miller.


The men were preparing for what is called
big shoot which consists OF series Of
blasts, the charges being set of stimuli
taneously. Five holes had been filled with
powder and the men we're at work on the
sixth when it -let 60" Probably sand got
into the hole and the iron bar with which
the men were tamping down the charge
caused spark by scraping on the sand.


John Shelter, a fireman working about
some donkey engines $50 feet away, says
There was one shock. then two heavier
shocks, and after that all could see was
shower Of falling rocks and fragments Of
bodies" Shelter was turned over three
times by the explosion. An Italian water
boy was hurled fifty feet and every stitch
Of clothing torn from his body. j. c. Miller,
sitting 200 feet from the blast, was blown
twenty-five feet. Wiseman's body was
identified only by the fact that he dyed his
hair. One Italian escaped because fellow
workman had playfully snatched his hat
and run with it The owner made after the
hat and got out Of range just in time. The
vacuum was so great that the side of a tool
shed nearby was torn clear out and drawn
twenty feet toward the blast. The explo-
sion shook the country for miles around


A purse belt containing $3.50 was found 100
feet from the scene.

The mysterious woman In blue was ar

Lee, and her home Is at Manhasset, L. l.
She tried to get to President Roosevelt a
half dozen times at Oyster Bay during the
last summer but each time was prevented.
The secret service people found that she had
left her home last Friday for Washington

time she got off the train here. Saturday
night about 10 o'clock she meandered
around outside the White House grounds
and then entered the Enclosure and talked
with an officer near the front Of the execu-
tive mansion for some time. She did not
make her appearance again near the build
ing until yesterday afternoon


Mrs. Lee Is married and her husband has
made every endeavor to prevent her annoy
ing the White House people, but was unable
to keep her from following the President to
Washington.


Mrs. Lee always dresses in blue with a
light colored short coat but the mystery
about her Is that no one knows why she
wants to see the President. She has never
given an inkling of her business and re-
fuses TO tell any one. The secret service
officials and police have put her through
most careful questioning but she will not
give them any satisfaction. She simply
says that she wants to see the President
and that Is all they can get out of her


She has been returned to her home

Not for many years, says an Edin-
burgh correspondent, have the pros

moors this year will provide splendid
sport.

look are not far to seek. To begin with
fairly good stock of birds was left
over from last season on many of the
moors and almost all parts of the coun-

WARRINGTON, Aug. l0.-In view Of the
prospect Of disastrous results to American
manufactures through the decision Of the
German Government TO end the tariff ar
rangement under which the United States
and Germany now operate, President Roose-
welt has decided to propose treaty Of
amity and commerce to Germany.


That President Roosevelt has reached
this decision can be stated on the authority
OF high Government official. The negotia-
tons have already progressed somewhat,
but for months the matter has been at a
standstill, the State Department deeming
it useless to present anything in the nature
OF a reciprocal tariff arrangement to the
Senate Already there are several treaties
before the Senate that apparently never
will be ratified.


But in view Of the Presidents decision
negotiations for an entirely new treaty will
begin. Germany has frequently expressed
its desire for treaty. The new German
tariff goes into effect on March 1, 1905, and
unless some arrangement is made by that
date manufacturers from this country must
pay much greater duty than the products
Of the European countries, with whom
Germany recently concluded treaties.


The exact lines upon which the treaty
will be drawn have not been announced.
Berlin does not desire to renew the present
arran cement, which is no more than an
agreement under which the two Govern
ments have operated since 1870, the German
Government taking over the treaty signed
between this Government and the King Of
Prussia in 1920. That treaty contained
the most favored nation clause and since
1870 this Government has enjoyed tariff
privileges equal to those Of any other coun-
try.


Next March themost favored nation clause
as 1t operates between the United States and
Germany will be a dead letter. the German
Government having 80 informed the United
States.


on Feb. ?? last the Reichstag by adopt
ing treaty of commerce with Russia
concluded the negotiations for seven sim
liar treaties with European countries, in
Guiding Russia. Italy, Rumania, Switzer-
land, Servia and Austria-FIungary. The
treaties grant the products OF those coun-
tries very low rates, which give them great
advantage over American producers.
The German agrarian party insists that
the United States be forced to make a
treaty. and the Government is apparently
following the dictates OF thr agrarians.

RENO, New, April 5.-George Pollock
and Benjamin Pollock, two Humboldt
County cowboys, were arrested at Col
conda. east of here, last night for fight
ing. After they had been in the town


Jail for time they planned escape by
setting fire to the walls. The flames
soon got beyond their control and they
would have burned to death had it not
been for passerby, who gave an alarm
and summoned the Volunteer Fire De-
partment. After much trouble the fire
was extinguished and the two men
were pulled from the ruins unconscious
and probably dying. They are now in
the County Hospital at Winnemucca
and still unconscious. Little hopes are
held out for their recovery That they
were not burned to death is a miracle.

Three members of a gang known

pany. They were charged with petty
larceny, but to-day the charge will be
changed to burglary.

were subsequently arrested.
