Shanghai Dec 1S.-The riot Is suppressed.
Twenty Chinese rowdies were killed, and few
Europeans were wounded. Otherwise the dam
age done was slight.


Police sailors and volunteers eo-operated in
suppressing the riots. One police station was
partly burned, barroom wrecked and a bicycle
store looted. No European was killed. The
streets are now deserted, except for armed pa
trolls, which everywhere.


The riot here was promoted by boycotters on
account of an incident involving the Mixed
Court. The German Consul was stoned, and
the American vice-Consul and several other
foreigners were attacked and injured. The Chi
nese closed their shops when the rioting began.
The local volunteers were called out to restore
order and detachments of bluejackets were
landed from the warships.


washington Dec 1S.-A dispatch received this
afternoon from Consul General Rodgers was
to the effect that all parts OF the city of
Shanghai had been put under martial law, and
that the foreigners all arming. A dispatch
received there from Chefoo said that all was
quiet in that city.


It Is gathered from earlier dispatches sent by
Mr.. Rodgers that the moving causes for the riots
were the anti-American boycott and a general
feeling of hostility toward foreigners. such as



Rodeers's statement was that all business was
SUSPENDED among the Chinese, and that incident
TO the general strike a number Of foreigners
had been assaulted Volunteers had been called
out presumably from the people in the foreign
settlements, whose efforts at maintaining order
were seconded by English marines. The war
ships in the harbor were cleared for action. At
the hour of sending the first dispatch, probably
some time last night two Chinese had been
killed In the riots and the Consul General had
telegrapf1ed for help from American naval ves-
sells.


A later dispatch from the same source re-
ported the continuance of the riotous conditions,
adding that the police stations had been burned
and number of people killed probably about
thirty, including some foreigners No Ameri-
cans however, had been harmed up to that mo
ment and the streets were being guarded by the
volunteers and the naval forces. Mr. Rodgers
added that he expected the American cruiser
Baltimore. which was yesterday at Chin Kiang

Montreal Sept. Fog, stranded vessels and
smoke from forest fires have practically brought
shipping to A standstill between Montreal and
the Gulf of st. Lawrence. Latest reports re-
ceived here to-day from the stranded Allan liner
Victorian at Cape Charles state that she is In
the same position and not drawing any more
water than when she first struck. Andrew
Allan is on the scene with special chartered
steamer and extra assistance was sent UP from
Quebec this afternoon. The passengers have
remained board


The Leyland liner Virginian, which went
ashore Yesterday at Crane Island, below Quebec
day Her agents here say that they still hope
to save the steamer.


Reports from points along the river tell Of
one of the worst fogs and smoke pals in many
years. The forest fires raging for miles along
either shore or the lower st. Lawrence have
spread dense cloud of smoke over the country
which added to the fog makes navigation espe-
ciafly difficult and dangerous. Word reached
the pilots office here to-day that all big liners
were advised TO anchor at Battiscan. above the
stranded Allan liner. while vessels In the lower
river have been advised to move very warily-


The fog and smoke still hang over the river
this afternoon and three Liverpool liners due
here this morning are detained indefinitely
Steamers which sailed from here this morning
are at anchor in the river above the stranded
Victorian, awaiting the lifting of the fog.

little girls. On a bench in Jefferson
Square they saw a dog asleep with
Just the tip of its tail sticking through
the Stats of the seat. The temptation
proved too strong to resist and little
Miss Glass was seized with the desire
to pull the protruding tail of the sleep

bit his tormentor on the lip before she
could get away officer Flynn saw the
accident and carried the child to the
Park Emergency Hospital, where the
lip was cauterized and the little girl
discharged. The dog belongs to Moses

NEW YORK, Dec. 6.--The steamship
Gerty of the Austro-American line,
from Venice, Trieste, Messina and Pa
lermo arrived yesterday with 719 immi-
grants who told story of five weeks
voyage through storms and terrors
which none cares to experience again.


For the better part of a month they
were shut between decks because of
rough weather. They had been fright
ened into at least one panic, a woman
had gone insane from terror, her fellow
passengers said; fire had started down
In the engine space at night; the ship
had been in total darkness; the drink
ing water got salty; passenger was
choked and robbed and death had
claimed three victims during the five
weeks trip.


The deaths were those of a mother
and her new born infant. and boy of
10 who, died of meningitis.

difnculty.

Special to The Herald.


KEN OSHA, Wis, Nov. There was
funeral at st. Georges Roman Cath
olic church this afternoon. Only five
persons were present, but the funeral
was the concluding chapter of one of
the most pathetic Incidents ever brought
to light in Kenosha. The little form
over which the service was read was
that of Adolph Rauer, months old,
the son of an immigrant who had just
come to Kenosha from Germany. Near
the lite white casket sat a woman
sobbing as If her heart would break.
The boy had died in a train near Pitts
burg on Wednesday afternoon and the
mother and father, having no funds
with which to bury the child along the
way, the mother had held the cold and
lifeless form in her lap for more than
forty hours, or until she could reach
Kenosha, where she had friends and
relatives.


The Rauer family had arrived from
Germany on Tuesday and had started
at once for Kenosha. Just after the
train pulled out of Pittsburg the child
was taken with convulsions and it was
evident to the mother that he was
dying. In the terrible presence of death
the mother thought quickly, and when
>he little boy died she made no outcry
but continued to sing to the lifeless
form in order to deceive the passengers.
Later she took clean white dress from
the grip and went into the women's
room of the car and washed the body
and prepared it for burial.


Then she began her long vigil to pre-
vent the train crew from discovering
the secret. The conductor came through
the train. and seeing that the babe had
been still for long time he talked to
,lnv .yonan and her husband. That's
the best baby ever saw" said the con-
ductor, and the mother, with tears in
her eyes simply replied, "Yes, he always
has been good baby"


AS soon as the train reached Chicago
the parents bearing the little corpse
walked across the city to the North
western depot and waited for train to
Kenosha. When the train reached
Kenosha she said nothing to the friends
who met her of the death of the child
but carried it more than a mile to the
new home. Then she broke down. Late
last night the remains were turned over
to a local undertaken and this morning
the coroner issued a permit for the
burial

ODESSA, Nov. g., 6 p. ma tour Of
the city and parts Of the suburbs today
found all quiet Shops that were pill
laged have been boarded up. The
poorer Jewish quarters suffered worst
and the principal streets, with few cx-
ceptions, were untouched. Russian
shops are marked with crosses painted
on the shutters and the private houses
with ikons so as to protect them from
the mobS. Peasants armed with knives
and scythes tried to reach the city
Saturday to loot the place, but they
were driven back by the soldiers.


The casualties in Sundays disturb
ances exceeded 140 and those of the
preceding three days, which have been
verified, number nearly 5000. The plum
dering continued early this morning in
the outlying districts, but today the
city was relatively calm, though the
population is still anxious.


The latest accounts of the devasta-
ton in the Jewish quarter added horror
to the situation. Besides numerous
mills all the bakery shops and nearly
600 homes have been destroyed.


The Jews killed were treated with
revolving barbarity. Heads were bat
tered with hammers; nails were driven
into the bodies, eyes were gouged out
and ears severed. Many bodies were
disemboweled and in some cases PEE
troleum was poured over the sick found
in cellars hiding and they were burned
to death.


1t is alleged that the police and
soldiers every where marched at the
head of the mobs melting them to de-
stroy the Jews by crying: THE Jews
have killed our emperor" and similar
expressions. While the mobs were en-
gagged in the slaughter the soldiers
busted themselves taking the cash and
jewelry, leaving the household goods
to the mobs. The owners of many
houses got rid of the bandits by the
payment of a ransom to the police.


The police prevented anyone from
arresting the looters and prevented the
Red Cross workers from aiding the
wounded, actually firing upon those en-
gagged in this work. A band of students
removed much of the stolen property to
the university while they also took
twelve dead bodies of anti-Jewish dem
onstrators whose relatives today be-
sieged the university, claiming the
corpses and demanding the release cf
those demonstrators who were con-
fined in the university They threatened
otherwise to burn the university ana
kill the professors. Measures were
thereupon taken to transfer these pris-
oners to the regular prison.

TACOMA, March 21.-The death of
Thomas Thurnbow to-day at Garfield
closes another chapter in one of the
tragedies for which Whitman County
is famous.


One Sunday morning in August, 1903,
G.. E. Brown shot Thurnbow on the
streets of Garfield. The bullet struck
his spine and caused paralysis. From
that day until his death Thurnbow suf-
fered untold agonies. For months he
was living skeleton. the dried flesh
dropping from his bones. Thurnbow
and Brown were rival real estate deal
ers.


There was much talk of lynching
Brown when the shooting occurred.
Had Thurnbow died within year after
the shooting Brown would have been
tried for murder. He was tried for
attempt to murder, found guilty and
sentenced to five years in the penitenf-
tiary. Thurnbow's funeral will be one
of the largest ever held in Eastern
Washington.

Thence from the Lake of the Woods, on the

taken through the wilderness and over the
mountains of the wild West to the Pacific
coast.


This boundary between the countries is
marked at regular intervals by pillars of wood
and iron, earth mounds or stone cairns


Beginning at the Lake of the Woods, cast
iron pillars have been placed alternately by
the English and our government, one mile
apart, until reaching the Red River Valley


Those set by our neighbor were brought
from over the ocean. while ours were made in
Detroit. They are hollow casting of pyra-
midal form, eight feet in height, having
base eight inches square and octagon fange
one inch in thickness, with top four inches
square, surmounted by solid cap.

ing One-half of the length Of the pillars are
firmly imbedded in the ground, SO that the
inscriptions on their sides, in raised letters
two inches high, face the north and south, the
first reading, Convention Of London" the
latter October 20th, 1818."


Beyond the Red River, earth mounds and
stone cairns seven feet by eight generally de-
note the boundary line. Whenever wooden
posts are used, they are of the same height
as the. iron pillars, and painted red above the
ground.


Through forests clearing has been made
rod wide, SO that the course is plainly indi-
Gated. Where bodies Of water are crossed.
monuments of stone have been raised several
feet above high tide.


Over the mountains. shafts of granite Ike
grim sentinels guard the way. Altogether the
fixing of the boundary marks was expensive.
but It was well done

, land sealer Neptune; chartered by the
Cana dian Government, left Halifax recently
for Hudson Bay with stores and equip
ments for the Northwest police posts
already established there. Her departure
marks another step taken by the Dominion
to assert her authority over the Hudson
Buy region.


During the last few years Hudson Bay
has been threatening to be the subject Of
an international dispute. Canada claims
the whole region. Yet American whalers
have been the only visitors to that lonely
sea. American explorers have chsrted
much OF the vast northland beyond, and
American capitalists have scented new
Klondike in the wilds Of Labrador and
Ungava.

ing that their Government call halt upon
American aggression 30 that the Alaska
boundary question may not be duplicated
here and the Dominion deprived Of another
substantial slice OF territory by new
arbitration. The Ottawa Cebinet, with
lively recollection OF what ensued after the
Alaskan award, has been doing everything
to demonstrate Canadian supremacy In
the north by despatching expeditions there,
annexing all the lands that surround the
bay and establishing police posts to collect
import duties from all comaIs.

sent up to Hudson Bay and spent twelve
months there. She conveyed an exploring
party under Prof. Low, which annexed all
the lands on the west side Of Baffin Bay
from Cape Resolution to Cape Sabine. and

farthest extremity where the early voyagers

Who bides his time, and day by day,


Faces defeat full patiently,
And lifts mirthful roundelay,


However poor his fortunes be;
He will not fail In any qualm


OF poverty-the paltry dime
It will grow golden in his palm,


Who bides his time.
Who bides his time-he tastes the sweet


OF honey in the safest tear;
And tho he fares with slowest feet,


Joy runs to meet him, drawing near;
The birds are heralds of his cause;


And like never-ending rhyme,
The roadsides bloom in his applause.


Who bides his time.
Who bides his time, and fevers not


In the hot race that none achieves,
Shall wear cool wreathen laurel wrought


With crimson berries in the leaves;
And he shall reign goodly king,


And sway his hand Ger every cline,
with peace writ on his signet ring,


Who bides his time.

Even the hopes OF the most sanguine

Evangelists chorus choirs ministers

cessful, and the result was such as

before.

dent what great throngs of people were

doors were closed there were still hum

the district meetings the buildings were
unable to hold the crowds, and over
flow meetings were held in smaller
churches, where the efforts of local pas
tors met with the same success as the
evangelists were having.

NEW YORK, December 20.-Men forgot
that they were convicts and remembered
only that they were men on Blackwell ISL

oners, marshaled by their keepers into
fire-fghting and life-saving corps, bore
from the flaming floors of the women's
wards 594 frantic women and from the hos
pital beds fifty more.


Starting In the sewing room of the work
house, and from a cause which has not yet
been definitely decided. the fire had reached
a fierce blaze at 2 O'Clock, when 1t was dis
covered. The fire engine On the island
proved inadequate, and call for help was
sent to the city department. Seven engines
we're sent over but were not sufficient to
save the women's workhouse from destruc-
ton. s


On the top floor of the building were calls
for the women, and every one held one or
two prisoners when the fire occurred. These
women became frantic with fright, and
were soon choking with the dense smoke
that filled all the halls and their cells.


That most of them did not perish is due
to the recent installation of system by
which in emergencies every cell In tier
can be opened simultaneously with all the
others.


When the extent and danger of the blaze
became apparent the warden marshaled his
regular fire-fghting force of employees, and
soon were all at work


The flames spread so fast, however, that
this force proved hopelessly inadequate.
Then it was decided to trust to the male
prisoners sense of manhood, and they bore
the test well.


Released from their cells and marshaled
into small bodies, they entered the burning
building and went at the work of freight
ing and rescue with utter disregard of the
danger to themselves The flames were
cracking all about them and they plunged
through the densest smoke when they
brought out in their arms the last of the
women prisoners.


The fire bells and the shouts of the men
at work could be heard all over the island
and in the hospitals and buildings of the
other institutions there was panic, which
was-queted with difficulty by the nurses.
physicians and keepers. The fire was con-
fined to the women's workhouse.

Mrs. Wilson arrived here Wednesday
night and walked to her home. She
had been riding in a warm coach. As

to chill. BY the time she reached home

mouth was wide open and she was un-

unusual appearance. She was unable

plight. Physicians were called and to-
day reported that she was able to close

Pedro Ontervaris was shot and fatally

morning.


Witnesses to the shooting assert that
Eli Lopez, night clerk at the house,
fired the fatal shot, but no one can be
found who knows how the quarrel
arose, what occasioned it nor why the
shot was fired.


Immediately following the shooting,
Lopez left the house and has not been
apprehended. Several of the roomers
at the house, who say they witnessed
the affair, assert that Lopez was not
concerned in the quarrel between On
tervaris and three other men near the
night clerks desk, and believe he fired
the shot by mistake.


Salina Ives, propritress of the
house, told the police that she heard the
loud and angry words of the quarreling
men and left her room to investigate,
but as she stepped into the hallway
Ontervaris ran toward her and the shot
was fired. Ontervaris fell at her feet.


Ontervars was removed to the re-

Smith operated on him. He was shot
in the abdomen and is in a dying con-
dition. the hospital surgeons giving no
opinion that he will recover.


Francisco Munez and Ben Madriga
are suspected of being implicated in

ing house Immediately after the shoot

guides and trapper named Macdonald.

nomination.. After the party had been
out two weeks, particularly cold wealth
er set in and it was with difficulty it
reached Sturgeon Lake, the point near
est to civilization in the almost unex-
plored territory that stretches away
north. .-~.

many dangers, particularly in making
the crossings of the turbulent rivers,
then running full of ice foes. Mac

glnes sdewise off the track. The
crews of both the freight engines

TOXIC, Jan. 4.-The Japanese cas-

sack raiders at the old town of New
chwang, Niuchiatun and other places
southwest of Liaoyang last Wednes-
day were one man killed and fifteen
wounded. The Russian losses were
more than 300. The Japanese report
that the supplies Of war munitions
stored at Newchwang and Niuchiatun
were not damaged.


GENERAL KUROKTS HEAD
QUARTERS, Jan. IA body of Rus
sian cavalry made raid south this
week for the purpose of harassing
the Japanese lines of communication.
They occupied the old town of New
chwang, whose population is entirely
Chinese. On Thursday, Japanese in
fantry attacked the Russians and
drove them from the town. They left
fifty dead. One Japanese was killed.
The raiders, who crossed the Lao
River into neutral territory, are sup
posed to have numbered about 5000
men. There was some interruption of
railroad communication with the south
yesterday as a result of the raid, but
the damage was Immediately repaired

STOCKTON. June 10.-Judge w. B.
Nutter to-day ordered Maria Josefa
Meza, a lunatic, deported to San Sal
vador. The woman was brought to the
United States only two weeks ago by
her sister, Jesus Maria. Although she
has been a demented person for ten
years. the woman was smuggled past
the immigration authorities in San
Francisco under the pretense that her
peculiar actions were caused by sea-
sickness. Immediately after arriving
here an effort was made to commit her
to the Stockton State Hospital for the
Insane. The San Salvador Consul has
provided transportation for the insane
women and her sister back to San Sal
vador.

Manned and bruised by the contact
of her delicate baby flesh with the
cruel wheels and trucks of a heavy car
little Bertha Dembowski beautiful
five-year-old child, died at the receiving
hospital last night.


Bertha lived with her parents at 42s
Turner street and last night about 2
o'clock, started with her older sister
Anna to take her father, Samuel DEM
bowski, who conducts cobbler's shop
on First street, his dinner.


The children reached the thorough
fare in safety and seeing a car coming
Anna told her sister to wait until it
had passed. Not needing the warning
and jerking her hand away from that
of her sister, little Bertha started to
run across the street.


Just as she reached the tracks of the
Los Angeles Railway company the car
bore down upon her. Confused by
the noise and the near approach of the
car the child became bewildered and
turned first this way and then that
She started to keep on across the
street, then changed her mind and tried
to recross to the starting point.


Before the brakes could be applied
and the car brought to stop the child
had been struck and dragged beneath
the fender. Her hips were crushed
and torn and both legs We're terribly
bruised.


The injured babe was a beautiful, fair
haired child and the pride of the
neighborhood in which she lived. When
she received news of her baby's in
jury Mrs. Dembowski tainted and re-
mained in a comatose state for some
hours.

wolves last night on the road from
Godfrey, Ill. The animals raced along
side the buggy and made repeated eff
forts to leap into the vehicle, but were
beaten back with a buggy whip and a
stick. The animals then attacked the
horse and drew blood repeatedly, but
when the buggy came into the out
skirts of the city the wolves fled.


Mrs Barr drove the horse and ham
died the whip, while Miss Coppinger
used the stick. The wolves deployed on
either side and snapped at the horse.
The first wolf then tried to leap into
the buggy, struck a wheel and was
thrown back on the road.


The other wolf snapped at the
horses flank and drew blood. Tho
whip drove 1t back. It's companion
Joined 1t and both tried to climb into
the buggy.


The frightened horse plunged forward
into a run and both wolves were tossed
to the ground. but the horse did not
stop. Mrs. Barr and Miss Coppinger
say this running fight kept up for
more than a mile.


Nearly dozen armed men. accom-
panied by dogs, have set out in the
woods along the Godfrey road. 1t IS
intended to keep up the hunt until
the wolves are killed.

man who walked into the Bank of Eng
land the other day and laid ten-pound
note On the counter was surprised to hear
the clerk say: I'VE can't cash this. The
note was stopped twenty-three years ago"


Over twenty years back the note was
stopped by clerk then In the employ Of
one of the provincial branches of the Lon
don and County Bank. It had been brought
In by an empioye of one of the banks
clients In order to be paid into the clients
account, with some loose change


BY strange oversight the clerk, after
Jotting down the number of the note and
after counting the change, omitted to take
the banknote. When he discovered his
error note and messenger had disappeared.
Neither was seen again.


The clerk took counsel with a colleague
at the counter. and for the sake of their
own prospects the two young men deter
mined to say nothing about the affair but
to bear the loss themselves. Each paid f5
to make good the loss and stopped the
number.


The man who presented the note for pay
ment the other day had found 1t among the
papers of his father, who recently died.


The two clerks instrumental In stopping
the note were traced, and though both had
left the employ of the London and County
Bank long ago. each has received back his
45 after the lapse of twenty-three years.

The tug William Fl. Yerkes, jr., of this
city had a narrow escape from being lost
in a heavy gale that swept over Chesa-
peake bay in the early part of this week.
The tug had left this city, towing light
barge found for Norfolk, and all went well
until she entered the bay. The gale which
had been blowing in the river seemed to
gather strength as the tug reached the
wider waters of the bay. and off the mouth
of the Rappahannock river it blew per-
feet hurricane. The tug, running before
the gale, was completely overtaken by big
seas that washed completely over her, and
on some of her rolls she would almost lay
fiat on her side in the water. Both Capt.
Bob Brown. the master of the vessel, and
Capt. Jim Marmaduke his mate, were at
the wheel of the tug. and they state that
they expected every roll she made would be
her last. They had removed their shoes
and had made every preparation to save
themselves for they never expected she
would live through the gale. Fortunately
the gale abated and the tug was able to
make better Weather of 1t, and after a hard
battle succeeded in reaching Norfolk and
delivering the barge at her destination I'M
harmed Capt. Brown and Capt. Marina
duke are both mariners OF long experience
on Chesapeake bay, and they state that
this was the worst storm they ever saw
and that they do not care for another eX-
The severe straining to which the tug was
subjected as she rolled and twisted in the
heavy seas split several of the planks form
ing the sides of her pilot house EXcent
for this, the tug passed through the ex-
perience unframed.

Municipal ownership is becoming the
most insistent issue in local politics. The
spontaneity of the issue indicates the deep
seated dissatisfaction with private monop-
oily. The elections In New York, Cleve-
land and Chicago are but political cross
sections OF the country at large The con-
viction has become well-nigh universal that
the franchise interests are responsible for
most of the municipal corruption 1t is
the desire for franchises whose values
run into fabulous figures, that explains not
only the positive corruption. but the indif-
ference of the Detter-tO-do classes and
the heavy burden OF reform These fran
ehises have been appraised at $500 900 600
IN New oTk city; in other large cities they
run into hundreds Of millions Their value
depends upon no labor except the labor
incident to control OF the council. They
are created by grant from the city And
they can only exist through a performance
OF this control. This explains the activity
as well as the corruption In local politics.
These conditions will be corrected through
municipal ownership.


When the city owns it's own franchises
all classes will demand good government
and efficient service. Populate can be
distributed into the countryside Cheaper
hight, water and heat will relieve the poor
OF their most serious burdens, while Incl
dental savings to the community Will be
tremendous.


OF HufIClpdl ownership pays. he net
earnings of the New York water works
amount to S,SOo,0o per year; OF the Chi
CagO water plant. s.. 269 621; the Cleveland
water works, $500, 600 and the Detroit water
works, S3iOOi Similar showings appear
from other cities. Detroit claims that 1t
costs but $50 per lamp TO light its streets
by electricity. New York city earns nearly
a million dollars a year from its docks.
and $4,000 from it's markets. The city of
Cincinnati, which owns the Cincinnati
Southern railway, enjoys a revenue which
will leave the property without indebted
ness in fifty years time. These results but
demonstrate the success of municipal own
ership even under present conditions. But
the financial gain is Incidental. The big
gain is an institutional one


The issue is government by the people or
government by privilege; and the big priv
ileges of our cities are those grouped about
the franchise corporations the companies
supplying transit, gas. electricity and tele-
phone service upon the streets. With these
In the hands of the city, all classes would
be free to work for good government. A
free city will come into existence when all
classes unite in demanding 1t; and class
antagOnism Will only pass away when the
temptations and opportunities which now
exist are removed.

VIENNA, Nov. 1-Extraordinary
scenes occurred this morning in the
death chamber of the late Don Jesus
Zenil, Mexican minister to Austria.


While the workmen were dressing
the apartment appropriately as NOR
tuary-chamber, a series of binding
flashes issued from the electric lighting
apparatus with which the room was
fitted


Instantly the whole salon, which was
richly furnished and hung with tapes
tries and valuable pictures, burst into
flame. and at great danger to their
own lives the workmen managed to
rescue the coffin containing the body.


The flames spread rapidly and several
persons in the house, mostly women,
became panic stricken and were about
to jump from the fourth floor window
when the fire brigade arrived and res
cued them with ladders.


The apartments of the late minister.
with nearly all their costly furniture,
were consumed by the fire. and three
firemen were seriously injured.

The steamship George w. Elder had a tough
experience coming down the coast from
Astoria which delayed her twenty-four hours
in reaching port The Columbia River bar was
smooth when she passed out. but she had only
touched her nose into the deep when she ran
into a heavy sea and a strong head wind.
The hurricane she ran into just before Christ
mas, on her down trip, practically a
summer sea compared with the terrible storm
she encountered on this voyage. The gale was
a furious one. The seas swept her decks from
stem to stern. At times the main deck was
flooded with water foot deep. When little
above Cape Blanco the storm ragged so frriously
that the vessel was hove to for several hours,
and twice she was obliged to slow down. Great
mountains of water constantly poured over
her and swashed down through her ventilators.
She was sixty-six and one-half hours making
the trip whereas her usual time is about
forty -eight hours.
headline: Elder Has Terrible Trip.

FLIGHT OF THE BOILER.


The explosion occurred shortly after
the operatives had settled down to
work for the day. Suddenly and with
out warning the air vibrated with the
roar Of an explosion. At the same mo-
ment the large wooden frame of the
factory quivered and then the rear por-
ton of it collapsed. This section of the
great building had been transformed
into mass Of iron and wood wreck
age, in the midst of which human be-
ings were pinioned. In another mo-
ment flames had broken out in the
debris, and death by fire and suffoca-
tion became the fate of scores of the
operatives.


When the boiler exploded it passed
upward almost perpendicularly tear
ing passage as il went, killing many
on the way. After rising high in the
air IT descended half the distance, and
then, swerving northerly, cut it's way
like some huge projectile through
dwelling house fifty feet away and
pierced another dwelling farther along


Scenes of horror followed the wrench

the rear the three upper floors, weight
ed as they were with heavy machinery
collapsed with a crash that was heard
for blocks. Men and women working
in departments of this section who were
busy at their machines had time but to
turn in an attempt to flee after the
first dull roar, when the flooring sank
beneath them and they were carried to
the ground, crushed and bruised amid
the mass of debris. Many fell into
veritable fiery furnace. In the sections
of the factory which remained stand
ing the operatives We're panic stricken
as they sought escape.


MANY ROASTED TO DEATH.


Many fled down the stairways and
reached the ground. Others ran to the
windows, the fire escapes in many
cases being torn away by the explosion
In desperation many jumped from the
second and third floor windows to the
ground and were dangerously injured.
The crush on the stairWays resulted in
numerous minor injuries.


Scarcely had the rear structure col

up from the boiler pit and reached out

splinters of the wreckage and immedi-
ately afterward with the standing
walls. Soon the entire story was in

women who We're working near the

age and heavy pieces of machinery A

rived to assist the employees who es-

not extricate him. and to help the girls

Boston, June 2s.--Miss Flor ence L.
Phelps, daughter of the late DR.. Phelps
Of Marlboro street, this city. committed
suicide by shooting herself at Weston,
early this afternoon. She was 81 years
old and hal been acting strangely OF late.


Miss Phelps's father was a prominent
physician, and after his death, about
year ago, she and her sister, Miss Della
Phelps. broke up housekeeping and went
to live at a hotel here. This spring they
went to Weston and had been boarding
at a farm run by Mrs. Adeline Hagar


Early this afternoon Miss Phelps started
for a stroll in the woods near the farm
and took revolver with her, as had cen
her ha' it when venturing out alone. Soon
after she had left the house the Hagar family
heard three pistol shots.


When Miss Phelps failed to return
the town constable was notified and he
found the woman's body in the woods
near Summer street Two bullets had
entered her side and the third, evidently
fired last, had penetrated her temple and
caused death.

afternoon while trying to save Charles
Sowensky, a nine-year-old boy who lives
at Kent avenue and South Second street.
Sowensky was on the stringpieoe when he
fell backward into the water. The tide
runs strong at that point and was bearing
the boy away when Weissenbaoh, who was
bathing near the granite pier OF the Williams
burg Bridge, swan to his rescue.


Sowensky had gone down twice when
Weissenbaoh reached him. As Weissen-
bach caught hold Of the boys head to hold
him above water Sowensky got tight grip
with both arms around Weissenbaoh's
neck. Weissenbach tried to free himself,
and while 40 engaged both sank. Weiesen-
bach managed to make his way to the
surface, with Sowensky still holding tightly
to him.

crowd assembled on the South Fifth street
dock and hailed him as a hero. Sowensky

tary executions In Warsaw. From per-
sonal observation here and at LODI, and
from constant telephone communica-
ton with other centers, these reports
can be declared to have been utterly
untrue.

any strike center since February 9.
Everything here Is normal except the
presence of an extra large number of
troops. The strike continues stubborn
ly, but the strikers are orderly. Wher-
ever the men have resumed work they
have obtained better conditions.

ton of false reports of violence lest ii
hinder the amelioration of their posi-

text:
From Harper's Weekly.


The great event at Cheyenne this
year was the remarkable feat of "Will'
Pickett, negro hailing from Taylor
Tex, who gave his exhibition while
twenty thousand people watched with
wonder and admiration a mere man.
unarmed and without device or appli-
ance of any kind, attack fiery, Wild
eyed and powerful steer and throw it
Picket chased the steer until he was in
front of the grand stand. Then he
jumped from the saddle and landed on
the back of the animal, grasped its
horns and brought it to Il stop within
a dozen feet. BY a remarkable display
of strength he twisted the steers head
until its nose pointed straight into the
air, the animal believing with pain
and its tongue protruding in its effort
TO secure air. A gain and again the
negro was jerked from his feet and
tossed into the air, but his grip on the
horns never once loosened, and the
steer failed in its efforts to gore him.
Cowboys with their lariats rushed to
Picketts assistance, but the action of
the combat was too rapid for them.
Before help could be given Pickett,
who had forced the steers noge into
the mud and shut off its wind, slipped
and was tossed aside like piece Of
paper. There was a scattering of cow
boys as he jumped to his feet and ran
for his horse Taking the saddle with
out touching the stirrup he ran the
steer to point opposite the judges
stand, again jumped onto its back and
threw it. Twice was the negro lifted
from his feet, but he held on with the
tenacity of bulldog Suddenly
Pickett dropped the steers head and
grasped the upper lip of the animal
with his teeth, threw his arms wide
apart to show that he was not using
his hands, and sank slowly upon his
back. The steer lost its footing and
rolled upon It's back. completely cover
ing the negro's body with its own.
The crowd was speechless with horror
many believing that the negro had been
crushed; but a second later the steer
rolled to its other side, and Pickett
arose unnjured, bowing and smiling.

BOISE, Idaho, March 2o.-Rendered

ing Miss Ida Roberts used a revolver
to compel her sick sister to arise from
her bed, then captured the S-year-old
daughter of the family with whom she
was boarding, forced the child, the
young woman and another woman into
a carriage, and at the point of the re-
volver rode fourteen miles before her
frenzy relaxed.


This happened at Silver City, re-
mote town, the other day. The little
girls mother entered the room just
after Miss Roberts had displayed the
first signs of violence. She saw her
child kneeling upon the floor with the
maniac school teacher holding the re-
yolver close to her head. The mother
tainted instantly. Then the crazy
young woman ordered a carriage. 1t
was so apparent that she was ready
to shoot the child at any moment that
her demand was obeyed.


Fourteen men mounted their horses
and rode beside the buggy, but did not
dare attempt to rescue the child. One
went on ahead to her announced des-
tination, and when the strange cortege
arrived at this house Miss Roberts was
willing to be disarned. She has been
brought here for treatment.

The following are the principal charges
made by the British statement read before
the Dogger Bank board at Paris yesterday
afternoon:


On the night in question there were not
any warships whatever in the neighborhood
of the fishing fleet, except those of the Rus
sian navy.


No warships had been seen by the fishing
boats since long time previous.


None of the boats making up the fishing
fleet carried any kind of material of war.


No Japanese warship of any kind what
ever was at that moment in the North sea.


There were not any Japanese upon any of
the fishing boats.


The Russian fire continued after their
searchlights clearly showed the vessels were
peaceful fishing boats.


None of the Russian ships gave or even
offered assistance.


The fire killed two men, wounded six,
sank one boat and damaged five others.


The statement concludes that the attack
was without any provocation, upon pacific
fishing boats, pursuing their usual and
rightful aVocation.


The following are the principal points of
the Russian reply:


At about midnight the flagship Kniaz
Souvaroff saw the outlines of two small
with all lights eXtingushed, directly toward
the battle ship.


When the two suspicious boats came
within range of the Russian searchlights
they were recognized as torpedo boats.
Thereupon the battle ships opened fire.


Thereafter number of small fishing
boats, not showing the required lights,
were observed. Precautionary measures
were adopted nevertheless. There was a
strong feeling of danger upon the battle
ships, and the imperious duty of protecting
themselves against the attack of torpedo
boats obliged a continuance of the fire
despite the evident risk of hitting not only
the fishing boats, but also the ships of the
squadron itself, which had arrived within
the zone of fire.


In the meantime the two torpedo boats
drew off and shortly after disappeared
Fearing that some of the fishing boats were
damaged, yet being certain that all danger
from the two torpedo boats or possibly
others was not completely removed Admi-
raj Rojestvensky considered it indispensab BILE
for the entire squadron to continue it's route
without stopping.


Admiral Rojestvensky, while taking into
account the damage caused to inoffensive
fishermen, subjects of neutral power, was
nevertheless compelled to use all the means
in his power to destroy the torpedo boats
which attacked his squadron.

The Curacao. which arrived from Mexi-

six bulls for Topolobampo. The ami

tination. 1neir arrival and the events
which in rapid succession followed
their landing on Mexican soil will not
soon be forgotten in that region Of hot
days and warmer nights.


The bulls were beasts OF high degree.
They were young and spirited. but
while on board the Curacao behaved as
well bred stock should. Their exem-
plary conduct continued right up TO the
time they were ushered, one at time,
into the horse box in which they made
aerial hignt from ship to shore.


The first bull stepped unreluctantly
from his stall into the crude airship.
A gate was closed behind him. Hoist
away" sang Chief oficer Quinn, and
box and bull were yanked high above
the Curacao deck Landed on the
wharf, the gate was opened and Taurus
the First backed on Mexican soil


The rancher TO whom the animals
were consigned had detailed six poems
for the duty Of receiving the bulls
Each armed with a short rope. the
Mexican iaborers stood smiling on the
wharf waiting TO lead away the horned
pets.


There's your bull; take him away"
said Mate Quinn as Taurus the First
stepped clear Of the airship and sur
veyed the neighborhood into which fate
and the Curacao's tackle had dropped
him.


The bull snorted. He paved the
wharf for a second or two and then
tried 70 uppercut with his starboard
horn the man who held the rope which
restrained his liberty. Somebody
laughed. The bul lowered his head
and made a rush at the gleeful one,
whose smile wore off as he and the
bull went sprinting through the crowd

and after throwing a few more scares
into the assembled Mexicans. the bull
started for the hills. Topolobampo's s
main thoroug hfare was deserted in a
second and long before the fear-strick-
en- inhabitants cautiously opened their
doors Taurus the First had disappeared
in a cloud Of dust over the high hill on
the face Of which sits the town

the same informal way, but created
more excitement before taking his de-
parture. With one throw OF his neck
he freed himself from the man with the
rope and then, selecting first one and
then another Of those assembled TO see
the fun, he ran about a dozen Topolo-
bampoites of various shades to the
tops Of lumber piles and into dark re-
cesses beneath the wharf.


He then made a gran rush through
the crowd. leaped from the wharf TO
the beach. marched through the surf
and swan out to the offshore side of
the Curacao. A boat was manned. the
bull captured and towed back to shore.
once on the beach. he resumed the Of

hands dived overheard Turning from
the empty boat, the bull discovered w.
G. Mccormick the stout and smiling
American agent at Topolobampo for
the Mexican and Oriental Navigation
Company.


He's killed" shrieked a woman from
the topmost tier Of a pile Of sugar Nc
Cormick had lost most Of his ward
robe, but still retained some presence
Of mind and. making a record standing
jump landed far out in deep water.


And then the bull. believing in VIC
torious glee, with McCormick's shirt on

west

railroad track. When the Curacao SAIL

name were still at liberty. Taurus the

pasturage to the eastward. Taurus the

Topolobampo.

The Pennsylvania Railroads eighteen
hour Chicago-New York train ran into
freight wreck yesterday while making
seventy miles an hour The incident
furnishes remarkable evidence of the
safety OF fast trains. The fier, instead
of leaving the rails, ploughed straight
through the wreck, and the passengers
aboard, asleep in their berths, did not
know until afterward how serious was
the accident which caused the stopping
Of their train The only person injured
was the engineer OF the flier, who
jumped from his cab and was bruised
Had he stuck to his post, it is likely that
he would have escaped unhurt.


A slower train probably would have
been derailed and many persons would
have been injured. But the tremendous
speed of this flier kept her on the track
and scattered aside the distractions.
The accident resembled in no way that
in which the New York Central's eighteen
hour Chicago train was wrecked, for the
Centrals mishap was due to misplaced
switch, which would have caused as
disastrous smashup TO train making
much slower time.


These two incidents point to the con-
clusion, long ago reached by railway
operators that the fastest trains are the
safest under certain conditions, and are
certainly not more dangerous than the
slower under Others. The public de-
nlands fast trains, and the railways
supply them. For the traveller in one
of the heavy cars that are hauled over
the tracks at the rate of mile in forty
five seconds it will be comforting reflec-
ton that il accident befalls his train his
chances are in no event worse than
those Of the traveller in an accommoda-
ton, and that under most circumstances
they are much better.

MOUNT VERNON Ohio, Nov 2.-Buried
beneath culvert, 200 feet from the spot
where Stuart Person, the Kenyon College
student, was ground to death by train,
the authorities have found three lengths
Of bloodstained rope. and a kind Of absorb
ent cotton also saturated with blood.


County Prosecutor Stillwell expressed the
firm belief that the boy was chloroformed,
the cotton saturated and bound across
his face, and that he was then tied across
the tracks as part Of his initiation into
a college fraternity. The authorities be-
lieve that the cotton was removed later
and the boy left stupefied. On these grounds
the prosecutor will lay the case before the
Grand Jury

President Roosevelts love for his baby
boy. Quentin, and his interest in children,
were brought out in pleasant little incl
dent of the Inauguration days. Charles n.
Teetor is the superintendent of car build
ing company at Hagerstown, Ind. He has
a little son named Lothair, eight years old.
The father had agreed to bring the son 20
the inauguration and the boy felt that he
would like to bring something along to
Quentin the seven-year-old son of the
President. The father suggested fine top,
and proceeded to plan one. He turned the
plans over to the little son. who began
work upon the bronze and steel his father
had given him. With the help of the work
men he soon turned out the finest top ever
given to the son of a President or to any
other boy. One night the little fellow
worked until nearly midnight at the lathes,
and the other hours Were put in before and
after school and on Saturday.


When completed the mechanism was so
delicately adjusted and the friction so little
that the top, with little pulling from a
string, would run twenty minutes. A small
steel plate was also made upon which the
toy should spin. The problem of the two
Teetors was how to reach the little son of
the President They finally secured a letter
of introduction to Colonel Crook, the dis
bursting officer of the White House, and he
acquainted Quentin with the details Quen-
tin, fine little fellow with kind word and
thought for all, went to his father Saturday.
during the rush of the inauguration. and
told him the story The father suggested
that he bring the little Indiana boy to see
him. The two boys met at the White House
Monday afternoon and Quentin arranged
for the visit. taking in both the Teetors.
Although the President was extremely busy.
he spent some time talking to his visitors
and had the little boy spin the top for him.
He made the youngster happy by giving

From Success.


Poverty and failure self-invited. The
disaster people dread often comes to them.
Worry and anxiety enfeeble their force of
mind and so blunt their creative and pro-
ductiye faculties that they are unable to
exercise them properly. Fear of failure or
lack of faith in ones ability is one of the
most potent causes of failure. Many peo-
pie of splendid powers have attained only
mediocre success and some are total failures
because they set bounds to their achieve
ment beyond which they did not allow
themselves to think that they could pass.
They put limitations to their ability; they
cast stumbling blocks in their way by aim
ing only at mediocrity or predicting failure
for themselves, talking their wares down
instead of up, disparagng their business
and belittling their powers.


Thoughts are forces, and the constant
affirmation of ones inherent right and
power to succeed will change inhospitable
conditions and unkind environments to
favorable ones If you resolve upon success
with energy, you will very soon create a
success atmosphere and things will come
your way: you will make yourself sue
cess magnet.

New York, Oct. 14-Alfred G. Vanderbilt and
Paul Sartori. the Italian automobile driver, had
narrow escape from serious injury while rae
Ing in Mr.. Vanderbilt's high-power automobile
over. the Vanderbilt cup course on Long Island
yesterday. They had taken the car out for 2
trial spin end were going at speed of ninety
miles an hour down the narrow road toward
the double reverse curve that is the dread Of
every driver entered for today's race.


To the watching crowd at the turn 1t seemed
that the machine was beyond control and would
shoot straight ahead into the field. Within
thirty yards Of the first sharp curve in the .fS''
was succession Of loud reports and the wheels
skidded across the gutter and against the soft
earth at the side where three big telephone
poles were directly in its path.


By fraction of an inch the machine missed
the first Of them and Its rear wheels actually
grazed the second. Then the machine turned
over on its side and threw its occupants out
into the soft earth.


Sartori was slightly bruised, but Mr.. Wander
bilt was uninjured. They righted the machine
and finished the course.

NEW YORK, July 25.--An unusual
case Of poverty and neglect has been
discovered by policeman on duty in
Tenth avenue. The bluecoat rescued
6-year-old John Mulqueen after the lad
had made his home for two months in
trunk and subslsted largely on
scraps snatched from garbage cans.
The little fellow was as timid as bird
after his pitiful struggle with the
world


Mrs. Mulqueen died six months ago
and the boys father disappeared, leav-
ing John in the care of neighbor. The
building where the latter lived was
condemned two months ago and she
moved away, leaving the child behind.
He sought out the house where his
mother died and found an old trunk
in the alley in which he had formerly
played.


Neighbors saw the youngster crawl
ing in and out, but he fled when they
approached, so they placed food near
the trunk and the boy ate it.


The story finally reached the police
and the young outcast was found nest
ling in pile of old clothing and bro
ken toys which he had gathered in the
alleys.

NEW YORK, March 27.-At a
meeting of the Central Federated
Union resolution has been adopted
calling upon every union to withdraw
from the Civic Federation. 1t was
further resolved to call a mass meet
ing and fight against giving private
corporations any more franchises for
subWays.


Adoption of these resolutions fol-
lowed the reception of reports from a
committee sent by the Central Fed
GRAFTON to confer last week with Pres
ident Belmont of the Interborough
Rapid Transit Company regarding the
unemployment of men who lost their
jobs as the result of the recent strike.


This report showed that Belmont
declined to make any concessions, say
ing that the road was equipped with
all the men needed and that the for
mer employees could only be employed
when vacancies occurred. Recogni-
ton of any union also was refused.


When the delegates representing
more than 10000 workers heard the
report pandemonium reigned. Dele
gates arose and shouted at the top of
their lungs against Belmont. Attack
after attack was made against the
Civic Federation, while some of the
delegates loudly demanded that every
labor leader should resign from that
body.


Samuel Gompers, president of the
American Federation of Labor, who is
vice president of the National. Civic
Federation, was also denounced.

TOXIC. Aug. 6.-Commander Akyama,
who participated in the battle of Japan.
has prepared for publication an extended
statement relating to the great conflict,
and its weight is on the side of gunnery,
the battleships and tactics as against the
destroyer and the torpedo.
He prefaces his statement by declaring
that good gunnery depends mainly upon
the division officers and asserts that the
Russian officers were lamentably lacking
In training.


In the early part of the battle the Rus
slams scored but one hit to three landed
by the Japanese. Under these circum-
stances it may be said that the Japanese
had three or four guns in action to every
one of the Russians, and there was moth
ing very remarkable about the disparity
in the losses


The admiral says that Admiral Rojest-
vensky had been criticized for electing
TO take his chances at the Tushima. On
the contrary, ii was the wisest course
open to him. Tsugara Strait Is long and
narrow, the season was foggy and there
were mechanical distractions. Distance
and coal were against Soya and the time
consumed in reaching that entrance
would have betrayed the design. and his
plight on emerging from Soya would have
been much worse than he might reason
ably hope for at Tushfma.


RegarQlnS the question OF SINKING ar
mored cruisers and battleships by gun
fire. the commander expresses the opinion
that the fact that the Russian ships were
exceptionally low in the water contribut-
ed materially to the result. The Rus
slams carried large quantities of COAL
stores and ammunition. and, thus weight
ed down and in a rough sea, suffered
badly from hits near the water line that
ordinarily would not have been fatal.


The commander says that the battle
did not as some claim, prove the SUI
perfority of arms to armor. He points
out that the newest armor on the Rus
sian ships, notably In the case of the
Orel, was not pierced.


Okyama defends Neboga toff's surrender
from severe criticism. Nebogatoff was
surrounded by twenty-seven ships, in
cluding the most powerful of Togo's feet.
Had the Russian refused to surrender his
ships would have been sunk forthwith.
Five or ten minutes would have sufficed
TO finish the unpleasant task. Any other
course than surrender would have con-
demned the needless death of 1000 officers
and men


Accurate estimates of the actual Rus
sian casualties are impossible to obtain.
but they are far under first estimates.
The rescued and surrendered exceed

room. Suddenly she arose and said,
IT must telephone my husband" and
then she started toward the telephone.


She raised the receiver to her ear

the sound of the voice that was dear
to her. While she stood there she
suddenly showed symptoms Of col
lapse and then, without a sound
slipped to the floor.


Her friends ran to her and picked
her up but death was instantaneous

noon at Pierce Brothers undertaking
rooms and heart failure was the ver-

icating their new joss house and driv-
ing the devil from the s;.cred precincts

The celebration was one of the most
gorgeous ever held In the Celestial
district For more than two hours

and Yung Wo societies paraded the
streets and in a fitting manner bade
the devil make a getaway forever.


The magnificent parade started from

of march was formed the pageant
swung down Stockton street, and be-
fore it ended every thoroughfare and
alley of Chinatown was visited, while
the multitude cheered and gave thanks
to Buddha.


Every Chinaman of consequence
walked solemnly behind an American
band that discoursed all kinds of mu
sic. There were Chinese musicians ga
lore, tomtom players, cymbal operators
and others who made hideous noises on
several weird looking devices. The dis
trict was in an uproar while the parade
lasted and citizens were attracted to
the scene from all parts of the city.


Thousands of dollars worth of fire.
works were exploded as the marchers
solemnly wended their way along the
streets and through the alley ways.
The paraders sang and yelled till they
were sure the devil had betaken himself
to other climes. Tnen they went to the
joss house, where the ceremonies of
dedication were enacted.


The exercising began about noon and
lasted for several hours. The place
was ablaze with glory. Lights repre-
senting all the colors of the rainbow
glistened brightly through the Oriental
ornaments, and the odor of the punk
and burning incense rose till it was
waited to- nearly every corner of the
Celestial quarter.


All the prominent members of the
two societies were called on for
speeches and they all responded, while
the onlookers and those who partici-
pated in the festivities looked on and
chartered with a sense of satisfaction.
The high priests and other officials.
gowned in robes ablaze with all the
colors and splendors of the Orient, were
prominent in all parts of the house and
Joined in with the rest in chanting and
giving praise.


The ceremony was followed by a
sumptuGus banquet, where more
speechmaking and glorification were In
order. The new joss house is one Of the
finest in Chinatown. and with 1t are as
sociated many of the most prosperous
and influential of the Celestial popula-
tion.

ST. PAUL Mimi, July 22.-The journey
of Baron Komura and the other japanese
peace commissioners eastward from Seattle
has been somewhat in the nature of a tri-
umphal progress


At almost every station throughout Mon
tana hundreds of Japanese, of whom great
numbers are employed by the Great North
ern railway, welcomed them with hearty
"banZais," with the waving of Japanese
and American flags and, at White Fish,
Montana, last night with elaborate dis
play of fireworks. Baron Komura has en-
joyed his trip exceedingly, the somewhat
trying heat of yesterday having given away
to perfect weather.


The party was much impressed with the
magnificence of the mountain scenery, the
baron being especially delighted with the
Kootenai canyon. At Malta little crowd
of Japanese workmen greeted the commits
sioners by waving an immense national flag
which they had made from white cotton
cloth, the emblem being painted with san
culinary grease paint


In reply to a telegram sent him extending
the hospitality of Minnesota and its capital
city upon their arrival here Baron Ko-
mura replied that, while gratified by the
courtesies offered, the party felt compelled
to decline special entertainment.


They had been travelling since July and
were much in need of rest For this reason
the dinner which had been arranged for
the party upon arrival here tomorrow was
abandoned and the envoyS will rest quietly
at their hotel until $40 In the evening, when
they leave over the Burlington for Chicago.

TOXIC, Feb. 1.-The Austrian steam
ship Siam, bound for vladivostok from
Cardiff with coal, was seized off Hok-
kaido Island yesterday.


The Emperor has issued rescript to
Field Marshal Oyama's army thanking
the troops for defeating a superior Rus
sian force in the recent battles. Oyama,
responding, says the men fought des-
perately day and night in intensely
cold weather.


Field Marshal Oyama reporting yes
terday said that the. Russians bonn
barded his center and right wing on
January 80 and sent small bodies of in
fantry to attack the Japanese outposts,
where they were repulsed. On the same
day heavy Russian guns fiercely sheiled
Piyentai and Chenchiehpao.


On January 81 the Russians lombard
ed Chenchiehpao, Lapati and Litajen-
tan, and two companies Of infantry at
tackled Chenchiehpao, advancing from
the south end, near Peitaitzu. The
Japanese repulsed them.


On January 80 two companies of Rus
sian infantry unsuccessfully attacked
Yatzupao, two miles northwest of
Chenchiehpao, and two battalions of
Russian infantry and a regiment of
cavalry failed in an attack on Tu-
taitzus


Field Marshal Oyama in reporting the
wounding OF Lieutenant General Mist
chenko, of which he had learned from
Russian prisoners, characterized Gen.
eral Mistchenko's attacks upon the
Japanese flank as brave.

ship February g. The immediate naval

penditure in the construction of the

CHICAGO, December 26-Holding up
crowded Ashland avenue electric car at
Seth street last night six armed men fired
a score of shots through the windows and
roof. and were engaged in robbing the pas
sengers. including several women and chill
dren, when the trolley pole was removed
from the wire by the conductor and the
bandits were left struggling in the dark
ness.


After battle In which the invaders were
pitted against the men passengers and the
car crew, and in which several persons
were trampled upon In the frantic rush that
was made for the exits. a wagonload of
policemen arrived and five of the robbers
were captured. The prisoners gave the
names Of Edward Lenehan, Edward Hig-
gins, c. Murphy. William Starr and Michael
Houlihan. They were all severely bruised
and scratched.


Two. men boarded the car at 66th street.
They leaped to the front platform, and,
holding revolvers at the head of the motor
man, James Callahan, they forced him to
stop the car. Four accomplices then got
on the rear platform. and while one of them
covered James Link, the conductor, with
his weapon, three men entered the car.


Everybody hold UP your hands. We
want your money, and will shoot the first
man who tries to stop us, said the leader
of the band.


Fired Through Windows and Roof.


Evidently hoping to thoroughly brighten
their intended victims before risking the
wholesale robbery. the trio fired repeat edly
through the windows and the roof. Several
women tainted and children cried in terror
When the uproar and confusion were at
their height the conductor striking away
the arm Of the man who threatened his
life, pulled the trolley rope, and the in
terror of the car instantly was plunged in
darkness.


Callahan, the motorman, gave battle to
the two men on the front platform. He
struck one of the robbers a blow in the
face, staggering him. He followed up his
advantage by lifting the controller handle
and bringing it down upon the bandits
head The injured man fell to the street,
but arose and fed. His companion went
into the car to the aid of the three men
who were engaged in hand-to-hand fight


A passenger who escaped from the car
informed the police, who came in patrol
wagon, entered the and drove the rob-
bers from it at the points of their revol-
vers. The bandits exchanged shots with
the policemen, but were overpowered.

TACOMA, Feb. 12.-Charles W.
Cook and Mrs. Rita Wolfenden have
lived through an almost unbelievable
experience. They are now at Kayak,
Alaska, recovering their strength after
gcing nine days without food, other
than the flesh of their small dog. Six
OF these days were spent at sea In an
open whaleboat, the seams Of which
opened, necessitating constant bailing.


Cook and the woman left Yakataga
for Kayak to overhaul two men who
had robbed them of $500. The boat
began leaking, but before they could
reach shore they were blown to sea by
terrific wind, which continued six
days. Their food was spoiled by salt
water. A drenching rain fell most
of the time. Becoming delirious, Cook
jumped overheard, but Mrs. Wolfen-
den seized him by the sweater and
pulled him back into the boat. Cooks s
delirium continued for Two days. when
Mrs. Wolfenden became delirious.


On the evening of the sixth day they
were blown ashore at Cape st. Elias.
The boat struck rocks and was wreck
ed. The couple waded ashore, fol-
lowed by the dog. They built fire
with difficulty and roasted seaweed,
but it gave them no strength. The
nearest habitation was White Head
Point, twenty miles distant. They
finally killed the dog. eating Its roasted
flesh without garnishment. Two days
later they were able to walk to White
Head.

NEW YORK. June LA short, fat, yell
low dog and second cabin passenger
delayed the departure Of the crack
French liner La Touraine fifteen minutes
to-day. The pups master was aboard
the liner, but he hadn't the slightest in
tention OF taking his dog to Europe. AS
soon as the master, who was a we'll
groomed Italian, accompanied by a dark
haired girl, presumably his wife, caught
a glimpse OF the animal following him
he dived after the brute and hustled it
down the gangplank.


Meanwhile the gong sounded for the
ship to start. The Italian hurried up the
gangplank, but the dog was close at his
heels. Back and forth he went with the
animal four times. while the big ship
waited. Finally the second steward
grabbed the cur by the hind legs and
hurled him ashore while the gangplank
was being drawn In.


The vessel moved out into the river, and
the poor dog looked wistfully after the
master who had SO shamefully deserted
him.

Another great audience crowded the
Grand Opera-house last night From
the proscenium boxes the view of the
magnificent audience was a picture of
rare beauty. White seemed TO be the
favorite shade for the fair sex and
that color predominated. The boxes
were all filled with lovely women in
magnificent gowns. Jewels sparkled
from swanlike necks and blazed in
brilliant tiaras.


Applause and recalls were the or
der of the evening. Everybody took
a hand in appiauding the great artists.
The enthusiasm was general from the
front row of the orchestra to the last
row of the top floor.


In the foyer between the acts a
general handshaking took place.
Everybody was congratulating himself
and his neighbor that he and she were
there. No such another lively and
enthusiastic atmosphere has pervaded
the great marble hallway since this
season of brilliant opera began.
Everybody liked the music of the
opera and they liked the great artists
who interpreted it. There was but one
sentiment and that was of delight.
The opera and its splendid rendition
struck great sympathetic chord and
no more delighted audience ever sat
within the walls of the Grand Opera
house.


La Gioconda' will be repeated for
the farewell performance of the sea-
son on Saturday night.

FRESNO, April 17.-While preparing
to take a picture of a rattlesnake yes
terday Miss Henrietta Savage of Clovis
was struck by the reptiles mate and
it was only the thickness of her stock
ing that prevented the venomous rep
tile from sinking it's fangs into the
calf of her leg.


Miss Savage went for Sunday out
ing on the San Joaquin River with a
party of girl friends. They lunched at
Lanes Bridge and soon afterward the
young lady saw a huge rattler summing
itself in the sand. She stepped forward
without fear and was about to snap
the camera when she heard a warning
rattle at her feet! The girl stepped
back in time to see a yellow body flash
through the air. The snake had mis-
calculated the distance and the fangs
only caught in her thick woolen stock
ings. The plucky girl knocked the rep
tile off with one foot and then killed
it with her parasol.


After the danger was all over Miss
Savage became deathly sick and was
delirious for several hours.

PINEHURST, N. c., April s. 1905.


Championship tournament week has with
in the past few years come to be recognized
as one of the merriest of the season from
social standpoint, for the hotels all keep

dances parties and entertainments, all In

past week has been notable, and dances at

the Berkshire and Harvard, numerous IN
formal affairs, together with afternoon tea
and music at the club house, haYe proven
most delightful


The special outdoor feature of the week
was equestrian contest held Monday
morning, the program including drill OF
cavalry movements and gymnastics, saber
head-cutting, lance and ring contest rib
thus E. Allen Of Newton Center, Mass. won
the mems, and Mrs Leonard Tufts of Med
ford Mass the womens prize.


Picnic parties are very popular, and hard
" a fine day passes that one or more merry
groups does not spend the day at some
nearby point, lunchng beneath the pines.


Spring is now well established and the
air fragrant with the odor of peach, wis
terra and dogwood blooms, and musical
with the notes of the hooking birds and
other songsters.


The largest number of April guests in
history is assembled here, departures are
few, and many are coming to remain until
we'll into May for the beauties of the
spring months are becoming more and more
appreciated each year.

INDIANAPOLIS, Ind. July 2l.-George-
town. a village Of Floyd county, was visited
by cloudburst this afternoon. and for two
hours the place was almost completely
submerged. Water stood four feet deep on
Main street and in lower parts Of the town
the houses were under water, while In other
parts the food reached to second story
windows.


The downpour was so sudden and came
with such force that there were many mar
row escapes. but it is thought that all the
people escaped from the town to the higher
ground Immediately surrounding, Sew
eral houses were moved from their founda-
tons by the force Of the food and the stocks
Of goods In all the stores were more or less
damaged. thus causing a heavy money
loss.


The water from tho cloudburst had not
subsidized before Little Indian Creek, which
runs through the town, came down with
a terrific roar and again flooded the place,
the water running through Main street
like a millrace and extern ding over the
entire town. Tons OF hay, farming imple-
ments and many small outhouses were
borne down on the crest Of the torrent.
and the entire country east Of the town
was flooded. All reports indicate that the
property loss will be very great.

SAN FRANCISCO, Feb. 1.-The SUI
preme court decided today that deed

for mineral purposes. The point was
raised in a suit over mining claims in
Amador county. The Central Eureka
Mining company was conducting oper-
ations under a mineral land patent

property attempted to work the same
ledge. An injunction was sought
against the new arrivals. The amount
involved amounts to about 100000

it's land to James and Eliza Toman
for agricultural purposes. The latter
Immediately laid claim to all the land
within their boundaries clear to the
center of the earth. The East Central
Eureka Mining company was formed
to work such part of the old ledge as
lay between the Tomans' lateral
boundaries.


The supreme court says the original
concern has the right to work out its
leads wherever they may run and that
the Tomans may have the full enjoy
ment of their land for agricultural
purposes alone.

Joined the Mormon church. They tray
eled with the Mormons thru Ohio,
Illinois and Missouri, and made the
overland journey to Utah with the first
Mormon pioneers in 1947. Their early
life in Utah was characterized by the
adventures that came to other pioneers

to change their residence.

old to care for, drove team from the
Missouri river to Salt. Lake in l947,

assisted her husband in building log
cabins, digging water bitches, sowing
crops and performing other manual Ia
Dor. Her husband died many years ago
and since that time Mrs. Woolf had
lived at the homes Of her sons, six of

Marquette, Kan, May 10-Twenty-
nine lives were lost and forty-four
people were severely injured by a tor
nado which struck this town at mid
night Monday night and cut clean
swath 100 yards in width through its
entire length. Coming as it did, the
people were caught without a mo-
ment's warning. A heavy rain storm
had preceded the wind and after the
tornado passed a scene OF complete
desolation followed.


The tornado broke upon the town
with great force, wrought its terrific
havoc within few minutes time and
continuing on into the rich farming
country north OF Marquette, caused
further damage.


In Marquette many residences were
completely demolished, the wreckage
being carried away entirely, while
others were picked up bodily. moved a
short distance away and dropped to
earth.


Many of the victims were killed as
they lay asleep. Others, manned and
bleeding awoke to find themselves
buried in the wreckage of their former
homes.


Monday afternoon had been hot and
oppressive. the atmosphere loaded
with electricity. Later in the evening
terrific rain storm broke over the
town. The rain continued to fall in
torrents until 11;55 last night, when
the tornado struck. Within less than
five minutes it had wrought its terri
BILE work and passed on. Telegraph
and telephone wires We're carried
down and it was several hours before
the outside world could be apprised
of the plight of the city.

Special Gable Despatch TO THE Sun.


SINGAPORE, June ?6-The captain OF
the British steamer Ikona, which was sunk
by the Russian converted cruiser Terek,
ascribes her sinking merely to the fact
that she carried rice. He vainly protested
TO the Russians against destroying his
vessel, After the crew, mails and pro-
visions had been removed from the steamer
the Russians exploded dynamite cartridges
in her engine room. This failed to sink
her. and they then bombarded her with
quick firing guns for two hours. The firing
lasted until dark.


The Terek stood by, intending to finish
her work in the morning, but the Ikona
sank during the night. The Russians
opened the mail bags, took some letters
from them and then resealed them.

four children when the flood came in

4:5o p.m.-Shortly after noon an
untimed dispatch was received here
reporting that complete anarchy
reigned at Odessa. The inhabitants
were panic stricken, and were hud-
died together in the houses. The
streets were filled with frenzled
workmen fighting the troops. The
warehouses, quays and some of the
shipping in the harbor were in
flames.


The correspondent of the Asso-
ciated Press who forwarded this dis
patch had to make his way to the
telegraph office through dense
smoke, which covered the city like
a pail. He heard volleys every few
minutes. In the darkness the mob
was beginning the work of pillage
and plunder, indicating that the dis
patch was filed last night, but was
DELAYED BY the authorities.


The correspondent added that
blueiackets with machine guns had
been landed from the battleship
kniaz Poternkine, in the hands Of
the mutineers, and they fought with
the strikers behind barricades
against the troops. Hundreds were
killed, and the streets were crowded
with wounded. There were rumors,
the correspondent also said, that
some of the soldiers had joined the
mutinous sailors in fighting against
the troops, but he was unable to
confirm this report.


The correspondent said nothing
about the arrival at Odessa of the
warships commanded by Vice Ad-
miral Kruger, but dispatch from
Sebastopol says the battleshlp
Georgi Pobiedonosetz and the
cruiser Griden have started for
Odessa, and are due to arrive there
tonight, when battle is expected.

rived here today from Nickolieff

joined the crew of the battleship

turned over the captain and other

1t is reported that the foreign con-

harbor was gutted by the fire started by

with large quantities of merchandise, as
well as four or five Russian steamers were

Probably three hundred rioters were
killed. Several Cossacks were also slain.
The troops are rapidly restoring order.


The losses are estimated at many millions
of roubles. The remnants of the wharves
and warehouses set on fire last night are
still burning today. and the city is en-
veloped in thick cloud of smoke.


Several explosions occurred in the port
during the night and a fierce conflict took
place between troops and rioters The dead
are now reckoned IN the hundreds. The
hospitals are overhowing with wounded
persons and the medical aid available is

and business and traffic is suspended The
streets are occupied by troops Many resi-

Two lines of torpedo boats suddenly

blundered.


Charged Between the Lines


When the Japanese torpedo boats
came within firing distance the Rus
SLAMS opened fire. Then it was the
Japanese executed maneuver that
threw the Russians into confusion. The
two encircling lines met south of the
Russians, but instead of continuing
in that direction they turned at a sig
nal from Togo and at full speed
charged between the three lines of Rus
sian ships, one division passing be-
tween the cruisers and the line of hos
pital ships and transports, and another
division passing between the trans
ports and the battleships on the other
side.


The Russian ships were unprepared
for an attack of this character, and for
q time were helpless against the dis
charge of the Japanese torpedoes.
Hardly a cruiser or battleship remained
unscathed. The Russians were com
pletely demoralized, and during the
last dash of the torpedo boats not
shot was fired to stop them. In the
meantime Togo with his battleships and
cruisers encircled the Russian fleet and
with his big guns completed the work
of destruction.

You're mistaken, my friend" re-

Speculation is rife as to the outcome
of the yacht races for the Upton cup
which will be held at San Diego dur
ing the last three days Of this month.
The time for listing entries expired
at midnight Monday, and seven fast
craft are entered for the contest.


There are five challengers, and the
crew Of each fully expects to win the
trophy The chances seem to favor the
Detroit however, for though she is a
long craft, 42 feet beam, she success.
fully defended the cup last year when
she belonged to the San Diego Yacht
club, and there does not appear to be
anything faster in this race than she
was pitted against last season. Other
challengers are Venus, Mischief, Ma
RTE and Typhoon, all belonging to local
yachtsmen and all fast boats.


Butcher Boy VIII Defend


The Butcher Boy will defend the cup
and the Nackey, owned by E. w.
Scripps, will be the only other entry
from San Diego.





The local yachts will start from San
Pedro August 26 and race to San Diego,
where they will get in trim for the big
event.


Most Of the boats which will take
part in the cup race have been entered
in other events previously and all are
known to be speedy craft. Reports
for entry show that none of the con-
testants has been changed in con-
struction since it was last raced, and
those who can figure the dope" be-
lieve that they know just about how
the yachts will finish.


There have been some changes in
crews, however, and this fact may have
decided bearing on the results. With
the crew which will man the Butcher
Boy trimming sails, the local tars re-
luctantly admit that the race will not
be walkaway for any one Of the de-
tenders.

BALTIMORE, April 3-This city was
almost encircled by forest fires yester-
day. Acres OF timber were consumed
by flames at Catonsville, Abutus. Mount
Winans, Landsdowne. along the Belair
road and at Canton, and for hours smoke
from different fires was visible In this
city. Fine groves on several valuable
estates were burned over.


There was a strong northwest wind
blowing, and nearly all the fires started
at the same time. about II o'clock in the
morning. The flames ate their way
through the dry timber with rapidity,
and soon the surrounding country was
covered with rolling clouds OF smoke.
Late last night, flames enveloped the
fine timber of the Winans estate near
Catonsville but the FIRE department of
that place has prevented the flames
reaching the houses.


At Landsdowne an acre of woods
along the Baltimore and Ohio railroad
tracks were burned, and the flames were
only kept from endangering trains by
forces of track hands. A dispatch late
last night from Blue Mountain, near
Hagerstown, Md, says the big Blue
Mountain Hotel and other hotels and
cottages are in great danger Fires are
sweeping miles OF tfmberland on the
South Mountain.

fered cuts about the face and heads. Inc

rounded by police, were escorted through

ing mob. Sticks and stones were thrown,

near by. Details Of police were left at
each barn.
