CHICAGO, November IA dispatch to
the Tribune from Ell Paso, Tex, says:


At the bull fight at Ciudad Juarez yester-
day, given for the American mining conVen-
ton, there was a panic when Felix Robert,
the French matador, who claims to be the
only matador of that nationality, was
tossed in the air and carried from the arena,
bruised and bleeding.


Later the same bull a ferocious beast
from the ranch of Gen. Luis Terras, gov
ernor of Chihuaqua, made run and plunged
its long, sharp horns through Matador
Francisco Alonzio Piquiro, tossing him into
the air first and then dragging him about
the ring, blood streaming from the wounds
in the mans body.


The spectators sickened at the sight, and
women tainted and SCREAMED to be taken
out. The arena was packed with Americans
from every section of the United States few
of whom had ever seen bull fight, and for
a time the situation was serious. Many men
rushed from the sickening sight in horror,
while the women in many instances were
carried out unconscious.


Order was finally restored but most of
the Americans left, deciding that they had
already seen enough of the Mexican and
Spanish national sport, although this was
only the second bull up for slaughter out
of the four marked for the ma tador's
sword.

Manila, May 16.-Fierce fighting has
been going on the last two weeks on
the island of Jolo between the outlaw
Moro chief, Pala, with 600 well-armed
followers, and troops under the per-
sonal command of Maj. Gen. Leonard
Wood. Pala's losses thus far are 300
killed, while those of General Wood
are seven killed and nineteen wounded.
Pala and his remaining followers, in
accordance with Moro tradition, prefer
death to capture.


General Wood, with detachments
from the Fourteenth cavalry, the Sew
enteenth, Twenty-second, Twepty-
third infantry, and constabulary scouts.
Lad driven Pala and his followers into
swamp which has been surrounded.


Pala was a noted slave trader and
warrior when the Americans occupied
the islands. Later he escaped with his
followers to the island of Pula Sekar,
near Borneo. One of Paya's leaders de-
serted and took refuge in the British
settlement at Lahad. Pala, discover
ing his whereabouts, landed with fol-
lowing and demanded of the British
magistrate that he turn the deserter
over to him. The demand was not COM
piled with and Pala ordered massa-
ere. Twenty-Five persons, including
several British, were killed. Pala es-
capped to the island of Joio and organ
lied the present uprising. 1t is re-
ported that the Borneo authorities re-
quested General Wood to- apprehend
Pala, dead or alive, and turn him over
to them.

NEW YORK, Feb. 12.-After a peril
Gus swift and enforced ride of more
than three-quarters of mile down the
East river in huge ice foe tonight,
seven persons, including women and
children, were rescued by a municipal
vessel. The foe, which stretched from
North Brother island to the Bronx
shore drifted down the river with the
tide, and in its passage tore from their
moorings the James D. Perkins and
the Eureka, two coal barges, which
had been fastened to the pier at 1S9th
street. On the Perkins We're Captain
Henry Flood, his wife and little daugh-
ter. Captain John Kratzner of the
Eureka had on board his wife and
two sons.


During their dangerous experience a
heavy rain fell, the river was torrent
and the barges were surrounded by the
foe, which headed for He'll Gate. AS
the barges were loaded with coal to
within a few feet of their decks. the
ice became piled on them to such an
extent that several times one of them
nearly capsized.


When the haWsers parted the women
and children were panic-stricken. The
men buckled life preservers on the
women and children and waved red
lanterns while they shouted for help.


Ice was forcing on top of the
barges so fast that the men were kept
busy pushing back the large cakes
to prevent the two crafts from over
turning. The captain of the steamer
Franklin of the department of chari-
ties and corrections became aware of
the barges' predicament, and ordering
full steam ahead, forced his vessel
through the ice to the aid of the endan-
gered occupants. After great effort
the Edison tied up alongside the barges
and the women and children We're
taken aboard,

SAN FRANCISCO, Feb. 12.-George
Heaton of San Jose, was driven into
San Francisco bay today with his air
ship California Messenger"


The aeronaut had narrow escape
from drowning. 1t seems that when
the airship was taken out for trial
this morning across the bay in Oak
land it was cold but very clear and
there was slight north wind.


This wind rapidly increased, how
ever and when the airship was fairly
well up it appeared to strike a current
of air of great velocity, for despite the
rudder and propeller it was driven
rapidly toward the bay. The aeronaut
tried to steer it south of Oakland, but
the airship was driven steadily across
the mud flats and then over the bay.


The wind had created sea and the
ship began to sink, so that the aero
naut was in dangerous position.


Apparently some gas had escaped
from the compartments at one end of
the machine and as it sank one end
fell into the water while the other.
fully distended, stood nearly perpen-
dicular above the waves


The aeronaut's predicament was seen
to his rescue. He was taken off and
the airship was slowly towed back to
Oakland.

The City of Mexico has been doing bust,
ness for about $50 years. There is prob
ably no capital in the civilized world that
during the same period has been the CEN
ter of more wars of conquest or revolution.
and yet, through all the troublesome days
of these centuries, this city has maintained
its financial reputation free from blemish.
Kings have come and gone, viceroy has
succeeded viceroy, emperors have -four
ished for brief regime, and rival factions
have striven for the presidency, loans have
been forced by general government
to be repudiated by the next, bonds were
issued during the French occupancy that
the republic would not assume. but during
all the strife the ancient capital of the
Aztecs cherished its financial integrity as
its choicest jewel. and today rejoices In
the record that not once in all its long
history has debt been repudiated.

BY Associated Prsss.


WASHINGTON, Feb. 6.--The wea-
ther bureau announced today that the
outlook is for continued cold weather
over large part of the United
States. Zero weather extends as far
south as Oklahoma, and the Dakotas
report 20 to 30 degrees below zero this
morning. The coolest point shown by
the official reports is Valentine, Neb.,
where it registered 80 below.


The snow and sleet storm which CEN
tered yesterday morning in the lower
Mississippi valley states has travelled
rapidly northeastward and is now off
the New England coast and the mari
time provinces, passing out to sea. An
unusually heavy precipitation of rain
has occurred throughout New Mexico,
Arizona and Southern California for
some days. While the cold snap con-
tinues undiminished in the northwest
and the Missouri valley, there are signs
of moderation in Assiniboia.

sissippi has risen six inches today and
two feet in the last three days, and is
still rising slightly.


In North La Crosse large section
is under water, people going about in
boats where the land is usually dry.
Manufacturing industries are greatly
inconvenience and can only be oper-
ated with difficulty.


Should the water rise another foot
several factories, both on the north
and south sides, will be closed.
The country districts are hard hit
large sections, both on the Minnesota
and Wisconsin sides of the river, being
cut off from market.


The bridge between Onalaska an6
French island is under water, prevent
ing communication between the two
places.

The weather bureaus monthly summary
of crop conditions is as follows:


Nearly the entire country has experienced
exceptionally favorable conditions for farm
ing operations during the month of March
The temperatures were mild throughout the
month, with the exception of the lake re-
gion. middle Atlantic states and New Eng
land. where it was cold during the first
half, but mild and favorable during the
second half Portions of gulf states suf-
fered from too much rain, and farm work
mas been considerably delayed in the CEN
tral ana western portions. Throughout the
central valleys, and generally on the Pacific
coast, farm work is unusually we'll adj
vanced. and, while slow progress was made
In the middle Atlantic states and New
England during the fore part of the month
operations were active during the latter
part.


Winter wheat is very promising, practf-
cally all reports indicating that this crop
has come through the winter in 1,n1suaIlv
fine condition in the principal winter-wheat
states. The outlook on the Pacific coast is
also promising, except in portions of south
eastern Washington, where considerable
was winter-kilIed.


Good progress was made with seeding of
spring wheat and oats. the seeding of oats
being nearly completed in Illinois and Mis-
sour, and in the more southerly states the
early sown is coming up to good stands
Il
vanced over the southern portion of the
spring wheat region and was in progress at
the close of the month in the extreme north
portion.


throughout the central valleys the soil
was in fine condition for blowing during
most of the month, and this work is well
advanced. Some corn has been planted as
far north as Kansas, Missouri, Tennessee
and North Carolina. while farther south a
considerable part of the crop has been
planted. and some is up.


Reports indicate that peach buds have
been extensively killed in the central VAL
leys and central gulf states. but in the
Atlantic coast districts peaches have been
but little injured so far The reports re-
specting other fruits are generally encour-
aging.


Some cotton has been planted in Texas
and IN South Carolina, Georgia and Florida
but practically none elsewhere and but
little land has been prepared for this crop
in the central districts

the mysterious disappearance of Midshp-

HENNIKER, N. H., Oct. 15.-This
town has no sons that she is more
proud of than the famous Bacon trip
let's, who have lived in their native
town since their birth, thirty-three
years ago, and who bear such a strik-
ing resemblance to one another that
even some of the oldest inhabitants
are often mistaken in their identity,
and many times the triplets have been
placed in rather peculiar situations.
Their names, too, are nearly alike, be-
ing Ellon r., Elgin S. and Elwin T.
Bacon.


When these remarkable babies were
born, thirty-three years ago, scores Of
friends called to see them, and the
news spread so rapidly that people
from other towns drove miles to view
the Bacon triplets, and such great
numbers came that finally the family
decided to close the house to visitors.
At that time they were bright, hand
some boys and so nearly alike in all
respects that to distinguish them apart
was quite task.


Red, white and blue ribbon was used
and to each one was tied bow of a
different hue. The striking resem-
blance strange to say, has always re-
manned the same. They have the same
shade of hair. complexion the same,
same blue eyes and, best of all, the
same sunny disposition that has
always clung to them since boyhood
and which has made them what they
are, the most popular young men of
Hennlker. At school there was no end
of the trouble that they caused the
other pupils and the teacher in dis
tinguishing them. When one would
become involved in a controversy with
a fellow playmate, he could always
rest assured that his two brothers
would be there to help him out, If they
were needed.


The lives of these three men have
been characterized with much same
ness. Each one graduated from the
high school at Henniker and after leav-
ing school they all engaged in the
dairy business. at which they have
been very successful. During the past
ten years they have been prominent
in town affairs and have taken keen
interest in all that has transpired in
their native town and elsewhere.


When they were eight years old their
father died. and although the family
burdens fell upon their mother, they
We're soon at work and during their
vacations were earning money for
their home which they loved so well.

Surrounded by a mob Of nearly q

Arlington for nearly twenty minutes

Again and again the officer blew his

1t was all that three officers could do

Several times before assistance ar

NEW YORK, Oct. 14.-Five lives are
known to have been lost and more than
thirty persons injured, one fatally and
some of them seriously, on the Cunard
line steamer Campania last Wednes-
day, when a gigantic wave rolled over
the steamer and swept across a deck
thick with steerage passengers. So sud-
den was the coming OF the disaster and
so great the confusion which attended
and followed 1t that even the officers
of the steamer themselves were unable
today upon the vessels arrival here to
estimate the full extent of the trag-
edy. 1t is possible that the five persons
known to be missing from the steerage
may not constitute the full number Of
dead. When the Campania reached
quarantine today ten of the injured
passengers were still in the ship hos
pital, some of them seriously hurt and
a score of others were nursing minor
injuries.


John Graham of Milwaukee was one
of the passengers washed overheard
and lost. He was travelling in the steer
age. The others who are known to
have lost their lives were Margaret
Cleary, Mary Cosgrove. Niels Ekberg
and Elizabeth Grunadotter.


The Campania was plowing along un-
der full headway last Wednesday att
ernoon. A heavy quartering sea was
running, but the weather conditions
were far from unpleasant and the big
boats decks were crowded with pas
sengers. The steerage deck was COW
cred with merry-makers and there was
nothing to indicate the approaching dis
aster, when suddenly the big steamer
lurched to port and scooped up an enor-
nous sea. The wave boarded the
steamer about midshJp on the port
side and swept clear across the steer
age deck. completely filling the space
between that deck and the deck above
and carrying everything with 1t. The
steamers side was buried and pas
sengers on the deck above the steerage
were submerged to their waists as the
immense volume of water rolled aft
and then surged forward. All the cabin
passengers on the upper deck succeed
ed in clinging to supports while the
waters surged around them and We're
saved, but the unfortunates in the
steerage deck found themselves ut
terly helpless.

ment over the wedding cake and a

LONDON, June 5.-Whitelaw Reid, the
new American Embassador, had an audi
ence with King Edward at Buckingham
Palace at noon to-day and presented his
credentials.


Three royal carriages were sent to Dor
chester house to convey the Em0assador
and the members of the embassy TO the
palace. Foreign Secretary Lansdowne
drove up to the palace at about the same
duced to the King. The latter wore
field marshars uniform, and was sur
rounded by his suite. His Majestys re-
ception of the American ambassador was
most cordial


While the ambassador was presenting
the King with his credentials, Queen
Alexandra was receiving Mrs. Reid and
Miss Reid. Her Majesty showed them
the interesting objects in the palace.


The conversation between the King and
the ambassador lasted for some time. His
Majesty recalled Reid's previous visits to
London, and expressed the greatest
pleasure at the good relations between
the United States and Great Britain. The
King also spoke few words to each
member of the embassy.


After the official reception, Reid was
ushered upstairs, where his wife and
daughter were with the Queen. and the
ambassador was presented to her Maj
esty. King Edward also came in, and
Mrs. and Miss Reid were presented to
him. The King and the ambassador
thereupon engaged in further converse
ton. The visit altogether lasted forty
minutes, after which the ambassador and
his party returned to Dorchester House
in the state carriage, with coachman
and footman garbed in long scarlet
cloaks.


Reid had already called at Lansdowne
house, the Foreign Secretary having
waived a formal call at the Foreign Of
flee, and requested the ambassador in
stead to call at his private residence.
Reid during the afternoon called on all
the ambassadors and Ministers accred-
ited to the Court of st. James.


Secretary Hay made a formal call at
the American embassy this morning.

Directly in my path stood an ancient
swamp white oak, the greatest tree, think,
that 1 have ever seen. 1t was not the
highest nor the largest round, perhaps,
but individually, spiritually, the greatest.
Hoary, hollow and broken-limbed his huge
bole seemed encircled with the centuries
and in this green and grizzled top all the
winds of heaven had some time come.


One could worship in the presence of such
a tree as easily as in the shadow of vast
cathedral Indeed, what is there built with
hands that has the dignity, the majesty,
the divinity of life? And what life was
here! Life whose beginnings lay so far
back that could no more reckon the years
than could count the atoms 1t had builded
into this majestic form. -


Looking down upon him from twice his
height doomed a tulip poplar, clean. boiled
for thirty feet. and in the top all green and
gold with blossoms. 1t was a Respondent
thing beside the oak, yet. how unmistak-
ably the gnarled old monarch wore the
crown. His girth more than balanced the
poplar's great height, and for blossoms
nature knows the beauty of strength and
inward majesty and has pinned no bouton-
Mere upon the oak.

The interesting letter printed be-
low has been received by The Call from
Frank w. Marston. Trustee of the
State Normal school. Marston has
been travelling in Egypt for some time
and has made the schools and educa-
tional institutions Of the ancient land
his special study:


Editor Call:-During comparative
ly recent period. very great advances
have been made in educational matters
in the Land of the Pharaohs. At pres
ent the Egyptian Government schools
are divided into Elementary, Primary,
Secondary and Professional schools.


1.-The Kuttabs are the Mohammedan
elementary schools. Here the Koran is
taught and the pupils receive lessons
in reading and writing Arabic to enable
them to memorize the Koran. If the
teaching proves to be satisfactory,
these Kuttabs may receive Govern
ment grants based upon the average
attendance, but before this Is received
the pupils must be taught arithmetic.
Children may attend these schools up
to the age Of eight years.


Private schools may come under
Government inspection by showing
that they meet Government require
ments as to standards. but the only
ones that receive grants are the ele-
mentary schools or Kuttabs.


1.-The greater number of these Kut-
tabs present a very primitive appear
ance.


'The rooms are dark with stone walls
and mud floors. Some have benches
without backs. but in many there are
no seats: both children and teacher
sit on the floor. The walls are rough
and bare. without decoration. The
children repeat their lessons in classes
or singly, swaying their bodies as they
recite. They present a bright, keen ap-
pearance and are furnished with tin
or wood states and Arabic primers,
while the teacher has rod to enforce
attention.

UKIAH, May THE prospects for a
full crop of pears and prunes in
this section during the coming season
are not as good as they were last year
The warm weather of February
brought out the blossoms, and the
heavy rains that followed washed out
the pollen, and as a result the fruit
did not set. There will be only about
one-half crop gathered. All other
fruits favorable to this section will
give an immense yield. No killing frosts
have been experienced and the trees
are heavily laden with fruit The vine
yards are all well advanced and give
promise of an abundant crop


Fhe hop industry, which is the most
important in this section, has been in
creased in acreage by many growers
The good prices that the growers have
received for the last three years for
their crops have stimulated them to
renewed efforts. The hop growers DUR
ing this spring have shipped more than
$40 900 worth of hop roots to other
parts of the State. This is a new In
dustry in connection with the hop
business. The roots from this valley
are free from disease and pests and are
much sought after.


The prospects for big yield in the
grain fields are most favorable. The
hay and grain crops are making a most
unusual growth. The same can be said
of the alfalfa fields. Truck garden
owners and small fruit growers are
very enthusiastic over the outlook for
the coming season

should be above the average. The late

NEW YORK, May 1S-This city paid it's

last of the veterans of the war of 1912.

especially after yesterdays noteworthy
pageant, wien the body of the fighter who
lived 105 years was brought here from his
farm at Boonville and escorted through the
town to lie in state at the time-honored
city hall, draped in black as that building
death. There were crowds again around

fore the final ceremonies this morning.

portico. Although crowds had filed past

night, there were hundreds more just as
eager today. They wanted to eye
witnesses this strange spare figure out of
the past.


Not since President Grant was similarly
honored and buried here, it was said, has
the body of patriot lain in state at the
city hall or gone to its grave escorted and
followed by more notable military pro-
cession.

known Philander Cronk, eighty-two years

Mrs. Sarah Rowley, seXenty-one years old,

wick avenue, and Jamaica avenue Brook

check their ravages, but to no avail.

from Chicago, became frightened and
started to jump out. She fell and

BY Associated Press.


PRESCOTT, Ariz., April 2.-As a re-
suit of an explosion in the United
Verde mine at Jerome, owned by Sena-
tor Clark, five men are dead and seven
others seriously, one or two probably
fatally, injured.


The accident happened just as the
shifts were being changed and all of
the men except twelve had been raised
to the surface. They were waiting at
the station of the three hundred foot
level to be hoisted from the mine when
a terrific explosion occurred, killing
five and injuring seven others.


On account of the recent heavy rains
the surface water found it's way to a
portion of the mine where a fire has
been burning for several years, and
steam formed, causing the explosion
and blowing out the bulkheads erected
to keep the fire froh spreading. The
men were suffocated by the smoke and
heated steam.


Had the accident happened fifteen
minutes earlier or later one hundred
men would have been caught, most of
the old shift having just left the mine
and fifteen minutes later the new shift
would have been at work.


The explosion caused the mine to
cave from the surface, and the rail-
road which crosses the property turned
over and the rails were twisted into
every conceivable shape.


The company has had trouble with
fire for years and has had constructed
a cement bulkhead. which was thought
would keep 1t under control for years,
and this has been destroyed.

The hostesses never had such state
ly, beautiful setting for their ball as
last evening. When it was announced
that they would give their annual ball,
which is quite the most exclusive and
elegant social function of the year, in
the Auditorium, many people We're du--
bious as to the possibilities of that
great hall for brilliant ball; but the
most skeptical of the doubters joined
in the chorus of admiration as the
guests entered and glimpsed the beau
tiful picture that lay before them.


The long corridors on either side had
been transformed into pergolas, with
a lattice of white thru which the leafy
tendrils of southern smilax wandered
riotously.> Here and there light,
shaded with pink petals, hung on a
green stem like some glowing blossom.
White pillars held great urns filled with
dropping swordferns, and thee lattice
was broken at intervals with cozy gar
den seats, pillowed in green and form
ing most enticing resting places be.
tween the dances. The leafy arbol
ended in circular lattice and seat
almost hidden by the tangle Of vines
Rich oriental rugs carpeted the corri


dors and foyer, where the simple deco
ration of palms and southern smilas
| scarcely prepared the guests for the
| wondrous beauty of the great hall.

The west end of the auditorium was
set aside as reception room, and tall
fir trees, redolent with the spicy breath
of the woods, separated it from the
ballroom. This hedge was. broken in
the center and on either side to give
entrance to the dancing floor, and tall
pedestals held high the urns filled with
ferns, whose fronds dropped low to
meet the branches Of the fir trees. The
pillars that support the gallery were
wreathed with smilax and pink tulle,
caught in Haunting bows. Palms in
quaint jardinieres were placed here and
there with chairs and garden seats,
over which the oriental rugs cast a
simmer of rich color. Smilax trailed
its glossy leaves over the balcony and
gallery rails and the circle Of pink
shaded lights cleaned thru the leafy
veil like stars. Around the balcony
were the prim-trimmed bay trees, and
above in the gallery palms were used
at intervals. Tall fir trees hedged the
orchestra pit where the musicians were
stationed, and encircled the east end
of the dancing floor. Everywhere there
were the fir trees, smilax and palms
giving an air of dignity and grace that
was indescribable. The punch table
was in one corner of the ballroom, the
bowl almost hidden by the mass OF
richly-hued fruit and lighted by q
| quaint ANTIQUE lamp.

text:
Nobody knows who was the first shoe
maker. There must have been time when
everybody went barefooted. and the first
shoes were probably made of woven reeds
or skins. The original shoemaker doubtless
sought comfort more than style.


The Celt, who at times wandered over
moor or morass at others over mountains
invented shoe that suited his purpose ex-
actly. A sole of heavy hides protected his
feet from the sharp stones while uppers or
legs of lighter skins protected his ankles
and legs from thorns and bushes. The
buskin was so constructed that the water
exuded from 1t as soon as the foot ceased
to be immersed. In the modern shoe the
idea is that water be kept ont, not let out.
The Celtic buskin was tough and elastic,
and could be replaced wherever there were
untanned skins at hand. Every Celt was
his own shoemaker.


With the Norman conquest came the in
PRODUCTION into the British Isles of tanned
leather which had long been in use In
Normandy. where it had been introduced by
the Romans.


Shoes then began to take on style and
the styles have never been duplicated In
later days. From close-fitting shoes fash
ion went to long, pointed toes, which, In
time. grew so long that they had to be
fastened to the wearer's knees.


Shoes were gorgeous affairs in the middle
ages. King Richard. the lion-hearted. had
his boots stamped with gold John Lack
land, his brother. wore boots spotted with
golden circles, while Henry III wore boots
checkered with golden lines. every square
of which was enriched with lion. Cardinal
Wolseys shoes were


OF gold ard stone precious


Costing many thousand pounds.


Sir Walter Raleigh wore shoes studded
with diamonds said to have cost fS0.0O0.
The gallants in Charles IFS time wore their
high boot tops turned down to the ankles
to show the gorgeous lace with which they
were lined

BY Associated Press.


NEW YORK, Nov. 13.-The famous
saying, Blood is thicker than water,'
never found a more impressive express
sion than 1t did tonight at the dinner
on the Bowery ct Coney Island, which
the enlisted men of the first squadron
of the United States Atlantic fleet gave
to the enlisted men of the second
cruiser squadron of his majestys navy
commanded by Rear Admiral Prince
Louis of Battenberg. 1t was the key
note of the cheering with which the
$500 British and American sailors made
the great pavilion ring to the echo. 1t
was the toast to which they drank
across the long tables which stretched
down the great hall beneath the over
hanging British and American flags.
1t was the theme of the speeches that
accompanied the cigars and the beer
of this mammoth feast, unique in the
history of all navies and which will
long furnish the theme of yarns on
many British and American berth
deck.


Coney Island in the vicinity Of the
Bowery pavilion looked as if midsum-
about the enclosure long before the
sailors and the all-the-year-round res
idents packed the approaches to the
hall. Irside the picture was one which
surprised even the men themselves
who had worked all night in it's con-
struction. Overhead a frieze of British
and American flags stretched around
the hall. From each of the twelve
chandeliers swinging from the ceiling
down the center of the hall waved four
American and four British flags. The
balcony railing was intertwned with
the colors of the two nations. Fes-
toons of bunting We're draped across
from one balcony to the other, caught
up In the center by great globes of
electric lights.


Arrangement of Tables


Across the lower end of the main
hall was long table with four smaller
tables adjoining at right angles These
were for the two commanders in chief,
their staffs, the flag officers and their
staffs and the commanding and execu-
tive officers from each of the twenty
one British and American warships in
the North river and other officers espe-
cially invited by the men. At the CEN
ter of the long table looking down the
hall sat Rear Admiral Evans and Rear
Admiral Prince Louis. To the right
of Admiral Evans. beside the prince.
were Rear Admiral Dickens, Rear Ad-
miral BrownSon, Capt Pierce, Col. r.
NJ Thompson. Capt. Dare and Capt.
Arnold. To the left of Admiral Evans
sat Sir Percy Sanderson, the British
consul general at New York; Rear Ad-
miral Davis Capt Farquhar, Commits
sloner of Police McAdoo, Capt. Emery.
Capt King Hail. Capt. Tilley and
Capt. -Ryan. The other officers were
at the adjoining tables, which were
prettlly decorated with pink and white
carnations. Champagne was the only
extra" not served Mt the six rows
of tables, which stretched from the
officers tables to the door on the main
floor and for nearly the entire length
of the balcony. The British and Amer
lean sailors were assembled on board
the hagships Maine and Alabama

Following one of the most thorough
examinations on a charge of insanity
ever held in superior court room, May
Godfrey, waitress, was yesterday de-
clared mentally deranged by commits
sion in department 4 of the superior
court, but was discharged upon her
mothers promise that she would take
the girl back to their former home in
Kansas and there provide for her.


The trial was the result of number
of allegations made by the young
woman against Dwight and George
Hart, proprietors in part of the Natick
and Rosslyn hotels. The girl made the
accusation that Dwight Hart had per-
secuted her with proposals of marriage.


The girl, who is 16 years of age, came
to Los Angeles less than year ago
with her mother. The mother obtained
position as waitress at the Redondo
hotel, while May went to work for
Dwight Hart as waitress in the Natick
restaurant. Some time ago the girl was
discharged, and then she declared that
she began to receive letters and tele-
phone messages that worried her.


Too Much Telephoning


Several times day telephone mes
sages would come to the place where
the girl was working and the messages,
which were all proposals of marriage,
were alleged to be from Dwight Hart.


Finally the mother took the matter
before Capt. Auble, and Hart was called
in. Hart told Capt. Auble that the
young woman was not in her right
mind and that she had been writing to
him for some time. Finally he had an
officer swear to the insanity charge.


Friends of Hart and of the young
woman crowded the court room yester-
day to hear the evidence in the case,
and Miss Godfrey stoutly maintained
her claim to sanity. She answered
Hart's qestions and again testified that
she had not written the letters to her
self.


You are crazy" said Hart. you are

young woman. Several young women

ally asking to talk to Hart. On one
occasion she is alleged to have threat
ened suicide because Hart was perse-

After the taking Of all the evidence
Judge Bordwell told the mother that
the daughter was mentally unbalanced,

Tibet has for centuries been a dependency
of China, like Mongolia, Manchuria and
Turkestan, and sent annual tribute to the
emperor at Picking until 1895 The Chinese
government, however. has not interfered
with it's local affairs. which have been
controlled from time immemoriaI by an &C.
ciesiastfcal government. The chief author
ity has been the dalai lama, or high priest
of the Buddhists, who has been assisted
by bishops, monks and priests. scattered
through the territory among the six or
seven million inhabitants, who are still
Buddhists.


The Chinese have had so many other
matters of greater Importance to occupy
their attention that they have never called
the grand lama to account for his neglect
to send the annual tribute, but they were
very much alarmed when, in 1900. they
learned that the Russian government was
taking the same steps to occupy Tibet that
had been successful in Manchuria Hence
when the British proposed to send an ex-
petition under Colonel Younghusband to

Buenos Ayres. Feb 6.-Government troops at
tackled the insurgents. who had fortified them
selves at Mendoza, at dawn to-day. Soon after
ward the insurgent leaders and officers fed to
the mountains. whereupon the men surrendered
unconditionally. The insurgents had sacked the
local branch of the National Bank of Buenos
Ayres and seized 100000 Many arrests have
been made, and the city is quiet


Late information shows that the insurrection
is now restricted to Cordoba. Generals Winter.
Benavides. Garcia and Roca, with largely supe-
rior forces are surrounding the city. 1t is said
that Colonel Delacruz, commanding the artillery
there, has been killed, and that the leaders OF
the insurrection have offered TO submit on con-


dition that their lives be spared President
Quintana has replied, however. that the surren-


der must be unconditional, and that the courts


VIII decide the fate Of the insurgents.


The insurgents holding Senator Yofre.


The police of Buenos Ayres have seized guam
tity of guns and revolvers and many copies Of


manifestoes and revolutionary documents. Night
! trains on the railroad between Buenos Ayres
and Rosario VIII be resumed tomorrow.
All the bankers here condemn the attempted
! revolution. and express the hope that the ener-
getic policy of President Quintana will prevent
any such attempt in the future.


The only group Of insurgents in the Province
Of Buenos Ayres, 40 strong. has been de-
feated near Pirovano Station. Two officers and
seven men were killed and 121 surrendered. The


rest. with Comnandant Villamayor, are retreat
ing. and government troops are IN pursuit.
It is reported that the troops in the Province
Of Santa Fe were misled by officers, who IN
formed them that they were marching against
rebels. When the troops learned the facts they
refused to go into action. The officers escaped
The transport Santa, Cruz has sailed for the


outer barbor with political prisoners Order
has been restored at Rosario


The insurrection is admitted to have been
failure and the government has the situation
well in hand. The prompt suppression of the
outbreak makes IT evident that the usual ele-


ments of a revolution are absent. Popular sym
pathy is with the government. which exhibited
unexpected strength. The rising was purely


military, and was limited in its proportions.

The United States naval yachts Hornet and
Siren, which arrived here Wednesday from
Norfolk with a party of landsmen aboard
for visit to the navy yard, have sailed for
Chesapeake bay. The yachts are used as
training ships for green men, ''landsmen,"
as they are termed, who are shipped by
the recruiting offices in the Carolinas. The
new men are sent to the Norfolk navy
yard to the receiving ship Franklin and
are detailed to the Hornet and Siren,
aboard which they are taken out for
cruises on the bay and short distances off
shore outside the capes. and broken in as
to their duties men-o'-war s-men. When
the men are sufficiently advanced in their
duties they distributed among the ships
in active service and become genuine jack
tars The little vessels visit this city two
or three times each year, and sometimes
remain two or three days at anchor in the
harbor while the men aboard them have
liberty in order to visit the points of in
terest here.


The yachts entered the naval service dur
ing the war with Spain. and saw service
off the coast of Cuba with the blockading
squadron The Hornet was formerly the
yacht Alicia and the Siren was the British
yacht Eugenia and was built in Scotland

Oregon, which took fire up the coast
off Crescent City night before last lies
beached on Mud Flats just below the
plant of the Bendixsen shipbuilding
company with smoke pouring from the
after skylight. The crew of the ves-
sci are working hard to quench the
flames between decks. Lines are being
sent ashore so that the vessel can be
taken still farther up on the beach, and
at high water this afternoon the
steamer will be high and dry on the
sand. The vessel is gradually being
filled with water in the hope that the
fire, which has smouldered along for
over sixty hours, can be subdued in
this manner.

other craft. Her progress was not
retarded by the fire, her pumps being
constantly at work and holding the

and the smoke rising from the sky

which released the ship from the stocks.

drew Noble proposed the toast 1.-THE Japanese
Empire" He said all the European nations, in
Guiding Great Britain, might learn lesson from
the Japanese. Their course prior to the out
break of the war and their splendid strategy
and bravery when compelled to strike, together
with the consistently dignifed attitude Of the
government made them an example for all
nations.

warships were built in England. He was sorry
the Kashima could not take part in the war
but hostilities must end some time, and there
after the powerful vessel would be used to main
tain peace in the Far East.

Older even than China, the oldest
existing nation, are the cliff dwellings,
of southwestern United States, homes
of a race whose very name has per-
ished from the earth. Explorers, puz-
zling through the Mancos and Casa
Verde canyons of Arizona and New
Mexico, found the houses of this
strange people in the widest and most
inaccessible of the mountain sides.
Did the cliff dwellers antedate the
pyramids of Egypt? Were they of
blood relation to early Inhabitants of
the land where the Nile is god? Some
students are prepared to answer both
questions affirmatively and to give
what is to them abundant proof. The
pottery from their long wrecked homes
suggests Egypt, and the few inscrip-
tions found have similar suggestions.
Mummies, bodies wrapped In cloth,
feathers from the breast of turkey
have been dug from burial places
among the cliffs, and in bone and hair
much unlike the Indian of today there

GIRARD, Kas, Dec. 6.-Mrs. Ina
Barry. VINO since Friday last has held
the town officials at bay from her fort
in the toilet room of a Frisco railway
coach on the track here. was removed
today shortly before noon after she
had been partially overcome by the
fumes of ammonia. A bundle of rags
saturated with the drug had been
pushed through the window of the toi-
let room. Before surrendering Mrs.
Barry fired one shot at her captorS,
but without effect.


Before she could shoot again Mrs.
Barry was overpowered by two officers.
After being reassured that the officers
and the people of Girard were her
friends and that the officers had come
to protect her the woman made but
feeble efforts at resistance.


She was removed in carriage to
the Jail and placed under the care of
the city physician. Once inside the
iail and made confident that the at
tendants were working in her behalf,
Mrs. Barry quieted down and talked
nationally.


Emaciated by the long fast and weak
ened from loss of sleep and from eX-
posure, the woman presented pitiable
appearance. Her clothes were torn,
her face and hands badly soiled and
her hair disheVeled.


Mrs Barry will be delivered into
the custody of the probate court, be-
fore whom the town marshal had last
night been ordered to produce her at
8 O'Clock this afternoon.


After Mrs. Barry had been in jail
some time the effects of the ammonia
fumes became more apparent. Her
throat and eyes were swollen and she
was seized with a fit of trembling that
practically amounted to paroxysins.


She improved rapidly. however, un-
der the treatment of DR.. L. p. Adam
son, who said the woman would suffer
no serious injury from the ammonia.

ment the driver assisted in getting the

It's rather a nice standard of beauty that
the Japanese have for their dear little,
queer little. most fascinating little women.


On the whole, the Japanese consider that
a woman should not exceed five feet in
height; should have a comparatively fair
skin and be well developed; should have
long, thin and jet-black hair; an oval face.
with a narrow. straight nose; rather large
eyes, nearly black; thick eyelashes; a small
mouth; hiding behind red full lips even
rows of small white teeth ears not alto
gether SMALL thick eyebrows and a me-
dunn forehead from which the hair should
grow in circular or Fujiyama shape-that
shape recalling the truncated cone of the
famous volcano.


Add to these the modesty. sweet humility
and gentle submission which the Japs deem
essential in their womaukind, and which
long centuries of practice have instilled
into them pretty thoroughly-and the result
might well be very interesting and ador-
able little creature.

The overdue British ship Verbena
came into port late Saturday night. 1So
days from Liverpool. Captain Lee re-
ports that the long passage was due to
a succession of gales and calms. She
had been listed among the overdues
at per cent.


The Verbena left Liverpool October
19, 1904, and at first ran into light
variable winds and very poor northeast
trades. She lost them in 20 degrees
north. She crossed the equator when
forty-four days out in 81 degrees west
She was then carried by the southeast
trade winds to % degrees south. When
OF the River Platte she ran into strong
head winds. For three weeks the yes
sci was buffeted about by winds and
waves, and when the storm supsideo
1t was found that no headway had been
made during that period.


The weather then moderated some
what, although the seas were running
high. On January IA the Verbena
passed Staten Island. She was then
81 days out.


On January IL, while the vessel was
hove to, owing to heavy gales and
high seas, great sea came on board
and filed the lee side of the deck. 1t
struck the vessel with tremendous force
and almost threw her on her beam
ends. In it's furious onslaught the
waves caught Ordinary Seaman James
Putt and carried him overheard.
Everything was done to save the man
life, but without avail. The seas at
this time were lashed into seethlng
foam.


From that time on the ship ran into
continuation of westerly gales until
she reached so degrees south. 86 degrees
west. She was then 119 days out.
From that point to the equator she
had favorable weather and crossed In
113 degrees west when 152 days out.
Next followed a succession of indif-
ferent northeast trade winds which
were lost in 81 degrees north After
that the vessel encountered Gains and
light, variable winds until she reached
port.

eral merchandise to ]. D. Spreckels &

heavy rain fell all day, and this is believed

legislature went into joint session today
confusion at once resulted when Lieutenant
Governor Haggott, the presiding officer of
the Senate, took his position beside Speak
er Dickson to direct the joint session. Mr..
Dickson refused to give way.


THE clerk of the house will cali" said
Speaker Dickson, with thump of his gavel.


The clerk of the senate will call the roll

Haggott.


Immediately the two clerks commenced to
call the rolls, amid great confusion. But
few names had been called when Repre-
sentative Frewen rose.


Mr.. Frewen has the foor.' shouted
Lieut.. Gov. Haggott, with thump of his
gavel.


Regular and Irregular.
shouted the speaker.


Mr.. Frewen, you have the foor," re-
peated Lieut.. Gov. Haggott.


Bang, bang, went the two gavels Two
men stood side by side behind the speakers 8
desk, both refusing to give way.


The confusion was so great that no voice
could be heard, and although Mr.. Frewen
continued to address the assembly, his
voice was not distinguishable.


A motion to adjourn was made and sec
onded. 1t came to a vote, the ayes and
noes sounding in about equal volume.


The ayes have it and the joint session is
dissolved shouted Lieutenant Governor
Haggott.


THE noes have it and the motion is lost
shouted Speaker Dickson.


Dissolved and Not Dissolved.


Whack! went the lieutenant governor s

The assembly is not dissolved" sailed

Il repeat that the session is ended; and

lieutenant governor. and out filed the SEN
ators, headed by the lieutenant governor
amid great confusion. Many of them did
not leave the room, but stood behind the
seats of the representatives watching the
proceedings. Speaker Dickson refused TO
recognize the passing out of the senate.
and declared that although the senators
had left the room the joint session was still

San Jose, Cal, July 19.-With women
fainting and men sobbing, Daniel Ma
loney, who has made numerous public
ascensions with Professor Montgom-
ery's aeroplane, fell 1900 feet to his
depth at Santa Clara yesterday morn

Professor Montgomery had an
nounced an ascension from the grounds
OF Santa Clara College in honor of the
League OF the Cross Cadets, who are
holding their annual encampment in
that town. The announcement at
tracted probably 1000 people, who
watched with interest the hugh ma
chine as it shot up from the college
garden attached to huge balloon.


AT height of 1000 feet Maloney
cut loose and began maneuvering the
aeroplane. He circled gracefully about
for some minutes, having the machine
apparently under perfect control. Then
he essayed a deep dip.


Suddenly the machine swerved, hes
itated and turned completely over. 1t
righted itself, sank down a consider
able distance and turned over again.
Maloney was clinging desperately to
his seat and evidently endeavoring to
regain his control, but all his efforts
were in vain.


Again the aeroplane turned in the
air and this time the wings came to-
gether and the man and machine
plunged straight downward, while the
Mortified spectators gazed helplessly
upward. Amid shrieks and groans,
many people rushed to the scene, while
others turned away weeping.


A number of cadets first reached the
unconscious man and, picking him up,
they conveyed him to the college hos
pital- his head was fractured and
blood was flowing from his ears and
mouth. He expired within short time.
The aeroplane, which was constructed
of the toughest oak procurable, was
ground into small fragments.

BLOOMINGTON, ILL.,, Oct. 2S-Mayor
Charles Nickel of Chenoa was shot
and killed this afternoon in the Bank
of Chenoa, Hugh Jones, brickmason
was shot and killed and two passersby
were shot and slightly wounded by
William LIE Due, a farmer who lives
near Chenoa.


LIE Due, after the shooting, dragged
the body of Jones into the bank vault,
closed the door and defed arrest.


Nickel, who was lie Dues brother
in-law, was cashier of the bank as well
as mayor of Chenoa. LIE Due came
in from his farm this afternoon, walked
into the bank and without warning
shot Nickel dead. In the bank beside
Nickel and Hugh Jones were Cashier
Nickers son and another small boy.
The boys escaped through the back
door.


After Nickel had been shot, Jones
attempted to grapple with the mur-
derer, but was himself shot by LIE
Due. Two men passing along the
street, whom LIE Due feared might
capture him were shot by him. one
in the head, the other in the hand,
but their wounds are not serious. An
immense crowd, we'll armed, gathered
at the bank in an attempt to capture
the slayer. He drew the door of the
vault almost shut after dragging
Jones body inside, and would allow no
one to come within range. LIE Due
told the officers that Jones was dead.


Ammonia and chloroform were used
plentifully in an attempt to overcome
the murderer, but he succeeded in get
ting enough air to thwart the effect
of the drugs.


Nickel married a sister of LIE Due
LIE Due was married some years ago.
1t is alleged that he had had domestic
troubles with Nickel adjusted, but LIE
Due always imagined Nickel had not
been square in the matter. For some
time neighbors had said lie Due acted
queerly, and 1t is supposed today's
crime resulted from LIE Dues broodtng
over his alleged wrongs.


Several hundred shots were ex-
changed between the posse and LIE
Due. He gave himself up to the
sheriff at 9 o'clock tonight and was
brought to the county Jail at Bloom
ington.
